stories.title: Ariel: Driven by Faith and Fashion
paragraphs: How Ariel Is Transforming LaRussell’s Personal Style and Pushing Him Beyond His Comfort Zone While Staying True to Her Tomboy Roots
Ariel’s “uniform” growing up was the combination of big white t-shirts and jeans, with either a pair of pink and white Shaqs or Nikes and clean, straight-back cornrows.
“I was poor, so we had to get what we get,” Ariel said.

In middle school, Ariel remembers walking around Lake Merritt with her mom, begging for an extra baggy pair of boys’ jeans each time she saw them in a store. As an avid athlete, most of Ariel’s early childhood revolved around basketball. She wore sweats daily and stayed clear of skirts, shorts and tight jeans.
“I was really a boy,” she said.

Ariel didn’t start carving out her style until 9th grade when boys came into the picture. Freshman year also meant the peak of her punk rock phase, full of colorful bangles and belts, which Ariel said was the first and last trend that she ever really tried out.

By sophomore year, Ariel started putting fits together daily. With the help of her first job in high school at McDonalds, she could start buying pieces to craft her style. She became obsessed with vintage items and the joy of a trip to thrift stores. With her finds from Goodwill and The Salvation Army, Ariel would get busy reconstructing pieces to fit her aesthetic, which was far from girly. Ariel remained true to her tomboy affinity for sneakers and comfortable baggy pants, steering clear of skinny jeans, shorts and skirts, for the most part.
“I was wearing ties, with shorts—denim shorts—tights and Timberland boots. Just doin’ stuff,” she said, laughing.

Ariel’s love of experimenting with textures, silhouettes, and unlikely combinations fueled her passion for creating unique looks and growing appetite for fashion. Sometimes, she’d even color her hair to coordinate with her outfits. Eventually, she started getting recognized by her classmates and peers. During her senior year of high school, Ariel won best dressed at Dewey Academy.

While Ariel loved that fashion allowed her to express herself, her priority through middle school, high school and through junior college remained basketball because she wanted to play professionally.

But when Ariel got pregnant with her daughter, Kylie in 2012, Ariel realized she needed to have a plan B. She thought about being a social worker because always loved kids and she considered becoming a dental hygienist, once she started realizing that basketball couldn’t sustain her financially as a new mom without a professional contract. The thought of styling passed her mind but Ariel chopped it up to a dream more than reality. She still loved putting fits together, often helping her friends just for fun.

In 2016 year, Ally Cocaine, a friend and artist, started asking Ariel for help putting together outfits in her early stages of being an artist. Ariel helped Ally out with styling a shoot, still not realizing that her career was forming in front of her eyes. When Ally stepped out in the outfit that Ariel put together, all eyes were on Ally.
“I looked around the room—it was like a movie,” Ariel said.
Creating Movie Moments

Styling Ally Cocaine expanded the boundaries of what Ariel thought was possible, leading her to many opportunities, including becoming LaRussell’s stylist—but not without some bumps along the way. A short stint in Los Angeles in hopes of gaining more experience as a stylist turned sour after Ariel realized that the energy and environment were not for her. While she was there, Ariel quickly hit the goals she’d set out to accomplish as a stylist—working with big names, brands, athletes and rappers—but it became clear to her that Hollywood was too Hollywood. Ariel moved back to the Bay Area, writing off celebrities and rappers forever.
“I told myself I would only work with another artist if I had the opportunity to come up with them,” Ariel said.
Redefining LaRussell’s Style

LaRussell and Ariel connected in late 2023, though they knew about each other’s work for years prior. For Ariel, it was a matter of waiting until she felt prepared. LaRussell wasn’t a “typical” client. He was known and loved for his laid back attire and authentic nature. It’s what made him so relatable to people and what really allowed his talents to speak for themselves. At the same time, Ariel wanted to see LaRussell switch up his everyday attire of Crocs and hoodies.
Ariel saw the opportunity to work with LaRussell as a chance to grow and journey with an artist, rather than be dragged along.

“Wow—I literally manifested this,” Ariel said. “I literally said, ‘I only want to work with somebody who is a good person who I can grow with,’ and that’s literally what I’m doing with the LaRussell right now.”

Ariel’s impact on LaRussell’s image was palatable. Suddenly, LaRussell’s tan Crocs and hoodies became paired with colorful beanies and knit jackets, echoing much of the symbolism that LaRussell spoke about like the work ethic of his favorite athletes and his hometown of Vallejo. Eventually, custom letterman jackets, fuzzy bucket hats and even sunglasses—something LaRussell initially said no to—became staples of his aesthetic.

Ariel spent a long time thinking about what would work for LaRussell’s style, and although she always seemed calm, cool and collected, Ariel couldn’t shake her nerves during her and LaRussell’s first fitting.
“I was about to cry, but he didn’t know that,” Ariel said. “I was shittin’ bricks scared.”
LaRussell put on the first outfit—a camo two-piece set with a purple beanie and pair of white shades. Ariel waited anxiously for his thoughts.
“NIGGA!” LaRussell said, looking at himself in the mirror.
LaRussell liked it, he really, really liked it. By the end of the fitting, Ariel gained the approval of Tietta.
“You’re hired!” Tietta said.
Just like that, Ariel became the newest member of Good Compenny.
“It was really a seamless integration,” LaRussell said. “My mom and them fuck with her—it was very very seamless, it was effortless.”

Soon enough, “The Ariel Effect” began—visuals for LaRussell’s “How Could I Not” and “Cali Bear” went viral, the hype reaching back to the buzz of the golden music video era of BET’s 106 & Park and MTV’s TRL. LaRussell’s comments became flooded with people reacting, all sharing the same sentiment: “Oh, he finally got dressed!”
“I remember we had this analogy—it was like, man, not putting on a fit, when the videos be so great, it’s like putting the kitchen chair inside of a Lamborghini,” LaRussell said.

The “Hit-Boy” visuals–where LaRussell wore a knit Michael Jordan pullover with a blue sky background that complimented the cool tones in both the classic Mustang and Hitboys teal Adidas t-shirts he often paired it with—landed LaRussell in Forbes.

LaRussell recalled finding out about the Forbes article on one of the last days of his Seattle residency. It happened to be the only day of the extended trip where he woke up in a mood that he just couldn’t shake, but when he saw the article, it made him step back and think.
“It was just like a, like a reminder, like, damn, bro,” LaRussell said. “Forbes, Lil nigga from the V? Independently?!? Black!?! Forbes, no major, no - no …. Forbes!?! Man…. What we doing?”

Since their initial fitting, LaRussell and Ariel’s relationship has grown. He’s even got a nickname for her—Mei Ling, but that’s a story for another day. LaRussell never felt like Ariel was trying to force her vision on him too fast, too soon. This slow building of trust led to a point where things that LaRussell originally said “fuck no” to are now a maybe, and sometimes, without much hesitation, a yes.
“Our agreement was I’ll let you do your thing, but to my level of comfort,” LaRussell said. “I gotta look like me and I gotta feel good.”
On January 2nd, LaRussell posted on Instagram:

“I NEVER wanted a Stylist. I wanted to just feel and look like myself and I felt a stylist would compromise my brand. I just wanted to wear sweats and shorts lol. Mei Ling really came in and just allowed a nigga to flourish lol. I still wear sweats and shorts but we make it fashion! IT WASN’T EASY! But we get it done! I’m super grateful to have you on the team dawg!”

stories.title: Behind the Beats: DJ Gutta Butta Presents 3-Point Play
paragraphs: The album DJ Gutta Butta Presents: 3-Point Play dropped in February, leaving us with one of the most iconic Bay Area LaRussell moments, including features from Keak Da Sneak, J. Stalin, OMB Peezy, and DB.Boutabag.

Though they created the album on a short two-day trip in Las Vegas, it was latent with versatility from bars full of life lessons, punctuated by LaRussell’s personal journey to hyphy shit that Tietta and Splash rapped for weeks like it was their own, before it came out.

DJ Gutta Butta is the mastermind behind the album. LaRussell was originally in Vegas to do an appearance for Zumeiz when he posted that he needed some studio space. Gutta Butta hit LaRussell, quickly connecting him with a spot. As soon as he landed, LaRussell headed to the studio.
“I wouldn’t care if I worked with anyone else, but LaRussell, till the end of my fucking time.” - Mike G.

DJ Gutta Butta, producer Mike G, and LaRussell teamed up a few years ago for the song “All About Fetti,” with DaBoii but the trio never had the chance to work together in person until this point. The two-day recording session was filled with an energy that’s still hard to describe. Good Compenny always seemed to bring something special to the table, something that, in the making of the feature-laden album, DJ Gutta Butta and Mike G matched with their own talents.

According to DJ Gutta Butta and Mike G, several things made LaRussell’s presence in the booth different but one thing in particular stood out: LaRussell did every song in one take, no hesitation. This is hardly the norm. It’s more common for artists to repeat their verse as many times as it takes, then the producer pieces the best sections together to make it sound as if it was done fluidly in one take. LaRussell spit effortlessly, erroneously, each time.
Mike G

Michael Gorbani, a 26-year-old record producer and engineer from Las Vegas, first started producing when he was 14 after his big sister bought him his first keyboard, equipped with Ableton Live—a digital audio workstation with software to record, edit, and produce music.

A self-described garage producer, Gorbani worked out of his parents’ garage until he eventually went to college, largely at his father’s request. It was during this time that he started putting 21 Savage-type beats on YouTube. After a few months away at college, Gorbani quickly realized that he wasn’t interested and wanted to pursue music and return home instead.

In 2020, 21 Savage’s producer held a contest that Gorbani and 60 others entered. Gorbani secured fourth place and received an email list featuring several artists, including Lil Keed and Young Thug, to whom he could send beats. Winning helped Mike G realize the caliber of his beats. One of his many strengths was his versatility—he could produce anything from West Coast trap to Detroit-style, even R&B, which set him apart from other producers.

Gorbani began selling beats without realizing he was also navigating a health challenge—a tumor had been developing in his pituitary gland for nearly six years, causing depression, weight fluctuations, and other symptoms. It wasn’t until Gorbani accompanied his sister, who has Crohn’s disease, to a doctor’s appointment that he realized something was wrong.

“I remember waking up from surgery and the first thing I saw was my mom on my right-hand side,” Gorbani said. “And I told her, ‘I want to do this, like I really want to push and just go for it and make beats.’”

As soon as Gorbani left the hospital, he was eager to start making beats again. Soon after, he got invited to his first studio session where he met a producer who’d help him get better doing what he loved and lived for.
Now, Gorbani’s has made music with LaRussell, Slimmy B, SOB, MBML and several others.

“He’s exceptional, ” LaRussell said, when asked about Gorbani and his love of producing. “He loves it. He loves it and he’s excited and enthusiastic about it. And he doesn’t complain…he’s hungry. He knows what he wants and he goes after it.”
Gorbani loves it so much that shortly after the 3-Point Play dropped, the Vegas-born producer moved to Vallejo.
DJ Gutta Butta

DJ Gutta Butta is a Bay Area legend hailing from Vallejo, CA, who now works in Las Vegas. A self-described connector, DJ Gutta Butta can be found anywhere from DJing to hosting events, producing singles and EPs of his own, to putting on concerts for artists like 310Babii, Stunna Girl and others.
“A great connector is a man who just loves to see everybody win,” Gutta said.
Gutta is the common thread between LaRussell and Mike G, making plays behind the scenes.
“Gutta Butta, I love, because he never came to me on no favor shit,” said LaRussell.
LaRussell went on to explain that everytime he connected with Gutta, Gutta came with a budget and added value.
“He is always of service and he’s always trying to pour into the pie,” LaRussell said. “It ain’t never on no other energy so it was dope to just cultivate from there.”
Gutta knows that LaRussell is particular when it comes to his music. There were several verses from talented artists that didn’t make the cut for the album.
“There was nothing wrong with the verse–he just wanted more energy,” said Gutta.

Growing up, it was The Temptations that first made Gutta want to do music. In high school, Gutta Butta described himself as outgoing, an athlete and a hustler, always making plays, like he still does today. He first got his start working in the music scene with his high school group the LRG, Little Rap Group, who he’d help throw parties across the Bay Area.

stories.title: DEO: Bay Area's Hip-Hop Ambassador for Over Twenty Years
paragraphs: In 2001, DEO got hired at 15 — a year before he legally was allowed —to work at the San Francisco Sam Goody record store, after persistently pleading with the manager, Paula, who finally said yes.
Paula was a young Latina woman passionate about music who’d interned at Universal Records when the company still had an office in the Embarcadero.

In the early 2000’s, every type of person came into the store, from teeny boppers and metal heads to elderly classical music lovers and rap fans. The two-level record store in the bustling Westfield Mall featured a movie room, thousands of CDs and tons of records. This was a time when walking into a physical store in search of an album was the typical way of acquiring music. iTunes debuted in January 2001 but streaming and buying music on your phone was not at all the norm then like it is now. DEO started learning about all the different genres of music while working at Sam Goody. At the time, Pop was the #1 charting genre. He sold a lot of Britney Spears, *NSYNC and Backstreet Boys.

DEO’s early days spent selling albums to all types of people reflect what has made him a successful and integral part of the music industry. His dedication to music, regardless of his personal preference, opened doors for him to navigate through different pockets of industry, from formerly managing Lil Kayla, whose demographic is 90% teen girls, to managing Dregs One—a hip-hop historian whose content centers the Bay Area, featuring the stories of OGS who helped shape hip-hop and rap.

Outside of what I’ve seen DEO accomplish professionally, it’s clear that he has a sincere, constant desire to see other people succeed. Whenever I ran into him he was often wearing a baseball cap, tucking away whatever drink he had in hand for a photo, in between conversations or introductions.

For DEO, connecting people is a part of who he is. DEO, now 39, a husband and father to three daughters, has spent nearly his whole life dedicated to the Bay Area. I wanted to learn about how DEO successfully became the Bay Area hip-hop liaison for decades, keen on understanding how he accomplished this while maintaining his signature brand of hospitality and humility. We met up at DEO’s recording studio in San Francisco for a conversation. As I looked around the room, I noticeds a 2x Platinum Lil Dicky plaque on the wall, an Amoeba flag hanging on another wall, near paintings of Mac Dre, with early 2000’s rap magazines piled high on a nearby shelf.
Can you tell me a little bit about what it was like growing up for you in San Francisco?

Homelife was, I mean, without getting too much in the details—it was a typical kid living in the projects. And music was kind of like art, our hub, it was our reason to kind of get out the way and go in a house and do something productive.
What else did you like to do growing up in the city outside of just kind of making music with your friends?
Once I decided to do music full-time which was like junior/senior year, it wasn’t really nothing that was more important than that, honestly.
What would you tell that version of yourself with what you know now?

Learn how to organize your finances better. Learn what it means to start an entity, like an LLC. We had one early but we didn’t really know what it meant. We just did it because that’s what we heard back in like, ‘04-‘05. But learn what that means to do that and learn how to leverage assets. That’s probably too deep. Yeah, find out financial literacy.

Being in an industry for so long and an industry that historically isn’t amazing for your mental health. What lessons have you learned along the way, about taking care of yourself? And remaining consistent?

Yeah, I think that you got to earn those breaks, you got to earn those mental health breaks. That’s probably not the right thing to say. This isn’t a corporate job. If you have to stop for mental health day, every month or every other week, then that’s not gonna work. You have to get to the goal, like finish some goals and reach some goals before you say, I need a break.
What part of being a manager do you think people don’t see?
It’s a thankless job. The manager is like, “the hidden hand.” A good manager is not all in the camera or in the spotlight of the artists.
What’s the first piece of advice you give to new artists?

The first piece of advice I usually give is put music out there. It starts with the music. Like if you’re not putting music out, it’s really nothing to talk about. Like seriously. People want advice before they even see what kind of fans they have or where their fan base is. Some people couldn’t even tell you what their fan looks like.

stories.title: Legacy. Humble. Myself. Reflection. Malachi's Story
paragraphs: Malachi had always dreamed of performing in the pouring rain, literally. Hit-Boy and LaRussell’s 2024 release for “Rent Due” made this moment a reality. With stormy skies forcing the crowd under the tarp, Malachi stood in a blue and white ombre jacket, black sweats and a black fuzzy beanie, rapping his heart out, all while raindrops made his dream a reality.
They tell me I’m so mature
My nigga I’m trynna be
I done hurt some people
did some things you won’t believe,
I wasn’t trying to hurt you
I was really trying to grieve…”

It’s a somber moment. The crowd is quiet and attentive. I notice several people with their heads bowed in what I assume was not sadness but rather what felt to be deep reflection. LaRussell stands to the right of Malachi on the bleachers, surrounded by his fans and family. LaRussell’s typical, beaming smile is replaced with a pensive look as he stares into the distance, each raindrop dampening his gray Good Compenny hoodie. As Malachi finishes his verse, LaRussell folds his hands at his chest then opens his arms wide, embracing Malachi with a hug.
From Merced to Vallejo

“Legacy. Humble. Myself. Reflection.” Those are the words LaRussell used when I asked him to describe Malachi, a 17-year-old artist from Merced, with no driver’s license and few months left of high-school. Malachi is most definitely the type of young person that you look at and think, “I didn’t have that much poise at 17-years-old.”

Malachi had a way of carrying himself that you seldom saw in teenage boys, let alone rappers. Malachi was notably the youngest rapper to regularly hang out with Good Compenny. He often came with his uncle, dad and sometimes, his two young brothers. Malachi was relatively quiet, but whenever he spoke, it was always with confidence. Every time he walked into rehearsal, the young artist was laser focused. While many people happily chatted in the corners or cut up with someone they hadn’t seen in a while, Malachi looked to always be studying, whether it was LaRussell’s performance or someone else’s. Malachi was wise beyond his teenage years. LaRussell recalled their impromptu walks, listening intently as Malachi would provide insightful thoughts on music, business and his experiences navigating the world. His emotional intelligence reflected in the way he spoke about taking care of his family, building his faith in God, being a good example for his younger brothers, and his discipline to his craft. Malachi was extremely consistent, something he credited to his dad’s guidance and mentorship.

Though only a teenager, there was no treating Malachi like a rookie. He’s profoundly dedicated to his craft of creating songs that tell stories that are deeply personal to him, songs that he’s learned resonate across generations. LaRussell first noticed Malachi in 2021 after Tietta came across a video of Malachi rapping on a local Bay Area blog and shared it with him. LaRussell was immediately impressed.
“That kid wrote ‘Hood Cry’ at 14. Some of these guys are 40 or 50 and haven’t written anything as great, intimate, or touching,” LaRussell said. “At 14, I was just trying to rap like Lil’ Wayne.”

LaRussell was astounded by how someone so young could infuse more lyricism and emotion into a single song than many do in their entire careers. To LaRussell’s surprise, Malachi crafted his lyrics entirely on his own.

Over the past three years, LaRussell has been dedicated to highlighting Malachi, inviting him to shows whenever possible and bringing him into circles that could open further opportunities. Today, LaRussell continues to mentor Malachi, who in turn teaches people like me—and the rest of the world—valuable insights about ourselves through his music.

Malachi’s hard work is paying off. He ended up on 13 of the 17 songs that LaRussell and Hit-Boy recorded during their brief two-day studio session in Los Angeles—one of which made it on the actual album. LaRussell is currently mentoring Malachi through the process of dropping his first album. His social media following continues to grow and in the past few months, he’s started throwing his own shows.
LA Hit-Boy Session

It was sometime in early January 2024 when Malachi was supposed to be coming to Vallejo just to record a few songs and to show LaRussell new music he was putting together for an album that was slated to come out later in the year. In typical LaRussell fashion, LaRussell asked Malachi if he had an outfit and ID with him (he did) and invited him to come to LA to work with P-LO and Hit-Boy. But because Malachi was still very much a teenager, LaRussell knew he had to call Malachi’s dad. On the phone, they ironed out the details, then, with dad’s blessing, hop on a flight to LA. LaRussell told Malachi before they even got off the plane that every time he sees LaRussell writing, he should start writing too.
Malachi entered the Hit-Boy studio session nervous but left feeling affirmed and inspired.
“Even the first verse I wrote I didn’t know if it was good enough,” Malachi said. “I just went in and I recorded it.”
Malachi recalled expressing his uncertainty about the first verse he wrote during the studio session. LaRussell disagreed.
“Nigga shut up!”
It was clear that Malachi was talented and no one was letting him think otherwise. Malachi wrote another verse. Then another, and another.

“Malachi is only the nigga I know who can write with me, like at that pace,” LaRussell said. “I aint met another artist yet that could go when I go—like I’m usually waiting. That nigga had one where he was done before me!”
LaRussell has no problem telling Malachi this. He sees the young artist’s talent and wants to affirm not just his talent but who he is—Malachi is simply different.
“That just inspired me, it helped me to continue to write even more, because I wasn’t nervous,” Malachi said. “They kept affirming and saying what I was doing was so great.”
When Malachi writes, he thinks about how his faith allows him to feel the presence of God during the process.
“I believe in God, I believe in Jesus and I feel like He be there when I’m writing,” Malachi said. “I feel like I’m not the only person that’s there.”

Malachi left the Hit-Boy session as a featured artist on a majority of the songs that were produced. The Hit-Boy session offered just a brief look at what Malachi has been doing since he was 12-years-old: writing verses. Five years, Malachi admits, isn’t much for people who have been in the rap game for 20, but for him, which he pointed out, that’s nearly a third of his life.
Early Childhood
When Malachi was around 11, he told his dad he wrote something. His dad was expecting a short story but instead, Malachi spit some bars. Instantly, his father, Alex, was impressed.
His dad said Malachi was so good at such a young age, it was nearly impossible not to push him to take it as far as he could.

From that point forward, Malachi’s dad committed to investing in Malachi’s music career. Some days it looks like driving long hours with Malachi’s uncle, Cory, to make sure Malachi could get to where he needed to go in order to access opportunities that would help him succeed and gain exposure. Malachi had both his uncle and his dad’s full support. His uncle would drive and even try to help Malachi run his social media and YouTube to bolster his online presence. Malachi’s dad basically worked as his manager, careful to make sure Malchi was aligned with the right people so that his career could continue to flourish.

This meant driving to Reno, Nevada, Los Angeles and regular trips across the Bay Area for Malachi to work alongside Good Compenny. With Malachi, his uncle and his dad, who Malachi fondly refers to as the “three-piece combo,” were his two younger brothers, both theatrical and full of energy, along for the ride.

Malachi alchemized all the encouragement from his mentors in the industry and family into his music. I’d just seen Malachi perform at the Hit-Boy release party. It seemed like each time I saw him, he was only getting better. On top of that, I heard him sing for the first time.

It’s a Tuesday evening in Vallejo and the sun is just about to set. I’m in the media room at the compound sitting across from Malachi as his uncle and dad watch from the side. The three had taken the hour and half drive from Merced to Vallejo so Malachi could record a podcast and join me for an interview.
I start by telling Malachi how impressed I am, surprised that he can not only rap but sing too, when his dad starts cracking up in the corner.
“What’s going on?” I ask.
“He’s been telling me to sing for ten years,” Malachi said. “Singing expresses things that I can’t say in rapping.”
Malachi’s dad, Alex, has the “I told you so” look on his face, then starts laughing as he tells me how he first found out how his son could sing.
“So the kid’s weird right?” Alex said, smiling as he begins the story.

He continues to tell me about the time when Malachi was in fifth grade, dressed in a button-up shirt and top hat, singing Frank Sinatra’s “My Way.” Alex was taken aback because Malachi was actually hitting the notes. His son could rap too, and write—well. Alex found himself asking the same question LaRussell first asked when he heard Mali: “Who wrote this?” It was Malachi.

Alex continues to witness many proud moments as he watches Malachi’s career grow. From small moments in the house overhearing Malachi rapping his verse from one side of the house as his younger son finishes the verse on the other side of the house, to Malachi finally listening to him and getting the courage to sing, to watching Malachi perform in front of 1,200 people. This moment nearly brought tears to Alex’s eyes, especially seeing everyone’s response to Malachi—his son—as lighters and phones lit up the room, praise and daps following each show.
Malachi is wrapping up his senior year in high school while continuing to work on his music career.
“I had trouble in high school trying to find my like collective, my people,” Malachi said.
Malachi goes on to tell me that he doesn’t have a lot of friends right now— most of them are dead, in juvie or in prison.

“And these are the people that like, aren’t, they aren’t obligated to be around me. They aren’t by default my people, right? But they accepted me,” Malachi said. “They accepted my family and they accepted my little brothers and my fathers and my uncles,” he said.
Malachi constantly reminds us of the next generation and their undeniable qualities—courage, grace, and creativity.

stories.title: Shanté: Music & Motherhood
paragraphs: As a child, Shanté’s morning routine began with stepping outside and singing—singing to herself, to the sun and to anyone else who happened to hear the notes flowing out of her grandmother’s East Oakland house. Afternoons were spent listening to the sounds of Charlie Wilson, Marvin Gaye and Oakland’s own Keyshia Cole. In the evenings, Shanté would be playing outside, drawing with chalk while her grandmother cooked, pulling ingredients from the garden.

For as long as Shanté can remember, she’s been asked by her family to sing, even if she didn’t feel like it. Referred to by her family as the “mini Alicia Keys,” particularly by her animal-print-obsessed aunt, Shanté found herself called upon to perform at every family function, from cookouts to birthdays and parties at her family’s ranch.

Years of impromptu performances at her family’s request may explain Shanté’s unenthused look when she walks into the backyard for rehearsals. LaRussell promptly hands her the mic, giving her barely a moment to catch her breath. Begrudgingly, Shanté takes the mic and settles into the bleachers, doing her best to blend into the crowd. No signs of excitement or nerves slip onto the 20-year-old’s face. At 4 ‘11”, Shanté prefers to go unnoticed but once she opens her mouth to sing, you’ll never be able to forget her. Eventually, Shanté pulls out her iPhone 7 to glance at her lyrics, then, with a single note, her angelic, soft, soulful voice draws the crowd into silence.

Somewhere in the crowd, a toddler stands mesmerized. Noel was endlessly curious, the type of child that couldn’t help but make you smile. From birth, Noel was surrounded by art, love, talent, light and endless hands from the Good Compenny crew, ready to pick him up. Michael Prince crouches down to let Noel blindly pull at his violin, Nef the Pharaoh drops to his knees to rap eye level with him, LaRussell holds him in his left arm while he adjusts audio with his right, Tietta catches him when he runs into her arms, pulling his pant leg down to make sure it covers the small part of his exposed ankle.

But the 1-year-old’s deepest connection is with Shanté, his mom. The melodies he sings just like her, the beat that he drums upstairs in the venue as she waits backstage, the turn of his head when she opens her mouth and lets out that first glorious note, the embrace that soothes when no one else’s will. Shanté’s love felt like her voice—angelic, soft and soulful. After rehearsals and performances, Shanté is often showered with compliments. New listeners who didn’t know her before are anxious to tell her how amazing her voice is. Often Shanté blushes and looks down as people gush over her performances.

For Shanté, the 20-year-old songstress from East Oakland, success came quickly. The standout track, “Party on Mars,” from her debut EP Protection, released in 2021, is approaching nearly 2 million plays on Spotify. Just recently, the streaming giant added her to the cover of their Fresh Finds playlist. In February, Shanté opened for Pink Sweats after he pulled up to Vallejo and happened to hear her sing. Her social media continues to grow, with several viral videos boasting views in the hundreds of thousands. Shanté is currently working with the well-rounded and infinitely talented musician and producer, Hokage Simon, to put out new music.

At the same time, Shanté is a new mom and despite quite a few successes, her career is still in its early stages. Each day, she navigates co-parenting, motherhood, love, and relationships. On some days, Shanté embodies the particular brand of exhaustion that only parents—particularly moms—understand.

Until this interview, Shanté and I communicated through side eyes, raised eyebrows, and an occasional side comment at the Pergola. In a moment of irritation, Shanté would say to me,“Did you see this big beefy nigga just try to hit on me?” or, in a moment of doubt, “Is what I said awkward? I feel like it was awkward,” or, in a moment of anxiety, “Do you have weed?” Shanté is only 20.

On a sunny day in late February, I convinced Shanté to come to my apartment for an interview, promising a present upon arrival. It didn’t hurt that it was just her birthday. I was determined to know more about Shanté. She had an energy that lifted hearts but when she wasn’t singing, Shanté seemed like she didn’t have much to say. I wondered who Shanté was at 16, when she first walked into the backyard of LaRussell’s family home.
Backyard Beginnings

In 2020, a friend invited Shanté to sing background vocals for LaRussell at one of Good Compenny’s Live Sessions–a series of short, live performances edited for YouTube. After she finished singing, LaRussell told her how good she was and that she should not be a singing background. They went on to record a live version of Etta James’ “I’d Rather Go Blind.” LaRussell asked if she had a studio space to record anything–she didn’t. Soon after, Shanté pulled up to LaRussell’s home studio and the two recorded her first EP, Protection, in less than three days.

For LaRussell, writing with Shanté was something new and fun. He typically only wrote by himself, but with Shanté, she would hum a bass line for LaRussell or a flow, he’d add his bars, then she’d add her lyrics, going back and forth until they had a complete song.
“It was great. I felt at home,” Shanté said. “I felt like I belonged.”
“She’s my favorite person to write with because it’s so easy,” LaRussell said.

The album easily became an instant success, independent of a major label or big marketing dollars. For LaRussell, this was proof that great music always prevails, because a similar kind of magic happened when he wrote the album “Field Trip’’ for Tessie, an original member of Good Compenny, as well as an artist and longtime friend.

stories.title: AdventureIsDre: Healing, It’s Different
paragraphs: In 2019, Dre took a trip to the Sutro Baths outlook in San Francisco. The waves crashed on what used to be an ocean pool aquarium back in 1894 and left jagged rocks behind. As soon as he got there, he got déjà vu and started wondering why it all seemed familiar.
“The minute I saw the outlook, every memory I had there came back. To the point where I could remember the sandwich saran wrap. How my stepmom folded the sandwiches up,” said Dre.
He hadn’t thought about the Sutro Baths, or the cliffs below, for over 15 years, but something called him to that moment.
It reminded him of his father, who was born in 1947 and loved nature. Dre’s dad used to take him to places like the Sutro Baths lookout and Yosemite.
“I saw snow, rain, hail, sunshine, all in one day, and it blew me away because I didn’t even know you could have all of that,” said Dre.

Dre and his family drove around the national park, and he witnessed feeding coyotes and wildlife he had never seen before. He remembered begging his dad and uncle to stay just one more day, but it wasn’t an option. He returned home solemn.

Dre first heard LaRussell in 2020 when he was living in Georgia. George Floyd had recently been murdered, and someone had reposted a video of LaRussell’s song “20 Shots,” which he released in 2018 under his previous name, Tota Shakur.
Dre was shocked that someone from his hometown was rapping like this.
“I was just like, damn, there’s nobody from Vallejo speaking on something like this, like, unheard of,” said Dre.
Dre described himself as old school, someone who grew up on lyricism and the other fundamental pillars of hip-hop. Music wasn’t hitting the same as it was before, but LaRussell’s sound was different.

2020 was also a time of immense grief for Dre. He had lost everyone close to him—his mother, his father and his grandmother - who he cared for up until the moment she passed. When his dad died in 2020, he had never felt so lost. There was no one to talk to, no one to get advice from.
“I used to weigh like 450 pounds. I was depressed, like I was a recluse. I didn’t go outside,” said Dre.
Dre dismissed his friends’ pleas to leave the house. He could never come up with a good reason to step outside.

One night, feeling overwhelmed, Dre decided he was going to crash his car while drinking. First, he reached out to a friend with whom he had a strained relationship, but there was no answer. Determined, he got into his car and turned the key, but it wouldn’t start. He tried again and again, but the engine remained unresponsive. A few minutes later, his phone buzzed—it was his friend returning his call.
“I was like, was that meant to happen?” Dre couldn’t believe it, but he took it as a sign.

He thought to himself, “since I didn’t go through with it, maybe I can get out of this and somehow change it. So eventually I did. I started turning things around, like weight loss and trying to get my mental right.”
Dre got into therapy at one point, but it was nature that brought him the most peace.
Rediscovering Nature

Dre described nature as something that happened upon him, rather than something intentional, but once he became committed and enthusiastic about discovering what it had to offer, he couldn’t stop. He hadn’t been outside in nature for years, yet there were many familiarities from his childhood. The urge to go find something, something that made him feel at peace, in awe, challenged, overwhelmed — a waterfall, an unexpectedly beautiful trail, a stunning look out.

In 2021, Dre moved from Georgia, back to California, with a purpose. He wanted to keep the weight off, continue to lose weight, and eventually start a hiking group. He treated hiking like a second job. He worked Monday through Friday taking pictures of cars for dealerships, and on Saturdays and Sundays, he would scope out trails, find waterfalls, and locate breathtaking spots across California. Saturdays and Sundays soon turned into Tuesdays and Thursdays after work and by the time he wanted to start his hiking group, it was easy. He had already built a consistent routine at that point, and now the job was just introducing other people to it. Still, he reflected on the days when just started hiking again.
“I was 300 pounds doing this shit — like this is hard.”
Now, when team members are winded, drained, and completely unmotivated they sometimes yelled, “We’re not you!” to Dre, to which he would respond:
“You could be me though! I was where you are right now.”
“I always tell people, do shit when you don’t want to do it, because that’s the best time to do it. You’ll be breaking down the bad habits.””

After watching Good Compenny from across the country and then moving back to California, Dre continued to follow Good Compenny but never managed to grab a ticket. When Shanese reached out to invite him, Dre insisted, again, that he didn’t have a ticket, but Shanese assured him he was welcome to come. He attended the June Pergola show in 2023 and was amazed, becoming an even bigger fan than before.

Since then, Dre has become a familiar face at Good Compenny events, known for his impressive edits, stunning hikes, and vibrant demeanor. He’s been seen editing videos for other artists, working with Manny at Momo’s, jet skiing with Coach Ott and his sons, and, of course, attending the next Good Compenny show.

Dre’s story serves as an inspiration for others finding ways to stay active and support their mental health. Still, he occasionally reflects on a different version of himself, one that struggled to leave the house at all.

“I don’t know how. Eventually, I just stuck with it. That’s all it is. I stuck with the goal. I knew eventually, if I found my purpose in life, I would be able to really grab it, hold on to it, and make it what I wanted to, and that’s ultimately what I did.”

stories.title: CallMeClaydough & Body Music
paragraphs: It’s the first Sunday in July in Vallejo, and the sky is a brilliant, cloudless blue. Clay walks through the back gates and begins setting up the stand for his keyboard, careful with the piece that will fall off if not held correctly. His keyboard is covered in purple and cheetah print stickers with part of his Instagram handle, “Claydough.” He’s dressed in tan cargo shorts and a white T-shirt, complemented by a patchwork bag made from colorful quilts and a multicolored trucker hat.

The cloudless sky is the perfect backdrop for the fourth Pergola of Summer 2024— an event Clay has graced all season. The occasion also celebrates P-Lo and LaRussell’s newest album, “Majorly Independent,” which features Clay alongside artists like Michael Sneed, MALACHI, and more. The green turf in the backyard is marked with a small baseball diamond, and a sign is hung on the fence showcasing the baseball inspired album cover art.

Soon to turn 21 in August, the Oakland native isn’t focused on drinking or smoking; instead, he looks forward to retiring his fake ID at the venues where he performs. The instrumentalist, producer, designer, and creative is on a roll—showing up on more song credits and shows each day. He’s producing alongside industry greats like Hokage Simon, P-Lo, and Mike G, performing with LaRussell, working on a poetry tape with Tietta, building his fashion brand DIZZY, and collaborating with artists nationwide— all while staying true to his musical roots. There’s no sign of him slowing down.
Clay’s journey with Good Compenny began less than a year ago, thanks to @Made.by.Harry. He progressed from attending rehearsals to joining studio sessions to performing on the road.

Clay’s presence is marked by an understated yet undeniable talent. Despite being only twenty, his calm demeanor and distinctive style, characterized by layered patterns and accessories, make a strong impression. “He’s talented but doesn’t flaunt it,” said Keith, Clay’s dad. “I love seeing how he operates in the world.”

On this particular night in May, Clay is at Grill Studios in Emeryville, California, where LaRussell has established a creative hub to push himself out of his comfort zone and embrace more collaborations. Clay, dressed in a blue soccer jersey and a DIZZY beanie, is behind the glass booth, clapping and drumming on his body. LaRussell raps over the steady beat of Clay’s chest, then partway through, switches up the pace. Clay responds by drumming on another part of his body, creating a distinctly different sound as LaRussell continues to rap. Tietta and LaRussell often cheered him on with shouts of “BODY MUSIC!”
Body Music!

Clay’s musical background really begins with his parents, Evie and Keith, two musicians from vastly different parts of the musical world. His mother, Evie, grew up on the East Coast, immersed in clogging, string instruments, and folk music. She went on to form a band, the Stairwell Sisters, which toured all over. His father, Keith, grew up in Waxahachie, Texas, where his passion for drumming and Jazz was born. His dad went on to tour with some of the most famous tap dancers in the world, he joined a circus at one point in his career and in the latter he created the International Body Music Festival, which Evie, Clay and Keith attended as a family.

Clay spent his early years traveling with his parents as they pursued their musical careers around the world. Most of what Clay remembers from this time is through pictures and videos of him at that age.

One video shows Clay at seven years old at the Body Music Festival. He’s standing with two mics in front of him on an empty stage, swaying in front of a crowd of adults. His bangs are close to touching his eyebrows and he’s wearing a white shirt with a car on it. Standing at maybe only four feet and some change, Clay performs to the crowd - first beat boxing, and then drumming on his body, then back beatboxing, but not before a crowd roars, cheers and claps for him.

Fé, a lifelong friend of Clay’s family, traveled with them to the International Body Music Festival. Fé remembers Clay as an open and receptive child, deeply immersed in the diverse musical experiences he encountered around the world.
“Clay was very open, like a big vessel,” Fé said. “He was surrounded by musicians in the U.S., Istanbul, Tenerife, Italy, Paris, and Bali.”

Cecelia, another close family friend and production manager for the International Body Music Festival, called Clay the perfect travel companion. She fondly recalled their first meeting on a warm summer day in the Bay Area and how they later embarked on new adventures together as they traveled internationally for the festival.

“These are people that you know, use their bodies [to make music] and make their living from doing this. So it’s a very, it’s not a huge community, but it’s a very unique community. And these people were the top of their field of what they did. So people from Spain, Greece, Inuit, two Inuit women from northern Canada, France,” said Cecelia.

Along Clay’s travels he was encouraged endlessly to experiment with sound. Whether it was a set of pots and pans and chopsticks, a rolled up flier that would act as a drumstick or his red ukulele, Clay was always encouraged to make noise.
“ It was like a big party, with music workshops, performances, food, and dance.” Clay remembered.
The community quickly warmed to Clay, finding every opportunity to involve him in both the performances and the production.

Clay’s mom described walking through unknown destinations with Clay, trying to not stick out too much, but Clay was quick to say hello to a stranger walking by and would quickly reveal that they were not from there, but as Clay’s dad described, traveling with a kid was like having a secret key - people approached them differently and it established a level of connection you wouldn’t’ get otherwise. Clay was always ready to interact, look people in the eye, shake people’s hands and absorb the information around him.
“He was wired for listening to the variety and musicality of how music can be played, and not just with instruments and voices, but how it happens in nature,” said Fé.

Clay’s mom, Evie, credited Clay’s dad, Keith, for developing his deep listening skills. Keith was always fascinated in the ability of the ear to tune out certain noises - to control all the chaos - and simultaneously tune in, like a microscope.

Keith recalled asking Clay as a child, “What do you hear?” To which Clay would respond, “I hear the cars,” or “I hear the wind.” Keith would investigate deeper, “Well what about that airplane that’s way in the sky? Do you hear that low rumble?” or “Do you hear that dog a few blocks away?”Keith described this process as adding a 3D element to the sound around him.
“He would stand in a hallway that was very resonant,” said Keith
“And either clap or go mm-mm-mm so he could hear the reverb in and he’d look at me and say, ‘it’s working!”
It was fascinating to watch the world through Clay’s.
“He will listen not only to the sound, but he can [hear] intuition, the meaning behind,” said Fe.

Keith’s dad emphasized that traveling didn’t mean vacation, they had busy schedules and spent time in people’s homes, with their families, and were often off the touristy path. With that, Clay was surrounded by a lot of different cultures, many of which the common language that was shared was music.
The foundation of traveling required flexibility, respect, listening, and collaboration skills, of which Clay learned very early on.
“He’s still growing, which just floors all of us who know Clay, that Clay is just still blossoming.” said Fé.

Fé described Clay as a century plant - a plant that normally looks like a regular large agave plant, but every 50-100 years it has the capacity to grow a chute that reaches roughly 10 to 15 feet high. “There will be a blossoming from Clay that will be unstoppable. And that’s what I feel about him.”

As Clay grew older, his parents joked that he quit the band, though he continued to enjoy music. By elementary school, Clay began experimenting with GarageBand on his friend’s iPad. By middle school, he was creating regularly, sharing content with friends, and attending beat camps with his friend Devin who introduced him to Logic Pro. Music production soon became a primary means of Clay’s expression, allowing him to explore various styles.

In high school, Clay transferred to the Oakland School of the Arts, a pivotal moment in his life where he met his main collaborator, Ajai Kasim. Surrounded by like-minded producers, Clay stayed collaborating, until hit during his junior year, forcing him to spend more time at home. All he could do was practice. “That’s when I really got good,” Clay said. “I got ten times better.”

Clay graduated high school in 2021. He knew he didn’t want to go to college, and his parents supported him not doing so. He did a quick stint in L.A. and worked at Trader Joe’s but he quickly realized his creative fuel was drained by the end of a long work day. He returned back to the Bay Area and soon after experienced a serious health scare, one that had the potential to end fatally.

As Clay’s health faltered he was forced to accept a new pace - one where he had to mainly stay inside, rest and not much more. He couldn’t make music - the bass and frequencies would cause him to feel terrible. This lasted for over a year, and he remembers the transition phase of slowly reintegrating as extremely difficult and depressing. Over time, he slowly began to see people again and went outside. Surprisingly enough - one of the first things he did was see LaRussell at New Parish. It was his first time he had seen him live.
By late 2022 and early 2023, Clay was back to creating music with renewed passion. He joined jam sessions, performed with Seiji Oda, Tia NoMore, Ajai Kasim, and others.

In late 2022, Harry (@HarryMadeThisBeat) invited him to a LaHearsal and told him to bring his keyboard. It didn’t take long to realize Clay was a good fit. Soon he was in studio sessions, on the road, and playing at every pergola show.

Keith, now 72, has enjoyed watching Clay’s growth and milestones. The collaborative nature of Clay’s work and the people he brings around remind Keith of his own experiences but in a new era, with Clay making it uniquely his own. Clay continues to expand his musical and creative repotour after a busy year. He produced “BIG DREAMS,” on LaRussell and P-Los Majorly Independent album, he’s been working with Tietta to create a poetry album, he continues to send out beats, loops and packs to artists, played at New York Fashion Week and continues to co-create with artists from the Bay and beyond,
“I love seeing what he’s doing now and how he’s growing as a musician, but also just as a person, as a producer,” said Keith.

“I see him with his friends and the people that come around the house, you know, for sessions and stuff. I really like them. I’m very happy with the people that he surrounds himself with. Really impressed by this generation, and gives me hope.”
A Brief History on Hambone Music

In 1739, during the Stono Rebellion —one of the largest and most significant slave uprisings in the British North American colonies—enslaved people along the Stono River in the Carolinas revolted against their oppressors. (1)

In response, slave owners sought to suppress the rebellion and quell their spirit by taking away the enslaved people’s drums, which were vital to the West African culture from which the enslaved people originated.

To further restrict their freedom, and in response to the revolt, the Negro Act of 1740 was implemented, which imposed limitations on their social interactions, education, food cultivation, and musical expression.

Left without their drums, many enslaved people began to express their creativity and rhythms by drumming on their bodies. This led to the creation of Hambone—a form of body music that remains vibrant and influential. Hambone has since impacted various forms of performance, including tap dance and line stepping, and continues to thrive in many communities today. (2)

Keith’s musical journey allowed him to play with some of the most legendary tap dancers in the world like the Nicholas Brothers, Gregory Hines, Chuck Gree, Steve Condos, Charles “Cookie” Cook, and Charles “Honey” Coles. During a rehearsal early in Keith’s career he experimented with drumming on his body. Both Charles “Honey” Coles and Charles “Cookie” Cook noticed his approach and told him it resembled Hambone music—a style they had performed as children and in Vaudeville. They encouraged him to pursue it, leading Keith to explore and embrace Body Music, a term he uses to describe creating sound with the body.

stories.title: Creating Kehlani’s Record Store Inspired Pop-Up for Her New Album “Crash”
paragraphs: It was 2:00 AM on a Tuesday night in June when Chalberto’s phone buzzed. David Ali, Kehlani’s manager, was on the line with an urgent request. Kehlani had a pop-up shop in Oakland the following Friday, and Chalberto was tasked with creating an old 80s/90s record store infused with her unique style for her new album release, “Crash.”

Excited and inspired, Chalberto immediately began sketching ideas and getting them approved by David Ali. The color palette was dark royal blue and black, and accents included window decals and wall art. The design featured album covers of greats like Lauryn Hill, Musiq Soulchild, Amerie, and other soulful classics. He quickly pulled together a team and shopped for supplies, including vinyl, ink, plywood, epoxy, and new tools.
His vision included window decals, floor details, custom wood designs, and framing canvases.

For three days, Chalberto and his team worked nonstop, posting Instagram stories of their progress throughout the night. They printed and framed canvases with Kehlani’s intergalactic visuals, wrapped walls, painted tables, installed acrylic shelves lined with lights, and created the iconic blue and black “Crash” tables for autographs. When the day of the pop-up arrived, Kehlani and her team were amazed by the transformation. The space perfectly the mix of a nostalgic record store and Kehlani’s new age visuals. Chalberto and his team managed to execute have every meticulously crafted.

stories.title: Fresh off the Gentle Gig Summer Tour, Sydney and Seiji are now planning their next big move - with intention.
paragraphs: The Gentle Gig video shoot took place on a particularly overcast day in the Oakland botanical gardens.

“How’s everyone’s day going?” Seiji asked, dressed in black pants, a black leather Raiders jacket, a white graphic T-shirt with “Free Palestine” written in a serif font, and a visor bucket hat with the top cut out and a yin-yang symbol.
“Peaceful,” responded one person. “Gentle,” chimed another.

Sydney arrived late, smiling and thanking everyone for showing up - while talking on the phone, giving directions to someone looking for the video shoot location. She had freshly done French curls and oversized tortoiseshell glasses perched on her nose. She wore brown sweats that matched her brown and pink New Balances and Hello Kitty phone case.

Sydney was a perfectionist and a multitasker. She ensured everyone knew their roles, always checking over their shoulders. She managed to drop location pins, chat with everyone who arrived, monitor camera angles, snap photos, and guide people back to the shoot. What started as Seiji’s 12-bar freestyle post on Instagram to a xylophone beat by Jake Chapman (@chappymilkshake), “The Gentle Gig” had grown into a full-blown anthem, capturing the attention of millions over the last few months. Now, Seiji was teaming up with Jason Hayes to produce a music video for the song that reflected Seiji’s personal experience in the Bay Area, one that was equal parts hyphy and grounded in nature. The video featured Seiji in the botanical gardens, with two other dancers on either side of him. As water flowed through the rocks, Seiji and the two dancers began to turf, gig, and smeeze in front of lush green trees to Seiji’s soft knocking lyrics.
“A very therapeutic thizz I’m gentle gig general Ya I go dumb but I keep it so minimal”
In the final music video, the botanic visuals were juxtaposed with two cars in a parking lot, drawing circles with screeching rubber tires, as smoke billowed behind.

Sydney sat in my living room in late July to talk to me about Seiji and her partnership, as well own experiences navigating the creative industry. We had just returned from a late birthday dinner for Sydney in Sausalito, and switched from our dresses and skirts to sweats for the interview. I asked her what she pictured for Seiji in the future,

“Everything? Um, I want to see Seiji, like, in his stylish fashion bag. I want to see him walk in Paris Fashion Week. Like, he got that model physique - I don’t know if y’all be seeing him — but, my boy be tall. My boy is tall, He’s handsome. Like he literally can do that, aside from music, right?”
I agreed.
And I could see it happening with Sydney by his side.

In mid-2022, Seiji mentioned on Instagram that he was looking to expand his team, and on a whim, Sydney reached out. Sydney was already a fan of Seiji’s work, and Seiji knew about Sydney’s reputation as a photographer through word of mouth and their shared creative scene. Their initial connection, which began with consistent collaboration and Sydney assisting with social media and marketing, eventually grew into Sydney becoming Seiji’s manager.
According to Sydney, two years ago, things were different for her and Seiji. People who had once ignored them were now reaching out.

“I never forget,” she said, looking at me with a gorgeous grin. And it seemed to be true —especially those who didn’t say happy birthday to her a few weeks prior. Sydney acknowledged Seiji and her were still fairly new to the game, but they’d been around long enough to see how things unfold in the music industry—both beautifully and tragically.

In the last few months, things had really started to ramp up. The Gentle Gig song went very viral and brought Seiji a ton of new fans, including some that Sydney was particularly hyped for, like Jhené Aiko, E-40 and Kehlani. While Sydney was excited - she witnessed first hand all the work Seiji put in up to this moment - she was always extremely cautious about accepting new business ventures and wanted to get things right, the first time. While Seiji said he’s always been comfortable putting things together in whatever way, Bay Area style, out-the-trunk, that’s not Sydney’s approach. She demanded the best, and beyond that, she knew that both she and the artists she worked with deserved it.

Sydney brought a high level of professionalism to everything she did. She managed to strike a crucial balance between being a persistent dreamer and staying acutely aware of the realities— harsh or not—of the path they were forging. Additionally, she was fiercely protective of the people she cared about. She often joked about not wanting kids because between being an aunt and a manger, she felt that was more than enough. Nevertheless, her motherly nature led to her approach situations with a protective instinct, a deeply fortified love, and a relentless attitude to get things done.
As Seiji and Sydney both grew, they were also paying attention to how they were feeling along the way. They agreed, early on, that they wanted to take their time and be intentional.

“Nobody has time to be sued. Like, let’s make music. Let’s do it the right way. Let’s make sure we have a nice plan for the majority of things that we do. And, you know, keep it pushing,” said Sydney.

“You have to rest in order to be present, like you have to not do — to be able to do at your fullest capacity. I think for me, at least, that’s what works for me, is to be able to have time to be alone so that I can fully show up when I’m around people and when I’m performing,” said Seiji.

Sydney had an expert ability to switch between what needed to be done in the short-term, and what she saw as the big picture. She’s been breaking Bay Area records since high school, she graduated from San Francisco State University with a B.A. in Photojournalism, then got a Music Business Marketing and Management degree from Berklee Music College and then just got accepted to be in a concert cohort for UC Theatre.

Seiji began making music in middle school and continued to experiment with his style throughout high school. He remembered being young and creating parodies for family members as birthday presents, including a remix of “Stuntin’ Like My Daddy” by Birdman and Lil Wayne for his stepmom, which he produced using the Audacity music program.

He went to University of California, Los Angeles to study arts, music and business. In 2018, during his sophomore year of college, Seiji and his little brother created a song called “Trapanese.” Seiji made the beat for his brother, Lil Ricefield (@lilricefield), on an hour-long car ride, a parody of their Asian heritage and the many bad jokes that came with it. The song went viral, landing Seiji and his brother an interview on Genius and started getting Seiji noticed in class.
At first, he was unsure of the attention.

“But then I’m like, it’s cool that people recognize me for something that I’m doing. And even if I didn’t feel strongly about that song as like, a representation of me, it made me realize that okay, if I make something that I really like and then people recognize me for that I will want that,” said Seiji.
Seiji was set on creating music that felt to be a more accurate representation of himself, he continued to experiment with his style, but not without a few bumps along the way.

Seiji got in a bad snowboarding accident the following year, which resulted in a broken neck. The injury had forced him to slow down a bit, and with it he — he created a comeback song, “Aero” which was released in May of 2019. This song, he said, marked the birth of his signature sound.
“That song is kind of the first step for me as a solo artist, doing and finding my sound like the Lo Fi hyphy sound. I feel like I was born with that song,” said Seiji.

Aero ended up doing numbers, amassing almost 2 million Spotify plays (to date), and marked the beginning of Seiji diving into his lo-fi hyphy sound. Seiji has received an overwhelming amount of love in response to his music. One woman reached out to let Seiji know that she worked at a lavender farm and played his music when they harvested lavender. However, he noted that one of his favorite responses was when a person described his music as “ya dameaningful.” Seeing music through other people’s eyes, for Seiji, is one of the most rewarding parts of being an artist.

stories.title: Grill Studios
paragraphs: Hip-Hop in May as LaRussell Led a Legendary Collaboration

Throughout May, LaRussell embarked on a venture to bring together a range of artists at various stages in their careers to create something special at Grill Studios in Emeryville. He reached out to the owner, pitched the idea, and offered royalties on all the resulting music. The owner happily agreed.

“It’s really dope because we did so much collaborative stuff in there that he gets to be a benefactor of all that taking place in the studio. It just continues the legacy of the Grill,” said LaRussell.

The studio sessions resulted in four mini albums, featuring artists like Michael Sneed, Nef the Pharaoh, 03 Greedo, Hey Kujo, MoneyHillCasino, Tietta and more. Producers and engineers included Mike G, CallMeClayDough, MadeByHarry, QuakeBeatz, and Link+Up, and was accompanied by instrumentalists Michael Prince and Hokage Simon.

“It’s not easy to work with us,” said LaRussell, sitting in his Vallejo apartment. “You gotta do it on the spot there. And people aren’t used to that, really. Richie Rich was like, one of my favorites. Watching him write in real-time and work was just a special moment. But everybody really showed up and balled.”
Michael Sneed was among the artists called upon to do quick turnaround verses.

“He’s like, ‘Yeah, we do this thing where we write verses in 15 minutes.’ So I did a 10/15-minute verse and wrote it real quick,” said Michael Sneed. “I ain’t gonna lie, the beat was pretty hard to write to, so I probably got maybe four or eight bars by the time it was time for me to record. So I wrote the eight bars and then had to freestyle the rest of the verse.”

What came from it was a range of four mini albums, showcasing the full spectrum of hip-hop, including storytelling and life lessons like “Goin Places” featuring MoneyHillCasino and Tietta, produced and engineered by QuakeBeats and Link+Up, to Cali Classics that make you want to roll the windows down with 03 Greedo. Oakland producer Link+Up, who has worked with LaRussell on projects like “Motion,” “The Fresh Prince of the V,” “Outstanding,” and more, reflected on the chemistry they’ve built over the years.

“Energy is unmet,” said Link+Up. “I haven’t met an artist like him yet, but it’s always good vibes when he’s in the booth. He kind of just blacks out, does his thing, and nobody can tell him any different.

He knows what he loves, and I love that I can be creative with him, and he doesn’t hold me into a box. He just kind of lets me be. And I feel like that’s how we end up coming up with the crazy stuff,” said Link+Up.

Also among the all-star roster was San Francisco native and producer QuakeBeatz, who grew up with an equal appreciation for Motown and Smokey Robinson, as well as the hyphy movement. While QuakeBeatz didn’t produce a song, he did engineer several.
“It’s just like his culture. I feel like what he stands for, the positivity. Always giving somebody a message within the music. I feel good to be a part of that,” said QuakeBeatz.
The album served as a cultural marker, showcasing what hip-hop unity looks like and, more importantly, what it sounds like.

stories.title: Lakefest Fashion Show
paragraphs: It was the middle of June, and Ariel was wrestling with a decision. She had been contemplating whether to ask her community on Instagram to contribute to a kids’ fashion show she had been asked to organize for the Lakefest Festival. The show was set for the mainstage and was a big opportunity, particularly for the 30 kids who would get the chance to showcase their individual styles. However, Ariel was hesitant to ask for help. She worried about the possibility of failing the kids if donations fell short and felt she would have to swallow her pride a bit. Nevertheless, she reminded herself that it was all for the kids. She decided she would cover whatever wasn’t donated with her own funds—and make it happen for her babies— regardless. Determined to make it work, she posted her CashApp details.
Within a couple of minutes, ping, she got a notification: a $10 donation.
“Wow,” she thought to herself, “That was pretty fast.” A few minutes later, she got another ping and flipped her phone over: a $150 donation.

Ping. Ping. Ping. Ariel was shocked. In a short period of time, she quickly met her $3,000 goal, with her biggest donation being a $500 cash donation. When she realized her CashApp had already surpassed the goal, Ariel began to question it—and then started to feel bad.

“Anxiety through the roof, because I just never want anybody to think that I’m getting over on them, and I always want to be seen as truthful and trustworthy, because I am.” Ariel explained that she quickly deleted the post once she realized she had surpassed the goal.

“I even started questioning, like, why? Mind you, I needed it—I wanted it for the kids. But then I was just like, why are y’all sending me money? Like, why are y’all doing this? It was just like a whole thing within myself,” she went on to explain.

Regardless, Ariel was excited. She said on her dollar, they probably would’ve been going to a thrift store, but she would’ve made it happen. However, with $100 each in their pocket, each kid was able to go to the mall and pick out their outfit—including accessories.

Among the shoppers were Avery and Major, two familiar faces you may recognize from Good Compenny. Major is often seen dancing, laughing, and jumping with LaRussell, Malachi, and Splash, and Avery went viral earlier in the year for her stellar cover of Hyphy 2020. Both Major and Avery’s families had become part of the fabric of the Good Compenny community. Avery was playing pickleball with Tietta and LaRussell when Tietta mentioned that Avery should connect with Ariel and be in the show. Tierra, Major’s mom, was contacted via a note that LaRussell’s mom left on the door after Ariel reached out and asked her to get in contact with Major.
“I was like, I need Major,” said Ariel.

“He’s just so confident, he’s so good at everything, he’s so brave, and he’s just like an innocent kid. He’s just a kid, like, he doesn’t try to be grown, he’s not too prideful, he’s just literally being a kid. And I love that energy. So I was like, I need him,” said Ariel.
Tierra, Major’s mom, was equally happy.
“I was excited for him. He is a kid that loves being involved in things, and he has a big personality, and so I could see that he was nervous at times, but he was really excited,” said Tierra.

Avery and Major carpooled to a park in Emeryville in preparation for the show. Ariel’s friends took time off work to support her along the way. The first rehearsal was shaky; everyone was very scared and nervous. Ariel gave them some homework and had them come back with a bit more confidence. She would also start practice in a circle, with everyone going around and saying an affirmation to themselves.
“It was just so dope to see that, you know, putting some self-esteem into the kids, and having them scream out positive affirmations, just for reassuring themselves,” said Tierra.

After several rehearsals and weeks of preparation, Ariel went with twenty-something kids to the shopping mall. Before they got there, Ariel told the kids to find something that made them feel confident. Ariel was adamant about not helping the kids out too much—this was an opportunity for them to gravitate towards something that would encourage their personal confidence and their own style.

“They could have picked up something I thought was hideous. And I’m like, I know that’s right. I like that. What you gonna wear with it, just because this is how they want to express themselves. This is what they like. And I think I just wanted them to know, to feel confident in their decisions, so they can feel confident when they wear it,” said Ariel.
For Avery, when she was shopping, she wanted to find something that really spoke to her.

“Oh, it was like, it was meant for me, because it was giving, like, cute, but then was also giving, like, the look of my poses, and I was, like, giving a sassy and slay vibe at the same time,” said Avery.
The shopping spree also gave them an opportunity to work in pairs and collaborate on an outfit.
“It was cool because we had a budget, and I was saving money, and my duo was too, because he had extra money,” said Major.
Major and his duo searched for something matching.

“He got a whole fit with a hat, some glasses, some fresh, brand-new Crocs to the socks, and even a little bust-down chain. I won’t say how much it was, because it’s real, but he got him a little chain from one of those little stations at the mall,” Ariel said.
Ariel would occasionally remind parents on the shopping trip to allow their kids to take the lead and remained steadfast in encouraging their individual style.

In less than a month, Ariel found nearly thirty kids to walk in the fashion show, organized several practices, and fundraised over three thousand dollars. The day for the kids to finally walk at Lakefest was fast approaching. Unfortunately, just a few days before the event on Juneteenth, there was a shooting at Lake Merritt, where the kids’ fashion show was supposed to be held later that week.

“What I saw was that Juneteenth was beautiful, and it was a beautiful event, and there were a lot of people out. All I saw was people dancing and having fun and just honestly, a lot of Black joy. So when I heard about what happened, I was just really disappointed,” said Ariel.

Being from Oakland, it made it even harder for Ariel. For a moment, she was fearful that they might call off the fashion show, but she felt confident that the kids would be safe and protected. She knew there was a very small chance of the same thing happening twice. The event was ticketed, with security and police.

“I was like, I trust God. Honestly, that was my biggest thing. I was like, God is not going to allow that to happen with all these babies. And we planned, you know? I was like, I really know that this is going to be great. Everybody’s going to be safe, we’re going to have a good time,” said Ariel.
Lakefest Festival was still set to go on, and on a Saturday afternoon in Oakland, Avery and Major waited anxiously with their duos to take the stage as Malachi opened the show.
“I felt nervous, scared, but at the same time, I was really excited. Yeah, really a lot of emotions were going through,” said Avery.
But once they got on stage, their confidence and practice shined.
Avery walked out in an orange Sublime t-shirt, blue jeans, big hoops with little hearts, a choker with a heart in the middle, a cute bag, and a fuzzy white hat.
“It felt amazing. I felt confident walking. I really loved it. At the end, I was like, we did that, we did so good,” said Avery.
Major and his partner walked out in their matching outfits, complete with their fresh white Crocs.

“I just cooled down, and I noticed a lot of people were smiling whenever I went up there. And my mom was actually excited. I couldn’t hear her because there were so many people clapping and yelling and screaming,” said Major.
It was also an important moment for the parents:

“It was definitely one of my proudest parent moments, seeing her just be so confident exactly as herself, because they were so encouraged to pick their own poses, style themselves, pick their own outfits. It was cool to just see her be so confident in exactly who she is right now. And it just made me feel so good inside and so proud,” said Avery’s mom, Tiana.

After the show, Ariel was bombarded. The kids who were part of the show were already asking for another one, and parents, grandparents, and aunties were all saying the same thing: we need this for our kids! They were half showering her with compliments, and half pleading with her. This was an important moment for Ariel: she had thought about starting a nonprofit but had been hesitant. Why would she need a whole nonprofit for what she was doing?
“God kind of told me then, like, this is why you need to do a nonprofit so more kids can come, so it could be bigger, so you can give more opportunities.”

Ariel laughed, reflecting on a drunk grandmother who asked to speak to Ariel about getting her granddaughter in the program. Ariel told the grandmother to give her a second and then forgot to follow up with her in the midst of the post-fashion show chaos. She tried to walk off, and the woman swiftly stopped her.
“She was like, ah, where you going?” Ariel said.
“I’m still right here,” Ariel responded.

stories.title: The Reintroduction of Richie Rich
paragraphs: And His Breakdown of Majorly Independent

It’s 2:30 PM at Boss Market Food and Liquor, just down the street from LaRussell’s parents’ house. Richie Rich stands by his caramel classic car, adorned with a black and yellow license plate that reads “7DULCE.” Mike G holds a massive speaker as Malachi rides his bike into the frame of the video, starting his verse. P-Lo and LaRussell are behind him, P-Lo in a black shirt, black Stone Island pants, and Timbs. LaRussell, styled by Ariel, wears a monochrome black and white outfit, including a letterman jacket and a black and white beanie. They’re surrounded by supporters who responded to LaRussell’s Instagram invitation to join the content day for LaRussell and P-Lo’s new album, “Majorly Independent,” which was set to premiere in early July.

The album, a Bay Area classic, showcases the full spectrum of hip-hop, featuring OGs like Too $hort and Richie Rich—renowned for his unforgettable verses on “I Got 5 On It - Remix” and “Ratha Be Ya Nigga” with 2Pac—to new era talents like Malachi, who just graduated high school, and Michael Sneed, whose unique sound continues to impress. The album tells a powerful story of Bay Area pride and community, with each feature and verse strengthening the hip-hop lineage to create something exceptionally solid.
Richie Rich got on the album by what he calls a fluke. LaRussell posted a snippet of a song, “What We Doin,” Richie Rich couldn’t resist and commented his first four bars:
“What we doin? Pulling off slow from the curb. What we doin? Smokin on herb that’s superb..”
LaRussell texted him, “You trynna get on this?”
Richie Rich responded,
“I said—do you think you could reintroduce me to the world? He said, ‘That’s exactly what I’m gonna do. I got you,’” said Richie Rich.
I hopped on a call with Richie Rich in late July to hear more about the album, his music, and his reintroduction to hip hop.
What do you think is special about this album?

LaRussell doesn’t need the assistance of anybody else, but he’s not greedy like that. Instead, he’s reaching back. He’s grabbing people from his era. He’s incorporating people from my era. And that’s just it’s, to me, it’s like strengthening the hip hop vine. Because basically, LaRussell to reach back and grab me is like LaRussell reached back and grabbed the Sugar Hill gang. You know? And they were artists in the 70s, ‘79, ‘78— I believe. A lot of people weren’t even born back then. So it’s just a breath of fresh air to see a kid who’s comfortable enough in his own skin to be able to include people from before him, you know, with him, after him.
What’s changed the most since hip-hop’s inception, for you?

When I first started –I didn’t aspire to be a rapper. I kind of just ended up rapping. But I came from an era where individuality was — was everything, like when you heard a record, you could hear who it was. It was okay to be yourself. What I saw that started changing for me in the music in the late 90s they seemed like they were taking away the individual and replacing that with, you know, everybody sounding alike or acting alike or having one look.

I saw music get to a point where it got away from the ear, and it seemed like it became more from the eye, like it had a look to it, you know what I mean? So a lot of people fell to the wayside.
