The more talented people who actually had something to say were seeming like they were being pushed out, and what was being ushered in with this, this baller type of image, this baller, rapper. The guy with the most money, the guy with the biggest car. I was always a floss rapper, too. You know, it was all because Oakland has always been about car culture. But when I came up in the music, you know, we were all hustling, so we were just telling the stories about the shit we was doing and putting the money back on the sidewalk.
What’s stayed the same, for you?

The thing that stayed the same, as far as my creation process, is I’m just a truth teller. You know? People, they say I’m a game spitter, but really, all I’m doing is telling the truth, you know? And one thing about telling the truth, it can work and it cannot work. People can love it and some people can hate it, you know? But the thing about the truth is, it never gets old, so my style has stayed the same.
How does this album pay homage to the foundational pillars of hip-hop?

Now it’s, it’s starting to get back to the individualisms. You got a kid like LaRussell, you got a kid like Malachi, who, they don’t wear any jewelry, none at all. You know what I mean. They come out the house with the house shoes on whatever, crocs, you know, sweatpants, just lounging. And once again, the music is coming through the ear, the message is coming through the ear, and then what people are seeing with their eyes is individuality, and it’s working.
You said your son had a strong reaction to the song, can you explain?

My son is a big Mali fan. So, I mean, by doing this record with him, it even made me cool to my son. I’m like, I’m cool now? Because I’m on a record with Mali? He’s 13. So I was like, so prior to that, I wasn’t cool? Like, dude, I have played records for you that I did with 2pac and, you know, and none of that resonated? None of that resonated with him, but when he heard I was on a record with Mali, it was just like - it was a whole different level.
What do you like about LaRussell’s music that stands out to you?

One thing I’ve never been able to do Kayla is be hella fun in my records. I’ve tried to, I’ve had some cool, fun records, but on accident. But like, everything he makes it fun. And he’s still saying a lot of the same shit that I’ve been talking about, but he has a way to make it fun. He has the knees to support those dances he does. My knees ain’t gonna support that!
What has been people’s response to the album?

Four days, 1.2 million views on a 12 bar post is ridiculous. Like my shit hit one 1.2 million. I picked up 12,000 followers off of that play, 12,000 people started following me, and my page has been hopping ever since, like with people talking about: what’s up with the music? what’s up with the music? I know he couldn’t have turned me on to people that are in my normal fan base. These have to be younger people. These are people who are finding out about me from other places, and then they’re tying it together, because they’re in the comments like: this is the dude who has a video with the orange motorcycle, my dad used to watch this. And then somebody’s like, Oh no, that’s the dude that did that song.
What’s next?

We kind of just getting started as far as collabing on shit, because whenever he need me to do something, I’m there, you know? I really want to work with the kid Mali, too. I like Mali style. I like a lot of the shit that he says in his raps, and it’s a fresh air. It’s a brother fresh air for me to hear kids saying some shit again.

stories.title: Curated 4 Selfworth
paragraphs: In conversation with Hokage Simon

Simon crafted a slow-moving love letter to himself with Curated 4 Selfworth, which debuted on streaming platforms in mid-August. The ten-track album holds your hand through loss, love, healing, resilience, and creative passion. Collaborations with Simon’s equally talented friends embellish the project, including Michael Sneed’s distinctive high-pitched flows, which capture a multi-generational love story marked by grief and immense growth; Shante’s one-of-a-kind vocals; and Seiji’s meditative letter to self. Contributions from P-Lo, Nate Curry, and Tommy Jumpman round out the album, giving it the dream team feel—like the U.S. Basketball Team at the 2024 Paris Olympics.

The album showcases Simon’s range—from singing to producing to masterminding unforgettable collaborations. While Simon’s name often appears in credits across the board (LaRussell, Thuy, P-Lo, E-40, Karri, Larry June, Rexx Life Raj, Elujay, Full Crate, G-Eazy, Christian Kuria, Serpent With Feet, and many more), it’s rare to see him release his own music. This project was a long time coming.
“This was, like, one of the hardest projects for me to put out because I was holding on to everything for way too long,” Simon admitted.

He added, “It makes me feel good too, because now that this old music is out, I get to put my mindset on making new music. You know, it’s like cleaning out your closet—when you want to get new clothes, you’ve got to take the old clothes out first.”

Take Changes, for example. The track, created four years ago, finally came to life and P-Lo jumped on it—once Simon convinced himself to release it. “I’m blessed enough to work with so many talented people, and I’m really just honored to play a part in so many artists’ creative worlds. So when it comes to me trying to water my own plants and build my own world, and people actually want to be a part of it... it makes me feel really great.”

I haven’t met an artist more consistent or highly spoken of than Simon. He’s effortlessly cool, endlessly humble, and kind to everyone. Simon has an unmatched ear for music and I’ve never seen him without his art. Every plane ride, car trip, pre-show moment, or post-gig downtime—Simon was creating. Whether it was his keyboard, laptop, or headphones, living and creating ran in one vein for him.

This commitment made Simon a go-to collaborator, always ready to say yes to close friends. That’s why this album is so special—it’s a moment for him to shine on his own. Simon started making beats in high school, though he didn’t have many artists to work with back then. Around 20 or 21, he began immersing himself in the Vallejo music scene, where his name first started spreading.

I discovered Simon’s work during COVID when P-Lo dropped STUNNA. Since then, I’ve slowly uncovered Simon’s endless G.O.A.T. lore. People would say things like, “Simon was traveling the world when he was 5!” or “He played in bars with bands as a teen!” The truth? He’s been playing in bands since middle school. His dad, filled with pride, would tell anyone who’d listen: “My son can play keys, bro.” That pride landed Simon gigs with Vallejo group CRSB, performing in clubs and touring while still in high school.
“Performing, especially with Russ, is like second nature because I’ve been doing this for so long,” Simon shared.

And it showed. Simon played a pivotal role in shaping Good Compenny’s iconic concert structure. Before 2022, it was mainly LaRussell and Simon doing shows. Slowly, new layers were added—Michael Prince with the violin during the 2022 Pergola show, Richy Cruz on trumpet, and dozens of musicians over the last two years. Through every era, Simon’s foundation has been instrumental.

“Simon, Hokage Simon, is one of my inspirations. He’s one of the most incredible musicians I’ve ever met,” said Harry (MadeByHarry), who joined Good Compenny at the end of 2023. “He just picks up the song instantly, playing chords, creating bass lines and melodies. It’s my job to fit in where I can.”

ClayDough added, “He’s a goat. So kind, so nice, and he works so hard. He doesn’t gatekeep, either. He’s given me so much game in production, piano playing, and live performance. Gotta give it up to Simon.”
At one point, someone said: “Nobody can outplay Simon.”

Simon has spent years building a community of like-minded musicians, working with close friends to create something beautiful. Slowly but surely, more people began recognizing his name. The same lore I heard from community has proven true—Simon’s story is one of passion, persistence, and unmatched artistry.
And now, with Curated 4 Self Worth, the world finally gets to hear Simon on his own terms.

stories.title: From Sierra Leone to Stockton, DJ Kenzo’s Journey Is All About Making People Smile
paragraphs: As a young boy visiting family in Sierra Leone, celebrating life was central to Kenzo’s upbringing. Large, extravagant parties were thrown often—for birthdays, holidays, and weddings. Unlike many other parents, Kenzo’s dad, as he recalled, loved arriving early to every event.

“I wouldn’t just walk into the party and, you know, the night would be made,” Kenzo shared. “I got to see the night slowly build—from eight o’clock all the way to maybe two or three in the morning, or depending on when my parents wanted to leave.”

Kenzo watched in awe as the celebration unfolded—guests arriving, the air filling with the rich aromas of jollof rice, fried plantains, cassava leaves, and akara, and once-empty spaces transforming into vibrant scenes. What fascinated him most was how music had the power to shape the mood and energy of the entire event.

While his cousins ran around or danced, Kenzo found himself drawn to the DJ booth. Standing near the speakers at a celebration, the pounding rhythm vibrating through his chest, Kenzo watched his uncle expertly navigate the turntables, swapping discs and CDs. Kenzo’s eyes moved between his uncle and the crowd, who were dressed in Ashobi—handmade, colorful intricately designed outfits that reflected their tribes, whether Krio or Mende.
These moments planted the seeds of Kenzo’s love for music, long before he built his first setup in Stockton.
Kenzo’s Story

At 13, Kenzo sat in his childhood room in Stockton, surrounded by his makeshift music setup: a DVD player, CD player, speakers, an aux cord, and a splitter cable. The walls were a shrine to his idols—music legends like DMX, Bow Wow, and Fela Kuti; sports heroes such as Marshawn Lynch, LeBron James, and Derrick Rose; and his celebrity crushes: Kelly Rowland, Beyoncé, and Meagan Good (until his religious mother eventually made him take them down which he said he eventually appreciated). His room overflowed with CDs, and though he didn’t have a TV, he repurposed his DVD player as a second CD player. In secret, Kenzo began experimenting with sound, creating his own mixes and mashups—a process that called back to his roots in Sierra Leone.

Kenzo described himself as a lively and expressive kid, full of fun—at least until he felt uncomfortable, at which point he would often retreat into shyness. Above all, he wanted to make the people around him happy, and he quickly realized that music had the power to do just that.

Kenzo continued to experiment with music, making mixtapes and CDs for people throughout high school, including one for a crush. He loved seeing people smile and music was a way to accomplish that. After high school, he began working at house parties and in the college music scene—sweaty, chaotic, and often wildly fun debacles.
He began growing his fan base, working in clubs, and driving Lyft or Uber on the side.

One of the defining moments came in 2019, when he was able to pay his rent and buy his whole family Christmas presents solely from his DJ money—without needing to drive for Lyft or Uber that entire month.

Then COVID hit. Kenzo faced the uncertainty many artists experienced during that time. He moved home, which ended up being a blessing, as he spent time caring for his father, who became ill and unexpectedly passed away during that period. As he grieved his father, Kenzo also felt energized, knowing his father would have wanted him to achieve everything he aspired to accomplish.

Post-pandemic, Kenzo began working for the Stockton Kings’ G-League. This lead to a chance to DJ for the Sacramento Kings. One opportunity after another led to a regular position with the Kings, something his dad had always hoped for him.
“It was sad that my dad wasn’t there to see it, but I knew he was a huge reason why, you know, we were at that level. So yeah, it was pretty crazy,” said Kenzo.

Today, Kenzo is booked and busy. He DJs for the UC Berkeley football team and the Sacramento Kings, has opened for major artists, toured the Philippines, works corporate events for companies like Apple, and is one of the newest members of Good Compenny.

Kenzo and LaRussell had known of each other since 2019 but hadn’t had a chance to work together. Kenzo said that even at that time, he prayed for LaRussell’s success. Of course, he wanted to be part of it, but whether or not that was possible, he wanted LaRussell to succeed. This year was the first time Kenzo and LaRussell really got to work together.

The first time I remember Kenzo performing was at the L.A. residency show. It’s August in Los Angeles County at the SLiC compound, owned by Baron Davis, where LaRussell is holding his first Los Angeles residency series. The stark, clear blue sky and beating sun resemble the backyard in Vallejo, but the graffiti outlining the compound and the palm trees scream Los Angeles. As the crowd piles in, there are familiar faces: Jayla and her family, and, of course, the Good Compenny team—Simon, Splash, Tietta, Coach Ott, Jason, and more.

LaRussell sits in a backroom, while Splash has the video camera rolling (as always), with a DJI drone sitting on the table. Jason snaps pictures. Conversations are typically filled with premonitions of the future. The year isn’t even over yet, and LaRussell continues to hit milestones—sold-out shows, massive brand deals, a country album on the way, and a persistent desire to push the needle.

From the distance, you can hear music starting to get queued up. What began as a mix of background noise—voices, food being cooked, teams running around—suddenly stands out. Splash jumps to attention, yelling expletives and sprinting through the back area, through the first door, and then the next room to make it to the outdoor stage. He leaps onto the platform, shaking his dreads, jumping up and down. The person responsible for the music is Kenzo, who is beaming with pride as LaRussell, Malachi, and Jason walk out to hear for themselves before joining Splash.

With an unpredictable blend of old-school R&B, afrobeats, West Coast rap, and oldies that many 2000s babies wouldn’t know, DJ Kenzo takes us across the map—from the West Coast to Sierra Leone—all in Los Angeles County.

Being a DJ requires being the life of the party before the party even starts. Kenzo is animated, always in great spirits, and curates an experience you can’t find elsewhere. DJing in California comes with its shortcuts; you can easily rely on an arsenal of popular songs that have kept Cali parties moving for the last decade. When Sexy Redd became popular, every DJ used her energetic tracks as an injection of adrenaline when the party was lagging. But Kenzo doesn’t rely on repetitive party songs to keep the energy up. Instead, he focuses on crafting unpredictable mashups that leave you no choice but to get up and dance.

Kenzo has no plans of slowing down, and Good Compenny continues to inspire and motivate him. In 2025, he aims to curate a DJ experience that incorporates live musicians. His aspiration is to become a global DJ—one who sells out stadiums, drawing crowds who come specifically to see him. He also wants to ensure that people recognize the artistry involved in DJing, just as they would with any other artist. Along the way, he’s bringing his infectious energy and the pulse of Sierra Leone.

stories.title: Kamaiyah & QuakeBeatz: Ms Everything
paragraphs: Kamaiyah’s album, Ms. Everything, opens with a smooth introduction that is impossible to misinterpret: Kamaiyah is a go-getting, bar-spitting, fashion-forward, Oakland-raised, self-made millionaire. The intro alone allows listeners to step into her unapologetic world.
The album, produced by QuakeBeatz, features 12 tracks where Quake lays down a smooth road for Kamaiyah’s sharp and assured lyrics.

She tells her story of Bay Area luxury—satin sheets, leather coats, Beamers and Bentaygas, courtside seats, and gold jewelry. Parallel to the glamour are honest conversations about mental health, loss, grief, depression, and the resilience required to thrive both in the music industry and in the Bay.

Whether you’re searching for a pick-me-up or a celebratory anthem, Ms. Everything delivers. It’s the perfect soundtrack to start your night or end a long day. It’s a reminder to indulge in life’s pleasures, big and small, because joy is worth savoring in a world that often demands resilience.
“I feel like to be my fan, they obviously have some type of self worth, self love and confidence about themselves, because that’s what attracts you to me,” said Kamaiyah.

I met up with Kamaiyah in an Alameda photo studio in November to watch her shoot the cover of Ms. Everything with QuakeBeatz. The two were coordinated: both wore black pants, Timbs, white leather jackets, primary-colored Tommy Bogo beanies, and sunglasses. Kamaiyah had on a large chain, stacked bracelets, gold cuffs on her braids, and large gold rings on her fingers.

Every time I saw Kamaiyah, she was typically with the same close-knit group: Quake; Tressie, her makeup artist; LinkUp, her producer, and his wife, Tati; Slimm, her manager; and maybe one or two other people.

That day, she was joined by Slimm, LinkUp, Quake, and a makeup artist (though not her regular one). LinkUp, Kamaiyah’s friend since high school, was the one who originally introduced her to Quake in 2022. During their first studio session, Quake didn’t hesitate to tell Kamaiyah when something didn’t work.
“I’m like, ‘Who the fuck is this?’” Kamaiyah said.
“But it just made me fuck with him because it’s like, Oh, you got your own opinion. You’re a free thinker,” she said.
The two have been locked in ever since.

The cover was being shot by Sydney Welch, whose eye for detail shined as she fixed stray hairs or caught a bead of sweat. While Kamaiyah and Quake posed for photos, Slimm texted a fan on Kamaiyah’s behalf. The fan had commented under a picture of Kamaiyah holding a Coach bear, saying she wanted it, to which Kamaiyah replied, “It’s yours!”

Twenty-year-old Andrea drove from San Leandro to the studio in Alameda. When she arrived, she hesitated at the door, unsure if she should walk in, until Kamaiyah invited her inside. Kamaiyah gave her a hug and handed her the teddy bear. The two snapped a picture together. I followed up with Andrea for a quick conversation. She shared that Kamaiyah’s A Good Night in the Ghetto reminded her of her sister, who would blast the album, and how she would hear it blaring through the walls as her sister got ready for a good night in the ghetto.
“I’m a youngin, like, really trying to get it and hustle and listening to her music makes me feel like I could do it regardless of my circumstances,” said Andrea.

Kamaiyah’s star quality showed in her ability to connect with her fans and make them feel seen. I witnessed it when she performed for a 30-person crowd on top of a small café on Lake Merritt. We witnessed it again when she performed in front of a sold-out crowd with LaRussell at New Parish. Regardless of the size, Kamaiyah performed with precision and strong delivery. Over the five or six times I saw her throughout 2024, she never faltered.

Kamaiyah’s 2016 hit A Good Ghetto Night in the Hood, with tracks like Out the Bottle and Fuck It Up, secured her place in Bay Area party culture, but with this album, she set out to do something different. To do so, she returned to the Bay Area’s laid-back, hard-hitting sound. The whole album moved like a night drive through the Bay with no traffic.
“I feel like there’s no constriction on what I can create. So I need to start playing in that realm, like, you know, every project should sound different and have a different feeling,” Kamaiyah said.

Completely independent, Kamaiyah has big plans for 2025, but she said that if she happens to regress—and not progress as she anticipated—she’s throwing the towel in. I highly doubt that will happen. Whatever she does next, the message is clear: Kamaiyah’s legacy is here to stay.

stories.title: Michael Prince
paragraphs: With a rare free day, Michael packs his backpack for a trip to the San Luis Reservoir. Inside, he carefully places everything he needs: a fishing rod, bait, camera, tripod, laptop, and his violin. The man-made lake is filled with fish, including salmon, striped bass and largemouth black. Setting off down I-5 South toward Merced County, he looks forward to the quiet shores awaiting him.

The air at the reservoir is crisp but comfortable, requiring little more than a hoodie. After a short walk through grass budding with spring life, he finds the perfect spot. Michael unpacks his fishing rod, baits the hook, and casts his line into the water, keeping an eye out for any movement. Next, he sets up his camera and tripod before reaching for his violin.

Usually, Michael would create a quick five-minute beat in his home studio, improvising and layering string recordings to build his sound, but today he was also doing a live recording of his song Finesse, released a few weeks earlier on April 19th. The song begins with a haunting elegance, transforming into a deep, yearning beat that somehow manages to slap—making describing it difficult.

Michael returns back to Vallejo with no fish, but a ton of new content to schedule over the coming weeks and months. Among the footage is the live recording of Finesse, ready to be shared with the world.

At first, the song gains traction slowly, finding its rhythm on TikTok. Then, it happens—Finesse blows up, Captivating everyone from car enthusiasts to the makeup and beauty industry, to celebrities and influencers. The ultimate stamp of approval? Its own viral dance. The song soared to chart in Apple Music's top sounds, rubbing shoulders with Mariah Carey's All I Want for Christmas, and amassed over a billion plays in less than six months.

While Finesse has been a massive success, Michael's career is still in its early stages. Without a lawyer to protect his intellectual property or handle publishing, many have profited off his work without proper compensation. Even well-known athletes have screen-recorded his beats, rapped over them, and then asked for his approval after the fact. Altogether, he’s only grossed a few thousand dollars and most of his money from streaming goes right back into Hood Orchestra.

“It's weird because I really have no idea about the music business, besides what I've learned from LaRussell,” Michael explains. “I assume it's big, but the other producer, Koncept, he has a lawyer and people collecting his publishing. I don't even have mine registered. For streaming, it’s maybe $2,000, but I feel like if I were doing everything correctly, it should be much more.”

Still, Michael remains grateful for the momentum. “This whole situation is like, I just have to be grateful that I just have something going crazy and just use whatever, like publicity and stuff to capitalize outside of the song itself.”

Though Michael had been consistently posting original content three times a day for the past two years, Finesse was the track that put him on the map. By December, when he returned to his hometown of the Third Ward in Houston, Texas, for his second annual Hood Orchestra residency, the buzz around his name was undeniable. It wasn't just his Houston community supporting him—the classical music world was paying attention, with whispers that Michael was the next big thing.

This was just the tip of the iceberg for Michael's whirlwind year—a series of seemingly impossible side quests that would only come with pure talent and luck. (I mean he randomly found himself in a New York jazz bar with Jon Batiste and ASAP Rocky, and on another completely random occasion, joined a massive bike ride with J. Cole)

In addition to these chance encounters, Michael released an astounding 49 projects on streaming alone, including albums, singles and live sessions. He's created multiple documentaries throughout the year that he shared on EVEN, fundraised thousands of dollars for music community centers in Houston, and took on roles as a creative director and consultant for organizations to help their fundraising. His year was a masterclass in creativity, hustle, and making the impossible happen.

When I caught up with Michael in mid-December for a follow-up interview—our first since Hood Orchestra had officially become a 501(c)(3)—he greeted me with unexpected news: “I got cut from Beyoncé's halftime show—they don't need strings anymore.” Even being cut from Beyoncé's show felt like a flex, a testament to how far he'd come. Michael's tone was light, almost amused, as if to say, “Even that's part of the journey.”

Michael's mission to bridge the gap for young people in music had only gained momentum. Fresh off a summer of non-stop touring with LaRussell and T-Pain, he was dedicating his rare days off to a packed December in Houston, filled with concerts, student workshops, master classes, jam sessions, and more.

He walked me through his day-to-day since returning home for the Hood Orchestra residency. Michael's roots were steeped in musical history. He revisited his old high school, the High School for the Performing and Visual Arts, whose alumni include Beyoncé, Robert Glasper, and producer Michael Cox. He attended a fundraiser for the late Theola Booker, a historic Black educator and musician. Through it all, he remained focused on expanding access to music education for students. He went back to his elementary school, to teach a class on improvisation.

“I'm starting to feel older,” Michael admits with a laugh. “I told the kids yesterday I made my first song in 2014, and they were like, ‘Oh, that's the year I was born.’” (Born in 2001, Michael is a Leo.)

During college, Michael took music education classes. While he enjoyed the teaching aspect, he struggled to connect with traditional methods of instruction, often recalling how punitive it felt to be a kid with boundless energy and ideas. He wanted to create a space where students could embrace improvisation and lead their own learning—two elements that were largely absent from his own music education.

Hood Orchestra became his way of offering free music lessons without bearing the financial burden himself. Having witnessed the scarcity of music programs in schools firsthand, Michael was determined to make music education accessible to as many students as possible.

As December comes to a close, Michael is wrapping up the Hood Orchestra concert series. General admission tickets for the final concert are completely sold out, with only a few VIP spots remaining. In between performances, he's filming, teaching, creating content, and, of course, fishing. This time, he heads to the lake armed with a Yamamoto bait—the one that always brought him luck back in college in Oklahoma. Michael casts his line and, at last, walks away with a catch.

stories.title: Sam Opoku
paragraphs: I'm sitting with Sam Opoku at Create Studios in Los Angeles, California in August. The singer and songwriter has just wrapped up his first session with LaRussell, and we're here to talk about his time in the booth, his music, and his background. Originally from West Ghana and now based in Phoenix, Arizona, Opoku first connected with Good Compenny for a Live Session. Since then, he’s performed with Shante in his hometown of Phoenix. Now, he’s in the studio recording with LaRussell, bringing a blend of soulful vocals to complement LaRussell’s ever evolving sound.
Sam says he aims to walk the line between Afrobeats and Frank Ocean, crafting a sound that’s unmistakably his own. His voice, both silky and emotive, instantly moves you.
What did you think when you first heard LaRussell & his music?

Just how dope and fresh and authentic it was. Yeah, it just feels, it feels like him all the way through. So it was something that it reminded me of, something that me and my team want to do, just go out and shoot what feels natural, what he always says is like his life is his content, and it comes through in the music as well. So it’s definitely palpable from top to bottom, and it’s inspiring to say the least.
And this is the first time y’all have hopped in the booth together?
Yes this is the first time, this is the first booth hopping. Yeah.
What is it like to actually be in the energy and the space to create together?

It's dope. It's like because I've experienced it online, experience at the compound. But when it’s like music making time, it’s a whole different energy, because now you're getting to actually create and put it down and watching the process is dope, too. Everybody has their own unique, takes and habits and stuff. So to be in that like, guy, let’s go, let’s move the machine. Energy is, like, It’s infectious. So, yeah, it is super, super dope. It’s inspiring.
Can you tell us a little bit about where you're from and what were your early musical influences, what you were listening to in the house?

I'm from Ghana, West Africa, and I came to the States when I was like eight years old, and I grew up in, a singer environment. But that’s just how our culture is. We have a song for everything. When we're to church or coming back from church and we're about to sleep or about to eat, when you're about to go use the restroom, you got a song for it, you know? So it just naturally fills up the house. A lot of stuff that I was listening to is like hymns and like old blues records and stuff that my dad would play.

And there’s a sound out of West Africa called high life, and it’s the origins of, like, Afro beat and Caribbean and that kind of vibe. And so a lot of that infused into what I was doing, along with in school, I was listening to, like, the oldies, like Ella Fitzgerald and even Frank Sinatra. Right now, I really love singer songwriters like the James Blakes of the world and Bon Iver and those type of people, just people who be like writing, writing, you know, that’s where, my heart and soul is. So as far back as you can remember, anybody who's a writer from the Temptations to Lil Wayne, you know, is an inspiration. So I take a lot of pride in the versatility of being able to jump from a hip hop record into like a soulful ballad into an afro beat. I think that’s the lane that I want to ride down. Whatever Frank Ocean would sound on that Afro pop record. That's, that’s the lane I’m trying to go into.
Do you have a hymn that really resonates with you?
Sam looks at me hesitantly.
You don’t have to if you don’t want to. I would love to hear.

My voice is very quavery, but so it goes like this. It’s very, very simple, but it’s one that we sing for any thankful occasion. And it can be for a wedding or celebration or whatever. And this is in tree, which is my language.
Sam goes on to sing a hymn in his native language, which I, unfortunately, won’t attempt to capture in words.
That was so beautiful. Coming from a culture where it seems like music and life are really intertwined. Do you kind of bring that into your creative process?

That's like every artist's life is meshing the art and the reality of your situations. Yeah, for sure, I’ve had a girl whose favorite color was yellow. I was talking to her for a little bit, and it kind of went south. So I made a song called Yellow. She said her favorite color yellow. And it’s like a therapy session to come to terms with what the color yellow symbolizes. It can be like all these nasty things, or it can be like the sunlight and you know what I’m saying. So bringing those two together really helped as a therapy session. Song called Boomerang of the girl going back and forth to her ex. And those all come from life experiences that only you can write, and it helps you process those moments and get, like a cathartic resolution from so yeah, for sure, life, the imitating art for sure.
What about Good Compenny? Do you really align with or resonate with just as a whole?

I think just the togetherness aspect, like, we're all going to eat together. And so, like, if you don’t have a skill, find a skill. And let’s get you in here thing that’s super dope. A lot of times we look outside for help, but usually it’s right next to us within our own family. So we just got to empower people and build them up to be able to sustain their own piece of the pie. And I feel like that’s something that Good Compenny does really well or emulates well, and it’s something that I want to do with my team as well, you know. So nobody feels like they're being dragged along, but they have, like, a tangible place that they could, like, feed themselves off of.
What can expect from you in the next year or so? What do you got going on?

Yeah, so I’m working on my own EP project. It’s gonna be a four part EP, and we'll tell the story of how I came from Ghana to America, and all the misconceptions I had, finding love, losing love, wanting to go back home, going home, experiencing that. Basically, my life story and a four part EP. So I’m super excited, because I wanted to all connect and be meaningful.
Is there anything I haven’t asked you about that you think we should be paying attention to do?

Yeah, I think you got everything. Just Arizona. Y'all gotta come out to Arizona desert. You’re gonna fry up, but it’s but it’s fire out there. Literally, the people are dope. The music scene is slowly growing, and they need to see more authentic, like artists out there that they can, like, latch on to and support. So, yeah, come out to Phoenix.

stories.title: Tiny Desk
paragraphs: LaRussell’s Tiny Desk performance, released on November 8, was a watershed moment—not just for him, but for everyone involved.
The morning the performance dropped, my Instagram feed was flooded dozens of clips and countless celebratory posts.
P-Lo was posting about “Give Me a Beat.”
Link-Up was posting about “TEST YA NUTS.”
Vince was showcasing the custom jacket LaRussell wore.
Each artist highlighted the section where they shined.
Ariel shared her styling everyone (except Simon),
and I shared Good Compenny Magazine going up on the wall to join the greats. Even the woman featured in the background of the magazine was posting about it.

I could have gone on. That was the beauty of the moment—a firm example of the kind of impact LaRussell had. He had built a community so deeply interwoven with his journey that his wins felt like our wins. And in many ways, they were. Good Compenny was a win for the Bay Area, for hip-hop, for entrepreneurs, for Black people—and each milestone represented so much more than a single moment.

The iconic Tiny Desk setup exists within an otherwise ordinary space. The NPR building in Washington, D.C., greets visitors with massive electronic news headlines running overhead the elevator entrance. As I made my way upstairs, I noticed most floors were practically empty—rows of cubicles left unattended as many staffers worked from home.

The NPR Music floor resembled a typical office, aside from the obvious star of the show: the Tiny Desk set. Its backdrop—a set of bookshelves adorned with music history—featured treasures like Mac Miller’s hat, Kehlani’s keffiyeh, and countless other artifacts of artistry. There was everything from sticky notes, to flashdrives, to signed setlists.

Everyone from the Good Compenny team was giddy with excitement. As we settled in and the production team adjusted cameras and tested the lighting, LaRussell sat cross-legged, palms pressed together—possibly meditating or praying.

Soon it was time to get everyone into position, the production team worked to squeeze the stacked lineup into the small space. The arrangement stretched left to right: Tione on saxophone, Jimmy Toor on flute (his second Tiny Desk!), Michael Prince on violin, Simon and Claydough on piano, Harry on guitar, Tietta delivering spoken word, Malachi rapping, Shante on vocals, and Splash—well, doing Splash. LaRussell sat front and center on a stool, with mic stand in front of him.

This performance forced a shift in style for LaRussell. Unlike his usual shows, where he improvised and went with how he felt in the moment, this one required a strict setlist and had a time limit. Simon assisted with the production side of it.

During rehearsal, the production crew seemed confused by Splash’s role, which involved shaking his dreads, smeezing, popping collars, ripping off his jacket, and occasionally stepping too far to the left—right in front of Claydough. Glances were exchanged as if to ask whether Splash was really supposed to be in the shot, especially given the space constraints. When it became clear this wasn’t a joke, they asked what his role should be listed as (it ended up being “vocals,” though “irreplaceable hype man” would’ve been more accurate).

After a short rehearsal, the team waited in a small room as a crowd formed around the set. Before the show everyone danced, laughed, and made last-minute outfit changes. It felt like a celebration—a mix of pure love, gratitude, and excitement, the kind you’d find at a baby shower or wedding. Then, it was showtime.
The set opened with Glory/Do That Lil Dance, two unforgettable songs. Do that Lil Dance paid homage to our ancestors with solemn storytelling. Claydough and Simon’s keys set the foundation to set.

“Made it off cotton fields, now we on Tiny Desk,” LaRussell rapped, grounding the moment in a powerful reflection. The song, released in 2022, felt timeless, a eulogy and celebration for the lives unjustly sacrificed for us to be here today.

The performance then shifted quickly into Give Me a Beat, a hyphy anthem and Bay Area love letter. Strong chords carried the energy, matched by sharp notes from Jimmy and Tione’s wind instruments and Michael’s violin, instantly making you want to smeeze and throw on your thizz face.

The set then transitioned into Caught Up in My Head, a soulful country track where Harry’s guitar playing truly shined. LaRussell sang about longing and life on the road, with the crowd responding in snaps and sways.
Before the next song, LaRussell addressed the audience:
“I’m here to keep it [rap] as pure as possible.”

Malachi’s Hood Cry, released in 2021, followed. It’s a story about grief, gun violence, and aspiration. Shante’s silky vocals eased the transition into LaRussell’s Perfect, continuing the themes of survival and generational trauma.
Tietta’s spoken word performance was next—a heartfelt reflection on her journey and a comforting message to herself.

The tempo then picked up with 10s 20s, What We Doin, and Test Ya Nuts. Instruments accelerated, chords grew more intense, wind instruments sharpened, and Michael’s violin plucks became brisk and urgent.

The concert concluded with When I Come Home, a reflection on LaRussell’s early days as a young artist balancing a 9-to-5 job and big dreams. The song seamlessly blended into GT Coupe, a Good Compenny classic representing a different era—smaller concerts, a different team, but the same unshakable goal. The set ended with LaRussell almost whispering the final line:
“Bitch, it ain’t over till it’s over.”

All six stories are now in the chat, separated by title, without magazine metadata. I preserved the source wording as closely as possible, while correcting apparent text-recognition errors such as | appearing in place of I. Because the PDF contains image-based text, I recommend comparing the transcriptions against the original pages before publishing.

stories.title: According to Avery
paragraphs: How Avery went from rapping at the Pergola to landing multiple LaRussell features, creating her own hyphy anthem, launching merch, and building her own lane, all before turning ten.

In March, I arrived at Rink Studios in Sacramento, California, for LaRussell’s show. The whole team was already there: LaRussell, Tietta, Jacob, Jason, and The Yee Section. Close behind Tietta was Avery, barely reaching her hip. I followed them into the green room.

A photographer walked in, introduced herself to LaRussell, and let him know she’d be taking photos. But the moment she spotted Avery, her jaw dropped. She dropped to her knees and started bowing, like Avery was royalty.
“Is this Avery?” she exclaimed.
“Well damn, say hi to everyone else,” LaRussell laughed.
The photographer quickly greeted the rest of the room. But reactions like that had become Avery’s new normal. Bay Area legends were introducing themselves to her.
This was the Avery effect.

Later that day, when Avery hit the stage to perform “We Be Hyphy,” the crowd erupted. Adults were rapping her lyrics word for word, holding up four fingers during her verse: “Four plus four, I know I ate!” Even I had been corrected on her lyrics by young adults who knew every bar.

The song itself was lyrically packed, from jumping off cliffs with Dre, to eating at Momo’s, to shouting out the girly pops, Avery told a full hyphy anthem from her perspective. The authenticity is what makes people, young and old, slap her music.
“It’s crazy,” she said, “because I thought only kids would know my stuff. But it’s wild how adults know it, and not just know it, they enjoy it. Like, they really enjoy it too.”

Last year, at the April 2024 Pergola Show, LaRussell made his usual call to the crowd: “Who wants to sing their favorite song?” You never knew what to expect. Some folks shrank back, shaking their heads. Others had to be coaxed onto the stage, while a few jumped up without hesitation. The stage became a mix of high-pitched screams, surprise renditions, and the occasional shockingly good performance.
Then 8-year-old Avery stepped up.

Wearing a red pullover, jeans, and a headband, she confidently grabbed the mic and requested “Hyphy 2020,” a long-time favorite in her household. Her parents stood front row as Avery climbed up on a speaker, moved her shoulders, grabbed her collar and nearly broke into a thizz face.
“Wow,” she said, rocking back and forth, eyes locked on the crowd.
“Wow,” she repeated, this time with even more focus.
The look on her face said it all, she meant business.
“Make some room, I’m a whole to take in,” she rapped, and the crowd erupted.

Over the next two minutes, Avery stole the entire show. It wasn’t just that she knew the words, it was her flawless delivery, her energy, her stage presence, and her confidence that left every single person stunned. The crowd went wild.

In the days that followed, LaRussell posted a recap on Instagram. The video went viral, amassing nearly 4 million views, 238k likes, 70,000 shares, and landing Avery a live session spot on LaRussell’s Spotify. The comments flooded in: fire emojis, love, encouragement, and, of course, the occasional hater.
Since then, Avery’s role in Good Compenny has grown exponentially.

She released her latest track “We Be Hyphy,” complete with a full visualizer. She attended her first influencer event at Foot Locker during NBA All Star Weekend, performed at E.L.I.T.E. Public Schools, and has become a regular member of Good Compenny.
People have even started bringing their kids to LaRussell, hoping they’ll have the same breakout moment Avery did. But as LaRussell shared in a passing conversation,
“I never chose Avery. She was chosen.”
It was happenstance at best. Her path was carved by the opportunity meeting the moment.
Now, Avery and her parents are at nearly every Good Compenny event. Recently, she joined Tietta on stage during House Rules, always announcing Rule #3: “Have fun!”
She’s interviewing artists, Good Compenny and beyond, on her own platform. She even hit the airwaves on 94.9 to share more about her story.
And the truth is, she’s just getting started.
“Honestly, it was crazy. I didn’t think I’d be able to do this,” said Avery.

Inspired by LaRussell and supported every step of the way by her parents, who are never more than a few feet behind her, Avery has been able to explore multiple creative paths, from interviewing your favorite artists to making music of her own.
Early on, her parents recognized that Avery didn’t just want to be a rapper, and they knew better than to box her in. It was clear: she was too talented to be limited to just one thing.

Every day, Avery’s stage presence grows sharper. She doesn’t just rap, she dances, controls her voice, stays on beat, and delivers her verses with breath and power, taking the crowd along for the ride. And by her side are her fellow GC kids, not just her peers, but her biggest supporters, rapping along to her lyrics like they wrote them themselves.
Now, Avery is part of a new wave of young kids leading their own hyphy movement, one rooted in a kid-friendly way to party.
Avery is proof of what’s possible when you give young people the tools to shine. She’s showing other kids that the sky isn’t the limit, it’s just the beginning.

stories.title: All Star Weekend 2025: Splitting the Pie, a Recipe That Never Fails
paragraphs: All-Star Weekend not only celebrated the legacy of basketball, but also its intersection with fashion, entertainment, music, and most importantly, the Bay Area. Before the weekend kicked off, Tietta sent out a meticulously crafted schedule that spanned from Wednesday to Sunday. The schedule itself took nearly ten hours to create, after revisions, without factoring in the time spent planning the actual event. It’s hard to grasp the sheer number of hours that go into producing an event like All-Star Weekend. Across the Bay Area, there were hundreds of installations, ranging from major sports brands to podcasts, and parties sponsored by nearly every brand under the sun. There was an undeniable sense of excitement leading into the weekend, but also a tinge of anxiety. With such a packed schedule, one mistake or delay could impact the rest of the events.

LaRussell is known for “splitting the pie.” He’s just as recognized for being an individual as he is for leading a team that stands out among the rest. It’s the professionalism, efficiency, and high standards upheld by Good Compenny that earned them the reputation. Maintaining that reputation required constant effort, and it was something none of us forgot, especially that weekend. With so many opportunities packed into the event, LaRussell had the chance to bring more people than ever to experience it. All-Star Weekend was about ensuring that everyone had a chance to shine, both on and off the court.
FCTRY LAB

All-Star Weekend kicked off with a business meeting in San Francisco to connect with the owners of FCTRY LAB. Good Compenny arrived in a sprinter van at an apartment near the Embarcadero. As we all piled in through the doors, the owner of the house remarked that he wasn’t expecting this many people. Everyone found a spot, whether sprawled out on the floor, sitting on a chair, or securing a lucky spot on the couch.

FCTRY LAB had worked with Kanye and YEEZY in the past, and more recently with NLE Choppa on his duck boot. LaRussell loved the idea of creating his first shoe, one that everyone would recognize and that could become a staple. They previewed the shoe during a slideshow: a foam shoe in several colorways, which the whole team loved. But once the first few price points were thrown out, the conversation took a turn.

“If there are four people in their family, that’ll cost almost a thousand dollars.” The quick math made LaRussell realize that an average family from Vallejo, who grew up like him, wouldn’t be able to afford it.

LaRussell went back and forth, exchanging ideas with FCTRY LAB, who traditionally made more expensive items, to come up with something that was both accessible and cool. LaRussell continued to emphasize that he wasn’t focused on short-term profit and loss. He was willing to invest more capital upfront if it helped make the project work on their end. The main goal was for every kid who looked up to him to be able to afford to look like him. This was one of LaRussell’s superpowers, he was able to think quickly in the short term and take action, while always keeping a long-term vision in mind. After a brief debate, both teams agreed that they could make something work. What that looks like, you’ll have to stay tuned to find out.
Rich Paul Panel With Klutch & E.L.I.T.E. Students

Next, we headed over to Union Square Shoe Palace for a panel conversation with Rich Paul, creator of the brand Klutch and sports agent to some of the biggest names in entertainment, including LeBron James, Anthony Davis, and Draymond Green. But instead of the usual room filled with influencers and sports fans, the space was packed with high school students from E.L.I.T.E Public Schools, the school based in Vallejo that LaRussell’s daughter also attended. The students were all gifted clothes with the signature black and yellow Klutch colorway and had been invited by LaRussell for a chance to soak up some free game from both him and Rich Paul. When asked about LaRussell’s invitation, Rich Paul said it was a no-brainer, when LaRussell wanted to bring the young people with him. The students took full advantage of the opportunity, asking questions about navigating life after graduation, Rich Paul’s unconventional career path, and hearing insights from leading sports journalist Malika Andrews, who is from Oakland. LaRussell reminded the group that when he was their age, opportunities like this simply didn’t exist.
NBA All Star Rising Game

The next stop on his NBA All-Star Game tour was the All-Star Rising Stars Game, where LaRussell didn’t just bring Simon and Michael to perform, he also brought a full lineup of dancers from across the country, including Diva, June, Storm DeBarge, Hurricane, and Lex. The 60-second performance highlighted national talent, bringing hip-hop culture from the Bay Area, the South, and the East Coast, all while staying rooted in the Bay Area.
Marshawn Lynch x Jordan Jam Event in Alameda

The trend of splitting the pie continued with the Marshawn Lynch x Jordan event, held at the typically empty Alameda hangars. A massive Jordan installation was built, with a huge stage in the middle and light beams coming down from every angle. The Jordan Jam event reminded me of Kendrick Lamar’s pop-out, and the lineup was absolutely stacked. The preshow included a dance battle featuring the Turf Feinz, and the main event had a once-in-a-lifetime lineup, including LaRussell, Kehlani, Mistah F.A.B., Larry June, 2Chainz, Seiji Oda, Quavo and more. The crowd was by far the most star-studded event we attended. It was a mix of athletes, influencers, rappers, Bay Area locals and singers. It was a moment to showcase Bay Area talent to a crowd that likely wouldn’t have made it out to the Bay otherwise.

LaRussell didn’t just perform; he brought the full Yee Section, made up of Jimmy, Simon, Claydough, Tione, Michael, Geo, and Harry, who played not only for him but for most of the show, backing a range of artists. LaRussell also took control of the show, at Marshawn’s request, orchestrating artists as they transitioned on and off the stage.

That’s one thing I’ve always admired about LaRussell, his unwavering standard for the way he performed. It often came down to the smallest details that were glaringly obvious to him and the instrumentalists but largely unnoticed by the crowd. Despite this, LaRussell was meticulous with the sound and the run of the show. Instead of focusing only on his own set or his team, he made sure those standards were applied to the entire event, from start to finish. It was another way LaRussell ensured no one was left behind.

There was a moment during the show when I looked to my right and saw the long stage that allowed the Yee Section to comfortably perform, something rare, as the big ensemble typically had to fit in wherever they could. On stage across from them was Mistah F.A.B., Seiji Oda, Michael Sneed, LaRussell, Tietta, Jason, Marshawn Lynch, and many more. It was a surreal moment to witness the talent, past, present, and future, being captured, all at a magnitude we rarely saw.

This came at a particularly important time for the Bay Area. Too often, the region has been faced with stigma from outsiders. The media frequently paints the Bay Area as run-down, dangerous, and practically unlivable. When I tell people where I’m from, their faces shift, they grimace, offer an apology, and reference the city’s “current state.” I find myself caught between defending my home and acknowledging the complexities of the truth. But for those of us who call the Bay home, there’s also a collective hope, that this moment wouldn’t reinforce the negative narratives that have long overshadowed our city. And the weekend delivered.
Steph Curry Court of Gold Brunch

To close out the week, LaRussell headlined at Steph Curry’s Court of Gold event at Club Thirty at the Chase Center. He brought along The Yee Section, as well as the CO-LLAB Choir, a powerhouse collective of singers based in Oakland.

LaRussell barely took up any time performing his own music during his set. Instead, he spent the time celebrating the other artists in attendance. He orchestrated an impromptu performance, pulling up Money B from Digital Underground to perform “I Get Around,” followed by P-Lo for Put Me On Somethin’, then Mistah F.A.B. for New Oakland, Richie Rich for I Got 5 on It, Saweetie for Tap In, and finally, the peak: Too Short stepping up for Blow the Whistle.

Steph Curry and Matt Barnes were posted on the wall, screaming Too Short’s infamous “Biiiitch!” ad-libs. The crowd of mainly industry folk were filled with thizz faces, the energy hyphy asf and very Bay Area. The kids were dancing, the whole stage was moving and it was another example of LaRussell’s mastery that showcased the lineage of hip-hop.

The effort it took to coordinate this weekend was unfathomable. Tietta’s attention to detail and planning skills were more important than ever and truly reflected her greatness. LaRussell’s work ethic also shone through. While it’s not something many question, it’s hard to comprehend unless you’re in his position, one very few people occupy. Mornings started at 6 AM and ended at 4 AM. While artists and people like myself could come later, leave earlier, or sneak off for lunch, LaRussell not only had to remain present, but constantly performed with a beaming smile, ready to interact with eager fans. Along the way, he also maintained a relentless pursuit of bringing in every person possible. That’s the true superpower.

stories.title: CO-LLAB Choir
paragraphs: “So much of music is philosophical and spiritual, especially with the voice, in particular, because the voice is inside your body. It has everything to do with how you think about yourself, how do you take care of yourself? How do you love yourself? How do you show up for yourself?”
— Cava, CO-LLAB Founder

LaRussell has been doing shows at the Empress Theatre for years now. And every time, the team grows bigger: more merch, more instrumentalists, more keys, more DJs. Just when I thought I had seen every iteration of the Good Compenny ensemble, I walked through the hallways of the Empress Theatre and saw a full choir onstage.

After soundcheck, seven members of CO-LLAB choir were huddled in the second green room, scattered between the floor, vanity, stools and the occasional chair, waiting for showtime. They hadn’t had much time to practice, and this would be their first show with LaRussell, the 2025 Empress series. The energy in the room was high, full of nerves, excitement, and joy. LaRussell had found the choir through Rexx Life Raj and Rob Woods and reached out to invite them to rehearse with him. Now, they’re at their first show.
“His energy is just so good and so refreshing,” said choir director Cava.
“Contagious!” another member chimed in.
Now, it was time to see how their voices would elevate his sound live.

When the show began, the choir staggered into two rows. Cava stands angled, facing toward the group, back turned to the crowd, guiding them with subtle, and not-so-subtle, cues: dropping down to signal a volume dip, widening her eyes for intensity, her hands moving with the pace of the song. What might go unnoticed to the audience is just how much she’s communicating with her eyes, and how attuned the choir members are, constantly reading one another for tiny inclinations that tell them to adjust here or there.

There’s an indescribable emotion that comes over you when more than a dozen voices converge at a single moment. Especially when it’s on the iconic background vocals of Overnight Celebrity, their harmonies rising and falling like hip-hop angles behind Twista’s rapid-fire delivery.
“We’re, like, painting with sound in the sky,” Cava says.

The CO-LLAB Choir was founded in 2022 by Cava, an Oakland-based teacher, director, painter, singer, pianist, and more. As a teacher at Oakland School for the Arts, many choir members are her former students. And while not all are from Oakland, their hub is there. The choir is made up of people from different backgrounds, some classically trained, others self-taught. What mattered most wasn’t their resume, it was what they brought to the group: authenticity, community, and voice.
“I look for heart first,” Cava said. “What is your heart like? Do you sing from your heart? Do you understand what it means to express music from this place that’s bigger than all of us?”
Their heart was matched by an undeniable Bay Area flare, a rhythm, a bounce, an attitude that came from being rooted in the soil.
“There’s a really unique vibration in Oakland that I don’t think exists in a lot of other places. It’s very authentic, very concentrated talent, gifts that are just here,” said choir member Zoe.

The Empress show quickly turned into many shows, including the Pergola, All Star Weekend and Sunday Service, with their sound evolving every time. Each performance became an opportunity to learn. While Cava is used to performing with a set list and a consistent band, LaRussell’s shows are entirely improvised. The songs they rehearse might not get played. The band lineup might change night to night. The result?
CAVA: “We’re getting stronger. We’re getting tighter. The rapport between everybody, it’s building confidence, for sure. It’s building our joy as a group. And I think it’s building our flexibility.”

ZOE: “It’s an artist’s dream culture. I feel like we all have this innate design, this authentic sound or pattern to each other. And when you have the space to just freely flow, that’s an artist’s dream. That’s where the divine lives. That’s where the magic is made, in the moment. The more present you are, the more you trust in your skills.”
B DEVEAUX: “That’s where the real fire is. The real magic of music, just having people in the audience, and feeling it as it happens.”

CANDACE GOODWIN: “To be able to improvise, especially as a choir, it’s one thing to do that as an individual artist, but when we can do that together as a collective? It’s really beautiful. It’s cool.”

SKYLR: “It’s sharpening, too. Sometimes something just gets thrown on the setlist and we have to catch it. We haven’t rehearsed it together, and we’ve got to come up with parts on the fly. It’s cool, it makes us better artists.”

Cava agrees. The improvisational nature of the shows keeps her on her toes as a director, and pushes her to grow as an artist. As a pianist, she also gets to learn from Clay and Simon, whom she described as symbiotic twins, seamlessly in sync.

Their process of preparing for LaRussell shows begun with listening, simply absorbing the music. Then comes the mapping: where do harmonies make sense? Where can vocal textures elevate the sound? Some songs are filled with layered harmonies; others just double the lead.

Once the arrangement takes shape, the fine-tuning begins. For CO-LLAB, this process happens over weeks of trial and discovery. They work on blending voices, playing with inflections and intonations to convey emotion. They navigate highs and lows, bounce and feel, tone and delivery, all the subtle choices that shape a song’s final form.
Ideas fly:
“Add a soprano here.”
“What if we echoed this line?”
Piece by piece, it comes together.
The finished product is a reflection of deep teamwork, each member offering what another lacks, and vice versa.
“It’s work,” Cava says, “but it’s joyful work. Fun work. I feel like it’s strengthening us as a group, and just building our relationship with him, it’s been so beautiful.”

The choir has become more than a space to sharpen artistic talent, it’s been a refuge. Often described as a family, the collective offers a creative hub where people from all walks of life can feel safe, seen, and free to share.

“These are kind of hard times to be alive,” said B DeVeaux. “A lot of people are struggling. Folks need healing. Folks need ways to feel and speak about things when there’s not even the right language to hold what we’re going through. And for us, this space has been a healing thing, just the ability to come together.”

The group supports each other both inside and outside of choir, collaborating on projects, forming deep bonds, and tending to each other’s spiritual and creative well-being. Members are deeply multifaceted, covering everything from design and visual art to music production and education.

Zoe spoke openly about what CO-LLAB has meant to them, especially in contrast to the space they left behind. After moving to L.A. to pursue what they thought was an artist’s dream, a production company offering in-house videographers, photographers, engineers, and a state-of-the-art studio, they quickly realized the reality was very different. What was pitched as a creative haven turned out to be a system of abuse. After leaving, Zoe came to understand that the environment was a cult, one in which she experienced multiple forms of abuse.

Joining CO-LLAB Choir was a turning point. It gave them a chance to rewrite their relationship with music and rediscover the joy in their art. It allowed them to remember the goodness still present in the world, even as they continued healing from her past.
“It’s not about what happens to you,” Zoe said. “It’s about how you handle it, how you heal from it, how you unpack it. Life continues, and it’s beautiful.”

stories.title: Empress Theatre
paragraphs: Throughout January and February, LaRussell hosted The Empress Theatre Residency, bringing hundreds of people to Vallejo to celebrate music, comedy, and the Bay. The Empress Theatre, with its red and gold interior and towering ceilings adorned with sculpted swirls, has long held a special place in LaRussell’s heart. One of his first major shows was thrown there, and he’s returned every year since. In October 2022, he celebrated his birthday at the Empress, bringing out artists like DaBoii and Mistah F.A.B. Now, he’s returned once again with a fresh lineup of special guests.

Every time I walked into the Empress, it felt familiar, but in true LaRussell fashion, he continues to expand the boundaries of his craft. This time, alongside the usual band setup, there was a harp and a full choir in rehearsal. The Co-LLAB Choir, an Oakland-based collective led by Cava (who is also music teacher in Oakland), joined the ensemble for a three-show run, with nearly a dozen singers rotating in and out.

The addition of the choir and harp brought another layer to LaRussell’s ever-evolving sound. The harp was soft, at times barely audible, but when its notes floated through the air, they were unforgettable. The choir was ethereal. Their voices elevated every moment, from offering ad-libs between verses to taking over the chorus entirely. It was an experience that lingered, pushing the audience’s expectations of what hip-hop performances could be.
Each show had its own standout moments.

Twista took the stage and performed “Overnight Celebrity,” with the Co-LLAB Choir singing the signature vocals. Their voices rose and fell like angels weaving through Twista’s rapid-fire delivery, it was a beautiful collision of grit and grace.

Comedian and actor Ron Funches flew in from Los Angeles to perform short comedy skits between songs. His humor was topical, slightly self-deprecating, and effortlessly lighthearted. He had the crowd in dying laughing, riffing on the struggle of resisting CRUMBL cookies, the hardships faced by actors during wildfire season, and even poking fun at LaRussell’s line “1.5 off rappin,” with a playful, “Hey, you’ll get there one day.”

Rexx Life Raj also blessed the stage, performing some of LaRussell’s favorite songs. His set was raw and introspective, each lyric offering a glimpse into his life. The vulnerability in his performance felt deeply personal, like the kind of music that had once walked LaRussell through pivotal chapters of his own journey.

Bay Area legends B-Legit and Spice-1 closed out a night with the classic “City to City.” The moment was unforgettable, a reminder that LaRussell isn’t just building something new, but honoring what came before him. He curated a show that paid homage to hip hop’s roots, spotlighted emerging talent, and still managed to shine in his own right.

The audience got to witness Avery perform “We Be Hyphy,” Tietta share a powerful piece of spoken word, and Diva show off her dancing skills. Throughout the night, there were countless moments where kids and other community members joined LaRussell on stage to speak about their experiences being part of Good Compenny. Malachi also took the mic, continuing to wow the crowd with his soulful vocals.

With each show, the collective grew stronger. The Co-LLAB Choir became more confident, finding their rhythm between songs and learning more of LaRussell’s music week by week. Geo quickly became woven into the fabric of Good Compenny, and alongside her, artists like Simon and Clay found creative ways to bring the harp into focus, letting its subtle beauty shine through the larger sound of the group.

There was something special about coming back to the Empress and seeing the same faces in the crowd, alongside new ones drawn in by the magic. Although this may be the last show at the venue (due to differences with management), the Empress will forever be a snapshot of LaRussell’s rise and the community that rose with him.

stories.title: Geo and the Hyphy Harp
paragraphs: The past three months for Geo have consisted of backyard shows, concerts, All-Star Weekend, studio sessions, 16-hour drives, national anthems, and countless fangirl moments. Signing up for LLCs and toting her harp across festival stages in the Los Angeles heat. Joining sold-out sets and sorting through endless DMs, all while her supporters grow.

In the middle of January, Geo showed up for a soundcheck and audition, but she didn’t know that. After passing the first of unannounced auditions, she was invited to play the concert. I remember that first show, Twista was performing and Geo kept looking to Harry for the keys to different songs. Harry didn’t look especially sure either. Still, the harp added something elegant and ethereal to the set, something that couldn’t be replicated. From that moment on, she was in.

She was quickly inducted into the legendary Yee Section. What started as quiet glances of reassurance while performing turned into effortless stage presence within weeks. The Bay Area music community was catching on too, artists, labels, and creatives alike were paying close attention to what Geo was creating.

By the time this magazine comes out, she’ll be at 20k followers on Instagram. Since meeting Geo, we’ve had countless conversations where she’ll exclaim, “I’m just being myself! I’ve never felt more myself!” a response to the continuous wave of opportunities that keep coming. The best part is knowing that the world is discovering and falling in love with someone who shows up as their full, authentic self.

Through meeting her friends and family, you feel the synergy among the people closest to her. She once told me how much she loved mixing friend groups, how they all got along. I (resident pessimist) doubted this. But after meeting her friends from all parts of her life, I got it. Geo has a spirit that attracts people who are very “come as you are.” And her greatest gift is her ability to share her talent with the world and reflect what’s possible when you show up fully as yourself.

stories.title: June
paragraphs: Back in the Bay, June is planting roots and building the future he’s been dreaming of, right at home.

June grew up in Richmond, California, spending much of his childhood immersed in basketball and enjoying the quiet comfort of solitude. Naturally shy, he poured most of his energy into sports. In seventh grade, he made his first appearance in a film. His older brother had developed a passion for YouTube skits and acting, transforming their dad’s Afrocentric store in Oakland, filled with incense, African art, candles, and other cultural treasures, into a makeshift set. June, not one for the spotlight, agreed to be an extra, sitting in the background with a newspaper covering his face as the camera focused on his brother.

Throughout middle and high school, June stuck to a strict routine: school, practice, homework, sleep, repeat. But as senior year approached, he realized basketball couldn’t be the only path forward, so he began exploring new interests. At Berkeley High, he’d always enjoyed drawing and being creative, though he wasn’t yet sure where it would lead.

After graduation, June took the energy and discipline he had developed through basketball and funneled it into dance. He studied videos, recorded and critiqued himself, then tried again. Soon, he was sharing videos on Snapchat, and his friends encouraged him to keep going.

That period also marked a turning point. He began stepping out of his comfort zone, attending parties, performing in front of larger crowds, and engaging more socially. He even started the “Tiny Glasses Gang,” where he’d pass around tiny frames at parties, and whoever wore them had to dance. It was June’s way of bringing something different to the party.

During that time, he met a photographer who taught him the basics of content creation, filming skits, incorporating dance, building narratives, and scheduling posts. He jumped on dance trends like the Milly Rock and Harlem Shake, broadening his reach. About a year into consistent filming, June posted a skit from the UC Berkeley parking garage about being from the Bay but wishing he were in New York. He went to bed with 2,000 followers and woke up with 11,000. Complex shared the video, celebrities began reaching out, and June realized this could be more than just a hobby.

One of his most viral moments came with the creation of the “June Bug Challenge.” The video took off, with some of his favorite celebrities joining in. Brand partnerships followed, and suddenly, content creation became a full-time career, even before there was a clear name for it.

Now with over 600K followers, June reflects on how far he’s come. Seventh-grade June couldn’t have imagined building a whole career around being on camera and performing on some of the biggest stages in the world. Most recently, he performed with LaRussell and a group of dancers at the NBA All-Star Rising Stars Game in the Bay Area. Basketball was his first love, he never imagined he’d still end up on the court, just in a different way.

Earlier in the year, June made the decision to move back to the Bay. After nearly a decade of creating content, he was ready to think about what’s next. LaRussell’s work in Vallejo inspired him to consider how he could give back to his own city.
“He’s doing things for his community in Vallejo, and I look at that and think, okay, what can I do for my city in Richmond?” said June.

Last summer, LaRussell invited June to the V to shoot some visualizers. The collaboration came naturally, and it reminded June of what’s possible when you create from home. Tired of being mistaken for being from LA or New York, June felt called to come home to the Bay.

Now, he’s back in the Bay and focused on what’s next. He’s interested in directing, knows he’s a great marketer, and wants to spend more time at his local community center. He’s also committed to building alongside Good Compenny, staying grounded in the place that raised him.

stories.title: Rent Paid
paragraphs: LaRussell returns to Los Angeles for his second album with Hit-Boy.

The hallway leading to Hit-Boy’s studio is lined with silver, gold, and platinum plaques, a testament to the decades of talent that have passed through the building. At the end of the hallway is a door with a ring camera attached. As I pass through the door, I’m immediately immersed in Hit-Boy’s legacy. Grammys are casually stacked on top of each other (one adorned with a VIP Baby Shark lanyard), a Racks in the Middle plaque hung prominently on the wall, and shelves showcase everything from a Magic Johnson Pop doll to Bape stuffed animals.

Hit-Boy was having another standout year. His production on Beyoncé’s Texas Hold ’Em hit #1, making her the first Black woman to top the Hot 100 with a country song, according to Billboard. Now, he and LaRussell had joined forces again for Rent Paid, the much-anticipated sequel to their first album, and with it came many unexpected guests.

The studio is packed. Everyone from Good Compenny, Tietta, Jason, LaRussell, Splash, Mike G., Malachi, Michael, and Vince, squeezed into every available corner. At the front, Bosnian engineer Davis Strauss, who also engineered Rent Due, worked behind a large monitor. Hit-Boy floated in and out, in straight-back braids and a plain white T-shirt. To the left of Strauss was LeftyGunPlay.

LaRussell’s process in the studio is always the same: catch the beat, write for a few minutes, 20 at the absolute most, and record the song. Malachi would step in next, with a process very closely parallel to LaRussell’s, sometimes even faster. Michael would go in after and add strings, and the entire track came together nearly seamlessly and pretty quickly.

Now, at Hit-Boy’s studio, the routine was no different. LaRussell laid down his verse in just one or two takes. Malachi followed, replicating his efficiency. Then it was LeftyGunPlay’s turn, shirtless, wearing a blue beanie, covered head to toe in tattoos, and clutching a Styrofoam cup, pen, and yellow pad of paper. Instantly, Lefty brought a chaotic and captivating energy to the mic. Draped in gold chains, he wrote and rewrote his lyrics on the fly, swapping out words as he said them out loud to himself, and chucking them out just as quickly. He was borderline self-deprecating at times, saying to himself, “Nah, that’s not it,” before diving back in, occasionally seeking feedback from his girl friend.

I hadn’t known of LeftyGunPlay before this session (it was months before Kendrick Lamar’s GNX album featuring “TV Off” would dominate the airwaves and the Grammys and climb the charts again). At first, I was hesitant about how his sound would mesh with LaRussell and Malachi’s. Lefty was far from a family-friendly artist, he self identified as a gangbanger. While Malachi talked about cracking crab legs and U.N.K., Lefty’s verses had gunshots in the background and as he spoke candidly about his life in the streets of L.A.
But the first thing that won me over was his avoidance of the N-word (which I had braced for and see too often unquestioningly adopted by non-Black POC communities). This quickly disarmed me.

The next thing that made me a fan was his process. Though chaotic, it was mesmerizing, his voice was a blend of enunciated mumbles and rolling rhythms. His words stacked like uneven, smooth stone towers that people make in rushing rivers. Through trial and error, throwing out and re-recording words and phrases, his lyrics began to find their center, and the verse took shape. He tried things that often left the room laughing. Whatever came to his head, he brought to the room, and nine out of ten times, it was pretty fucking hilarious.
After Lefty recorded his verse, it was time for Michael to add strings. The room fell silent, which was typical when Michael played, it was always deeply moving.
LeftyGunPlay broke the silence with a laugh:
“He’s gonna steal my girl, foo! He’s gonna steal my girl with that violin.”
We all cracked up, but Michael didn’t respond, though there may have been a slight smirk.

I couldn’t help but reflect on the contrast between the session we had just left, when Sam Opoku closed it with a traditional African hymn, and now, creating music with LeftyGunPlay in Hit-Boy’s studio. It was a session born out of pure happenstance, a scheduling overlap that brought LaRussell and Lefty together.
But that’s the beauty of music: unexpected collaborations that just work.

stories.title: Sausee: From BART to the Big Stage
paragraphs: “I dance my heart and soul out. And I have fun. I enjoy life, and I just love to create.”

In 2015, Sausee was in his early 20s, taking BART from Richmond to Oakland for work. After a long ride, he finally arrived, only to find out he’d been taken off the schedule. So, he got right back on the BART and headed home.

He hadn’t been particularly attached to that job, or the ones before it. Something always went wrong. Either he got fired, or something happened. On the ride back, he ran into a friend and fellow dancer on the BART who was performing and asked him, “Why don’t you just dance?”

He wasn’t working anyway, so why not make some money and have fun? It had been years since he really danced, but it had always been a part of him for as long as he could remember. Still, after high school, he’d tried to take a more traditional route: college, a steady job, the “safe” thing. But that day, something clicked.
He couldn’t think of a good reason not to dance.

Like no time had passed, the passion came back instantly. It felt easy. Natural. And better yet, there was money in it. A lightbulb went off. The 9-to-5s weren’t working, but maybe this could. Maybe this was his shot to do something he truly loved, and make it work.

So, Sausee started dancing on BART more regularly. At first, it was just to make ends meet. But the more he did it, the more his passion grew. He found himself quickly immersed in the culture he’d loved since he was a kid. On top of that, his warm inviting spirit allowed him to connect with people from all different walks of life on the BART.
That moment became even more important in 2018, when Sausee became a father. His daughter was born visually impaired.
“Once I had her, I was like, forget this. I’m gonna dance or die trying. Whatever comes with it, I don’t care.”
He didn’t care what it cost, he was going to make a name for himself dancing, no matter what.
“My daughter gonna know that she had a dad that was really out here doing something. Somebody’s gonna be able to tell her, ‘Your dad was doing this, your dad was doing that. Your dad was on TV.’”
Her birth gave him a new kind of fuel. A whole new energy to turn his dream into reality.
Sausee’s love for dance started young. Around five years old, his grandmother noticed he had an incredible sense of rhythm, better than most adults. From his earliest memories, he loved to move.

His early influences included Michael Jackson, B2K (especially Raz-B), and Chris Brown. He danced at every family function, every gathering in the neighborhood. He was a Richmond kid through and through, dancing, playing basketball, hanging out at Nicholl Park, and sometimes getting into a little trouble.
He always had it.
