During community celebrations like Juneteenth, he’d perform and quickly built a reputation for his skill. People began pulling him on stage just to turn the crowd up. He remembers times as a kid when whole buildings would go wild, people standing up, clapping, yelling, captivated by his energy.

One of his most defining early memories came when his mom took him to a talent show at Richmond Community College. He was about seven years old and was his older cousins’ “secret weapon.” His family, Kool John, Jay Anthony, and Rossi, were part of a dance crew called The Main Event, before HBK became a rap group. The crew also included IAMSU, LoveRance, Young Bari, Jay Rock, and others.

His mom used to take him to their rehearsals. There was no choreography planned for him, his only job was to hit the stage and dance. When it was his time, he went out and gave it everything. The crowd, around a thousand people, went crazy.
And sitting in the front row? Missy Elliott, who had performed earlier that day.
That moment was unforgettable. It was one of the first times Sausee knew he wanted to keep dancing.
“Yeah, this is what I like. I like this. Because my love language is making people smile.”

Throughout his journey, from childhood into adulthood, he was shaped by the dancers around him: his family, the community, and the teachers who taught him how to show up on time, how to read a room, how to turn his energy up or down when needed, and how to navigate the entertainment world while staying true to himself.
Even as a kid who wore his heart on his sleeve, Sausee knew:
He was meant to dance.
This all culminated in 2020, when the pandemic hit. While most people were stuck inside scrolling on their phones, collecting unemployment, and laying low, Sausee had a plan.
He poured all his money into a cameraman and spent his days shooting five or six dance videos in different outfits, every single day. He kept it up for weeks straight.
And people noticed. His audience started growing. But more importantly, they felt what he was doing. His energy, his authenticity, it resonated.

After the pandemic, he started walking around the Bay, and it became clear just how many people had been watching his grind. Strangers would come up to him, telling him he was their favorite rapper. That’s how magnetic his presence was.

LaRussell had peeped Sausee years before. The first time was at Cornerstone, when fellow artist Poo$ie was performing. Unbeknownst to Sausee, LaRussell and Tietta were in the front row, watching closely. They exchanged numbers after the show, but nothing came of it for a few years.
Then, last year, LaRussell hit him up out of the blue and invited him to come through to The V.

Sausee was playing video games with his boys when he got the call. LaRussell asked if he could pull up for 20 minutes. He lived just five minutes away, so of course he said yes. But he didn’t show up alone, he brought his friends too.
LaRussell’s only instruction: “Get off.”
And Sausee did exactly that.

Their connection was instant. Sausee’s presence, his crew, his movement, it was all appreciated. He ended up appearing in multiple visualizers with LaRussell. So when it came time to build a performance crew for the 2025 NBA All-Star Rising Star Showcase, LaRussell didn’t hesitate, he brought in Sausee.

For Sausee, it felt like a moment straight from the universe. He had just been in talks to be part of the 2025 Kendrick Lamar Super Bowl performance, but it didn’t pan out. The very next day, LaRussell called with the All-Star opportunity.

“He called me a breath of fresh air. It felt like God was in the building. I literally wanted to cry. I’ve been working so hard, dancing for so many years, and sometimes it felt like nobody was watching. But he reminded me, we see you. We love you. And we’re gonna make sure you’re in here.”
For over a decade, Sausee has brought joy to the Bay Area, through his art, his energy, and his unwavering passion.

These days, he teaches kids how to dance Monday through Friday, while still pushing his own career forward. Every step he’s taken has been about more than just himself, it’s about giving back, inspiring the next generation, and moving through life with purpose.

stories.title: Solano County Fair
paragraphs: I came to the Solano Fairgrounds on Friday afternoon with a heavy heart. It’s the middle of June, and across our screens are horrific images of people being ripped from their families, stripped of due process, and abused by those in power. The sanctioned ICE raids, sweeping across the United States, with a large concentration of media attention on Los Angeles, are a racist attack on every community. They’re part of a larger operation meant to instill fear, convince us we have nothing in common, and scare us into inaction.

But we know the truth. We know the Bay Area wouldn’t be what it is today without immigrants. We know the Bay Area sits on Indigenous land. And we know that we share a vision for the future, one where every child, regardless of identity or homeland, is welcomed into a community that accepts them fully as they are and provides the resources they need to achieve their biggest dreams.

All of this is weighing on my mind as I drive through the Walnut Creek backroads, stuck in 1.5 hours of traffic on the way to the fair. I arrive and park across from the livestock, not to be confused with a petting zoo. The concert is in the same spot as LaRussell’s birthday party last October, except this time the backdrop is filled with pink and yellow carnival rides, their lights flipping on and off behind a spinning Zipper ride.

Vince and his son Liam are setting up the merch table, stretching the cloth across the folding table, only to realize it’s inside out. Liam tells me he’s on summer vacation and staying up until 2 a.m. with his dad. On stage, Geo is tuning her electric harp. To the left, a barn full of goats and pigs echoes with bleats and squeals.

Slowly, the rest of Good Compenny starts to roll in, Clay, Drew Banga, Reece Beats, Jimmy Toor, Simon, Coach Ott, and more. After Vince and Liam finish setting up, they toss a Nerf football across the long lawn. More and more GC kids begin to fill the space, increasing the use, and chaos, of the football game. Sarai is here with Cairo, who just turned six months old. Jacob finds a pair of adult-sized noise-canceling headphones to set over his ears.

By the time the show starts, families have piled in. There’s a grass area in front of the stage and bleachers behind it, but most people stay in the grass. A breeze moves through the crowd as the sun begins to set. Fog pours from the edge of the stage as LaRussell jumps front and center.

His performance captures the crowd immediately. He starts by leaping over the rail into the audience. When he hops back on stage, he asks what people want to hear and pulls up a young kid in a Warriors jersey and GC beanie to sing his favorite song. Throughout the show, LaRussell invites dozens of kids onstage: Avery performs We Be Hyphy, individual kids take turns singing their favorite song, a dozen kids dance together at one point, Blu leading from the front. He brings up kids from E.L.I.T.E. to perform their school anthem that he wrote. One little girl stole the show with her thizz face (the cover of this magazine) and he handed her $100 out of his pocket and offered her unlimited access to future LaRussell shows, she couldn’t have been more than three or four years old.
As kids rejoiced onstage, others did cartwheels in the grass, flipping and stumbling over their own feet as they ran to their moms.

After the show, the team hit the carnival with eight to twelve kids in tow at all times. Tietta was caught between three girls spinning the ride as fast as possible. Avery was convincing everyone to get on the Gravitron, even Clay, who looked unsure about every ride. Occasionally, there were glances that screamed help, but those looks were always eclipsed by the love and admiration each kid had for the members of Good Compenny.

I noticed how many parents felt safe letting their children roam freely across the field. They knew their kids were protected, that multiple sets of eyes were watching over them. I watched the kids on stage being celebrated, having fun. In those moments, no child questioned where the kid next to them was from, what their worth was in this country, or whether they even belonged.

That realization filled me with both despair and hope, because right now, this kind of safety isn’t a reality for all children. And so I prayed: that every child might one day experience what I witnessed that night, a community where they are loved, looked after, and safe.

stories.title: Sunday Service
paragraphs: Amid smoke, a new healing sound emerged, part prayer, part protest.

In a time of immense grief, LaRussell and Sunday Service’s performance at their Grammy weekend benefit concert served as a powerful reminder of music power. Held during the first weekend of February, just a month after the Palisades fire began, the event supported those affected by the L.A. fires and offered a moment of healing for both performers and the crowd.

The concert united three creative forces: Sunday Service, the CO-LLAB Choir, and Good Compenny, coming together to blend gospel, soul, and LaRussell’s one-of-a-kind flow. The performance reimagined LaRussell’s discography and popular rap songs, like “Ballin” by Mustard ft. Roddy Ricch, by transforming their lyrics into gospel renditions.

The Good Compenny team arrived a few days before the February 7th concert. At first glance, much of L.A. looked unchanged, billboards advertising the latest Netflix series still towered over Downtown and Hollywood, palm trees cut into the clear blue skies, but there was a quiet weight in the air. Grief was present, even in places that appeared untouched.

Rehearsals took place on the 12th floor of the W Hotel, where panoramic views of Los Angeles stretched in every direction, including a perfect view of Capitol Records. At the center of the rehearsal room stood a small stage with a piano and mini organ, sheet music placed neatly on top. On the opposite side, nearly two dozen members of the Sunday Service Choir filled the rows of seats. At the center of it all was Jason White, the choir director.

Jason’s roots in music ran deep. Raised in the church, he’d been singing hymns and fusing genres since childhood. Over the years, he worked with legendary artists like Jennifer Hudson, Beyoncé, and Mary J. Blige. Now, he stood before us, clapping rhythmically, motioning with his hands, and, most of all, communicating with his eyes. His expressions were animated and full of life, occasionally prompting bursts of laughter from the choir. But with so much of the performance depending on facial expression, it was all intentional.

The choir was dressed comfortably. Some singers moved their hands with each note, raising or lowering them in sync with the melody, others waved along with the rhythm. Rehearsals were occasionally paused to clarify subtle distinctions between notes. Every song centered around themes of resistance and rebirth. Unlike the fast-paced delivery often found in rap, the gospel reworkings gave space for the lyrics to land, clear, powerful, and intentional.

The organ provided a cinematic backdrop to the choir, turning each voice into part of a larger emotional landscape. The piano shifted the mood, adding mystery, intensity, excitement, depending on its pace and rhythm. When a section hit the right note, Jason would offer a soft nod of approval. And when the harmony locked in, he’d loosen up, smiling, dancing.

He called on individual singers, clapped with his hands raised, stomped in time with the beat, and occasionally stepped over to the piano himself to play a chord or demonstrate a note. His energy was contagious. As his excitement built, the choir rose to their feet, clapping and dancing with him.

By noon, the choir broke for water, still humming melodies under their breath. LaRussell and the Good Compenny team arrived to begin full-group rehearsals. The following day, the entire crew was present: CO-LLAB Choir, the Yee Section, Sunday Service. Waiting for them were matching outfits, brown sweatsuits and socks for Good Compenny and CO-LLAB; long, cream-colored shirts for the sound crew; and cream sweatsuits for Sunday Service. The fashion coordinator explained the choice: brown for grounding, cream for healing and purity.

Early in the practice, Jason remarked, “I’m being bombarded by music.” With nearly 40 voices and a dozen instrumentalists, blending everything into one cohesive sound was no small feat. But with time, the sweet spots emerged. CO-LLAB and Sunday Service found their harmonies. The musicians carved out space for one another. A unified sound was born.
By the time the show began, every seat was filled. Guests arrived in their Sunday best.

LaRussell, Good Compenny, CO-LLAB Choir, and Sunday Service entered down two aisles to the haunting opening note of Kanye’s “Runaway.” The entrance was marked by a captivating stillness as everyone moved toward the stage in neutral tones, slowly forming a circle around the center.

Over the next hour, Sunday Service brought the crowd to church. Words fail to describe the experience. When dozens of voices meet in perfect harmony, a frequency is set in the room that reverberates beyond sound, a vibration technology still can’t replicate. It was something you had to feel.

“Runaway” was reimagined as a prayer, for the children, for the families, for the hurting. LaRussell’s own tracks, like “GC Coupe,” “Caught Up in My Head,” and “Peanut Butter Insides,” were transformed into gospel, layered with a Bay Area rhythm and style. At one point, the music faded out completely, leaving only the instrumental of “Tell Me When to Go” and “Gas Break Dip,” giving the hyphy movement it’s own moment to shine.

Tears welled up. Smiles stretched wide. Some bowed their heads in stillness, others stood with arms open in praise, singing along. The energy in the room was palpable. Every song became a sermon, every harmony a hymn. Music, once again, proved itself as a balm, for grief, for loss, for all of us. It reminded everyone in the room of the strength found in community, and the healing power of sound.

stories.title: !llmind
paragraphs: As !llmind steps into his role at EMPIRE, he looks back on a career defined by sound, service and community.

Since the early 2000s, !llmind has built a career as a producer and tastemaker. Along the way, he’s achieved industry-wide milestones: winning a Grammy for a Jay-Z and Beyoncé record, producing on one of Drake’s biggest albums, and contributing to the major motion picture Moana. Yet, as he wraps up his first year in the Bay Area as Empire’s lead A&R, one of his favorite parts has been being surrounded by people who look like him.
“Shout out to my entire Filipino community out here. It is an honor to be around you,” said !llmind.

!llmind first connected with Ghazi Shami, the founder of Empire, and Nima Etminan, Vice President at EMPIRE Distribution, nearly fifteen years ago, when they were just starting Empire. Many of the underground records and songs !llmind was producing in the early 2000s and 2010s were distributed by the company Ghazi worked for at the time. !llmind’s manager of the last fifteen years, Jonathan, was also one of Empire’s earliest employees. Now, nearly two decades later, the experience is coming full circle.

As Senior Vice President of A&R at Empire, his primary role is to “be !llmind.” That means using his skills as a producer and tastemaker, along with his love of bringing people together. The goal is to cultivate a creative ecosystem built to flourish into perpetuity. While !llmind’s success is indisputable, he joined Empire to take that success and share it with as many people as possible. He wants to continue pushing the culture forward and to be of service wherever he can.

He is also tasked with strengthening the connective tissue between Empire Publishing, which includes all the producers and writers signed to the company, and the artists signed to Empire on the distribution side of the label. He gets to play all these roles in Empire’s newly remodeled ten thousand square foot building in San Francisco.

Growing up in a Filipino household, music was always part of !llmind’s home. There was a deep love for karaoke, for singing, and for playing music together. !llmind’s dad played the guitar and was also really into jazz, classic rock, and the greats like Stevie Wonder and Michael Jackson. Every weekend, the house was filled with instruments. His dad would carry the melody on guitar, his uncle would drive the rhythm on drums, and another uncle tied it all together with his vocals. When !llmind was around seven or eight, they would sit him at the drum set, inviting him into the family tradition of creating music together.

It was not long before he became curious about how music was actually made. What did a producer do? What about a singer, an audio engineer? How did they merge all these elements in a studio to create something that felt so complete? And how did the entire process work?

His curiosity only grew as he entered high school and discovered hip-hop. He became fascinated with the producers behind the beats. Without a computer of his own, he would take the train from his home in New Jersey to a record store called Fat Beats, a place filled with soulful vinyl from the seventies and eighties. At the time he was broke, taking on whatever odd jobs he could to build his vinyl collection, and slowly it began to grow.
The first time !llmind made a beat, it was not on studio equipment but on a PlayStation game his girlfriend gifted him: MTV Music Generator. The moment !llmind loaded it up, something in him ignited.

He eventually began adding small pieces to his setup: an Akai S20, then an Ensoniq ASR-10 keyboard, the same model used by many of the producers he admired. Over time he acquired a beat machine and a computer and started learning how to create beats from scratch. He studied the greats, from J Dilla and Dr. Dre to The Neptunes, Timbaland, Mannie Fresh, and DJ Quik. After years of working with that equipment, he moved into Pro Tools, started tracking vocals, collaborated with local rappers, and posted his work on MySpace.

In 2006, !llmind received an unexpected MySpace message from an A&R named Derick Prosper, who said he had been listening to !llmind’s beats. Prosper was working with 50 Cent and had just signed Mobb Deep, during the peak G-Unit era. He invited !llmind to come to New York. !llmind boarded the same train he used to take to Fat Beats to meet with D. Prosper, and he left with a production deal.

!llmind’s beats, made in his mother’s basement using a one-dollar record, were now being rapped over by 50 Cent. He walked out into the streets of New York with his first rack of cash feeling like he had made it. That moment became the motivation to keep going and never turn back.

From there, word began to spread about !llmind. He moved out of his mother’s basement and into Brooklyn, where he started working with local rappers. In 2012 he produced “The Morning” for Kanye West, which was rare at the time since most of Kanye’s producers were signed to GOOD Music. In 2014 he produced the classic “Love Yourz” for J. Cole’s Forest Hills Drive album. In 2015 he produced “You and the Six” for Drake’s If You’re Reading This It’s Too Late. He worked on Khalid’s first album when he was just starting out. He worked with Future. He worked with Travis Scott and Quavo on the Huncho Jack album. He produced for Schoolboy Q, Kendrick Lamar, and the Black Panther album. All of this ultimately led to his first Grammy win for Jay-Z and Beyoncé’s collaborative album, followed by a Latin Grammy for Nathy Peluso’s Best Hip-Hop Song.

“I think the underlying common denominator for me was that as long as I stayed true to myself, kept working, kept connecting with people I resonated with, and continued to provide value, the momentum would keep going. And that is still the journey I am on now.”

!llmind’s discography expanded quickly, and while there were many producers in the field, a few specific qualities made him unique. First, he was not afraid of failure. That did not mean he never failed. He failed often, intentionally, because every misstep brought him closer to where he needed to be. He had zero fear of something not working out.

Second, he loved trying new things. Throughout his career he experimented, tested ideas, deployed new sounds, got roasted sometimes, and kept it moving. Years later, when he was already on to something else, those same sounds he was criticized for became popular. That constant game of hide-and-seek with new creative pockets allowed !llmind to continually expand his artistry.
The final thing that set him apart was his instinct and taste, something impossible to replicate.

After two decades of shaping the sound of modern music, !llmind is not concerned with defining his own legacy. He leaves that for the world to decide. He only hopes that when people look back, they see a man who brought people together, pushed sound forward, and inspired others to believe they could build a world with their own sound too.

stories.title: 12 Tips for Small Artists Building a Big Name
paragraphs: By Lazā

Lazā is a Seattle-based artist whose love for performance began in church, where she grew up surrounded by prayer, hymns, and a congregation that doubled as her first audience. Raised by pastor parents, she was introduced to music early through gospel legends like The Sheri Sisters, Deitrick Haddon, and Marvin Sapp, with her mother writing raps for her to perform during church plays. That foundation shifted in middle school when her brother handed her an iPod Nano, opening her world to Drake, T-Pain, and Cash Money and solidifying her desire to rap.

By her early teens, Lazā was performing at talent shows and by fifteen she played her first ticketed show, secretly pursuing music despite her parents’ uncertainty. Refusing college and committing fully to her craft, she began releasing music independently, dropping her first single “Zoom” in 2019 and steadily building her sound and team in Seattle. A major turning point came in 2023 when her EP All In One Night gained traction on TikTok, dramatically increasing her streams and marking a new level of confidence in her sound.

Her momentum has continued, with 2025 becoming her most-streamed year yet and a performance at Capitol Hill Block Party signaling her growing presence. Now learning to produce her own music and releasing consistently, Lazā is focused on expanding her reach, collaborating with new producers, and building her career brick by brick, shaping her vision in real time rather than waiting for permission.
12 Tips
1. Build a small, committed team. Find people who genuinely believe in you. This might include a producer, engineer, videographer, or friends who support your vision.

2. Work with collaborators who are willing to grow with you. Look for producers who will create original music for you and videographers who are willing to pull up and shoot because they believe in your potential.
3. Create a plan for your artistic output. Decide what consistent action looks like for you, such as releasing a song every month.
4. Execute the plan with consistency. Put up shots even when you’re unsure how things will turn out. Consistency builds momentum.
5. Use the resources you have. If you cannot pay for shoots, set up your phone. If you do not have a producer, use accessible tools like BandLab to experiment and begin creating.

6. Use YouTube beats strategically (but do not rely on them long-term). You can start practicing or writing over YouTube beats, then work with producers to recreate the vibe or BPM in an original way.
7. Take advantage of affordable options. There are producers selling beats for as low as $25. Getting started does not require a lot of money; it requires initiative.
8. Leverage TikTok and short-form content. Posting daily 30-second videos can introduce your music to new listeners. Many artists are discovered this way now.
9. Collaborate horizontally. You do not need to reach out to the biggest artist or producer. Look for peers in your city or online who are building at the same pace you are.
10. Document your process across platforms. Share your music on TikTok, Instagram, YouTube, and any space where it can find an audience.
11. Keep improving the quality of your music. Consistency will help you get better. Over time, your craft will catch up to your ambition.
12. Trust the brick-by-brick approach. Build slowly: a team, a plan, steady releases, daily content, and ongoing practice. If you stay consistent, the work will eventually take hold.

stories.title: 2EZ: In an Era Obsessed With Self-Sufficiency
paragraphs: In an era obsessed with self-sufficiency, producer duo Cam and Tajin offer a counterpoint, showing what becomes possible when two people commit to building a legacy together.

All relationships required trust, but two producers, sharing one board, required a deeper kind, an instinct like knowing your left foot will follow your right. Cam and Tajín, better known as “2EZ,” worked with that same unspoken rhythm, stepping in at the perfect time for each other.
I sat with Cam and Tajín in my Lake Merritt apartment during the summer to talk with them about their standout year, their growing partnership, and what the new year has in store.

Tajín had recently been laid off from his job. It was a welcomed transition, and he greeted it with excitement. He had been waiting for a moment like this, a reason to pour his full energy into music. He moved back home and began dedicating himself completely to his craft. By happenstance, or divinity, this was the exact moment when he and Cam started their fourteen day run of endless studio sessions, back to back at any hour of the day — something that would not have been possible with Tajín’s previous work schedule.

Just based on their Instagram, it was clear the producers were picking up speed. Working with the likes of Tyler Lauren, 3lise, Alien Mac Kitty, Frak, Ozer, Easweh, Nef the Pharaoh, John Mackk. They were just getting started.

Artists loved working with the duo, and that was partly because of the space they carefully crafted. Both Cam and Tajín honored how delicate and vulnerable the process of making music was, and they worked together to build an environment where everyone felt at ease. They often started sessions with long debriefs that sometimes took up the entire time and left with barely any music made.
Artist and collaborator Alien Mac Kitty spoke about the impact of working with 2EZ on her latest project.

“We’ve cried in the studio, we’ve laughed, we’ve screamed. We’ve all had moments of vulnerability together, and with that comes trust and responsibility. That allowed me to open up and give them the same.”

Creating a safe environment allowed people to do their best work. It required a level of emotional intelligence to read when people were feeling uncomfortable, holding back, or frustrated. This was particularly important when working with women, who too often felt unsafe in studio settings.

While in the studio together, the two grounded one another. Making music can be notoriously high-pressure, depending on who is in the room. And more often than not, it wasn’t just the artist and the producer(s); it was also the artist’s friends and team, each with their own opinions. Being a pair navigating the ever-changing landscape of making music meant they always had each other’s back. It also meant that when one started getting in their own way, the other would step in.
“I feel like us together, we are truly better versions of ourselves, which is wholeheartedly important,” said Cam
“We fill in each other’s blanks, it’s super dope” said Tajín

2EZ shared an open-mindedness when they created music. They both honored each other’s ideas and created a process that always prioritized the music over ego or individual pursuits, like two good parents from different backgrounds raising one child.
The Origins of 2EZ

Raised in Berkeley, California, Cam grew up in a household shaped by art. His father, an artist, was part of the Bay Area’s 1970s hippie scene, while his mother, a painter, left the Midwest in her early twenties to find community among like-minded artists in the Bay. Their family home was filled with canvases, watercolors, acrylics, and the sounds of the Grateful Dead, James Brown and Jimi Hendrix.

From an early age Cam gravitated towards music and pulled inspiration not only from his home, but from his school teachers. He fondly remembers his kindergarten teacher introducing his class to Chuck Berry, commonly known as the “father of rock,” and recalls a time when he was engulfed with knowing everything about the electric guitar: how it was invented, the first person to play it, how it became popularized.

In fourth grade, Cam was required to play an instrument in school and he thought to himself: what’s the loudest instrument I can play? He chose the trumpet. He continued playing the trumpet throughout middle school and soon he was playing in jazz ensembles in high school, falling in love with creating music that made people want to dance.

Tajín grew up across the Bay Bridge, in San Francisco, in a home with his grandfather, his great grandmother, his mom, and his auntie. He was the baby, his mother’s only child. He was doted on by his family, and his earliest memories with them, even before any images form, carry a love so deep it brings tears to his eyes.

When Tajín was a child, he would sit with his legs crossed in front of his grandfather’s tape deck. On either side were massive speakers boasting a height nearly equal to his own. He slipped on the over-ear headphones and listened for the whir of the CD player spinning into place or the click of a tape rewinding. The music system allowed him to explore all corners of the world, from Michael Jackson to the Beatles.

Music was an intrinsic thread to the culture Tajín grew up in; his dad played percussion and the bass guitar, his uncle was a drummer, his aunt was a dancer and part of a carnival group. Around seven years old, Tajín began going to the Mission Cultural Center, where his aunt worked, and joined the percussion program, salsa band and theatre class.

At the cultural center, Tajín got to bang on every instrument there was, focusing mainly on instruments from the Afro-Latin world, including: congas, bongo, bells, campana, the repinique and the cuíca. He loved being in community with people, and similarly to Cam, he loved to create music that made people want to dance.

Tajín continued playing music in high school, where he joined the school band. Instead of playing for people dancing, he performed at sports games and school events, and his passion for music continued to grow.

The two first met after high school, when they both joined an Afro-Cuban and Brazilian ensemble at San Francisco State University. Tajín had already been in the group for a year, and growing up in the city, he already had artist friends in his circle. Cam, by contrast, commuted from the East Bay, entering both the group and the San Francisco music scene as a relative newcomer.
“He had such an easy going personality and was just hella adaptable. He was just himself. I think that’s just what made him cool,” said Tajín.
The ensemble, spearheaded by John Calloway, was made up of a dozen or so artists: Tajín on percussion, Cam on trumpet, and others on congas, timbales, trombone, piano, upright bass, and bass guitar.

The group practiced three or four times a week and often hung out long after rehearsals ended. It was in this environment that Cam and Tajín’s friendship began. Post-jam sessions were spent going to viewpoints, smoking, and walking around the city. Gentrification was sweeping through San Francisco, leaving the streets busier and emptier at the same time. The ensemble wandered through neighborhoods, pointing out to Cam the homes that had once been filled with familiar faces and were now occupied by generic techies. The group sat on stoops that technically weren’t theres, wearing shirts adorned with “Bay vs. The World” and poking fun at the gentrifiers who stuck out like bones in broth.

Cam ended up leaving SFSU in 2016, just one academic year later, and transferred to Laney Community College to avoid the long commute and the cost of BART tickets from hopping the gate. He later finished his degree at UC Santa Cruz. Tajín stayed at SFSU to complete his degree, and the two naturally went their separate ways during those school years. Still, they kept up with each other on social media, checking in, cheering each other on, and periodically saying they should cook up.

After graduating, Cam began searching for internships, hoping to break into audio and recording. One evening, he received a call from a friend inviting him to an internship informational session at Secret Studios off Potrero Hill in San Francisco. When he walked into the building the next day, Tajín was already sitting there.

After class the two stayed late, caught up, and finally cooked up like they’d always said they would. Their bond was seamless, their styles blending like watercolor. It was this effortless dynamic that marked the beginning of what would become 2EZ.

The two began getting into the studio more often. Tajín was already comfortable creating beats from scratch with the artist in the room. For Cam, this felt daunting; the pressure of finding a sound that flowed between artist and producer is a delicate dynamic for anyone in the booth, especially someone just starting out. There is no guarantee the end result will be something everyone likes. But when Tajín asked him to join, he said yes. And in 2022, 2EZ became official.

As 2025 wraps up, the duo is ready to keep growing, aiming for global reach and household-name status. Their bond continues to shape the culture, creating space for people to create, grieve, and be seen. And in a culture that doesn’t always make space, they make it look 2EZ.

stories.title: Alien Mac Kitty
paragraphs: An intimate look at how Mariah transformed lineage and loss into a multiverse of sound, character and survival.

From a young age, Mariah would gaze into the mirror to study herself. She noticed the finest details, the curl of her lashes, the arch of her collarbones, and the ellipses in her eyes. At the same time, she was sharply aware that something deeper was not reflected back. She never felt fully connected to her body. Instead, she felt tethered to the world around her, certain that her spirit existed far beyond this realm.

Mariah was born in San Francisco to her mother Gloria and her father Ronald, more widely known by his rapper name, Cougnut. Both of her parents were artists. Cougnut is a Bay Area legend. Mac Dre would often tell people that Cougnut was his favorite rapper. Mariah recalled that when her father walked into a room, the energy shifted. People lit up in his presence. She also remembered feeling pestered by the constant flow of his fans who rushed up to him, excited and eager to talk, while she stayed protective of him.

Her bond with her dad was different from his relationships with other people. They were always joking, always silly. But she also remembered his rebellious streak and admitted he could be an asshole. Most of all, he was sensitive to energy. He either fucked with you, or he did not.

Mariah’s mother, Gloria, was an artist as well. She was born in Louisiana but moved to San Francisco, where she had Mariah in the 90s. Mariah described her mom as militant, extremely intelligent, and spiritually disciplined. Her mother encouraged prayer, persistence, and affirming the parts of your life you want to keep, alchemizing the energy you wanted to get rid of. Repetition was paramount. She taught Mariah through raw examples, not just instruction, showing her how life could unfold depending on the path she chose.

Both of her parents were go-getters and hustlers, raising Mariah through the nineties and early 2000s. They taught her to be genuine, to be direct, and to never be skeemish. They gave her game in their own ways. Most of all, Mariah was able to see both her parents for who they were. Their imperfections allowed her to mourn them in their entirety when they did pass. They shielded her from some things, yet she still saw them in their full kaleidoscope of colors, and in turn, she loved them exactly as they were.

Now, as she raises her son without the physical presence of her parents, Mariah made a clear choice: she would not shrink or hide any part of who she was. She was eccentric, sensitive, devoted and imperfect. Those very traits would become the foundation of the rich, explosive multiverse she created, a world layered with characters, complexities, stories, and color.

Mariah, also known as AMK or Alien Mac Kitty, is a singer, songwriter, rapper, painter, and explosive creative on a mission to carve out her own legacy. One that honored the hyphy lineage she was born into and also subverted what people expected from Bay Area artists. Her music moved freely across genres. There was her remake of “Toxic” by Britney Spears, an upbeat, raunchy, playful, and chaotic love story. There was her hyphy hype track “GAS ME UP,” an affirmation of self that blended her galactic lyrics with a direct message to anyone who might take offense to her showing up as her most authentic self — a clear demand to get on board or get left behind. And then there was “Passion,” produced by 2EZ, where her sharp, over-the-BS bars glide over soft, melodic vocals.

On stage, AMK was unforgettable. Every performance she felt fully connected to the crowd, and simultaneously in her own world, almost like the wonder of a newborn with no object permanence. All of her attention was locked onto the moment in front of her, yet she occupied a world you could not penetrate. Nothing in her drifted toward yesterday or tomorrow. Every part of her existed on that stage, in that exact moment.

She moved on stage until she was breathless. She shifted from sweeping motions to jumping up and down, to lying on her back with her legs kicked up in the air. Her emotional range was impossible to ignore. Her brows furrowed and pinched when she spoke on something real, her eyes rolled back when she addressed the BS, thizz-faced and whipped her hair when she broke into the hyphy energy that defined her.
Still, it seemed impossible to capture Alien Mac Kitty into words.

Alien Mac Kitty had always been a part of Mariah, for as long as she could remember, even if the name did not appear until later. The little girl who searched for something beyond her reflection in the mirror is the same woman now on stage in reflective white contacts with no pupils, platform reflective boots, long pink braids, and grills screaming “FUCK CHARLES” (a recurring shady character in her art) to the crowd.
The stage name also offered Mariah protection. Many people knew AMK, but far fewer knew Mariah, and that was by design.
“I don’t think everyone should have access to your true, vulnerable self,” said AMK.

Being an artist meant living in a state of exposure, always open to criticism and reaction. There was courage in stepping onstage, but it also invited parasocial attachments and blurred boundaries. AMK became the shield that protected Mariah, the softer, quieter soul beneath it all.

The lines between Mariah and AMK began to blur when she joined the short film “Whatchu Mixed With,” directed by Maya Cameron, in July of 2024. Mariah was cast to play Precious, the big-sister figure in the neighborhood to 14-year-old Alexis, who is navigating life in San Francisco without her father and living with her white mother. The film illuminates many realities: searching for pieces of your identity through community and culture, the importance of kinship when family is absent, and the complex dynamics San Franciscans navigate as they continue to survive in continually testing times.

When AMK was approached about the role, everything in her life felt like it was falling apart. She had just lost her job, she was going through a terrible breakup, and she was living out of a suitcase while trying to stabilize her housing situation. On top of that, filming took place during the anniversary of her mother’s passing. The movie, the team, and the set arrived at the worst and the best possible time. Maya Cameron encouraged her to push through and take the role.

Mariah showed up every day, despite everything working against her. The character Precious was a version of Mariah she was less comfortable with sharing. It reflected the quieter more introverted parts of herself. It reflected Mariah. As she stepped into the role, she realized it wasn’t just Precious’s story she was telling. It revealed parts of herself she had intentionally kept tucked away, pieces that would now be seen on a large screen.
“Mariah is Precious. She is super powerful.”

One of the first things she had to do was change her signature look, the pink accent she had woven into so many of her hairstyles. The moment did not come easy, and for a second, she began to panic. Her hairstylist reminded her that they could always add the pink back in and encouraged her to embrace this moment.

While filming, Mariah had to tuck AMK away, locking her in the closet for the duration of filming. She prayed daily, went to the gym to release excess energy, and stepped away to cry when the weight of everything felt too big, or when the pressure of not wanting to let anyone down became overwhelming. The whole crew surrounded her with love and encouragement, becoming a haven as she worked through the emotions as they surfaced. She tried to stay present, taking each day as it came.

At the same time, she was still performing as AMK, but she realized her energy onstage had shifted because she was so deeply embedded in Precious’ headspace. Those performances would become the place where she poured out all the AMK energy she had been suppressing, leaving it fully on the stage, before she got stuffed back in the closet.

When the night of the premiere finally came, in the middle of June the next year, Mariah finally got to see Precious in her entirety. She described the night of the premiere, at the iconic Lakeshore Movie Theatre, as surreal. She was a natural on screen, her character embodying so much of her own ethos: raw, authentic, nurturing, gamed up. There was Precious. There was Mariah. The role felt like a flawless match and told a story of identity that is often lost in writers’ rooms where diversity and culture are too often left out.

When filming ended, AMK was ready to step back into her bold, unencumbered persona, but what she did not expect was that AMK had drifted much farther than she realized. She almost had to look around the corner to find that part of herself again. Still, she returned stronger than ever, and pieces of her life slowly began to fall into place. She found a beautiful apartment in the city for her and her son, she was on a roll producing and creating music, and she was focused on what came next, which was GIANT.
GIANT

For the past year, AMK had been working with production duo 2EZ to create her latest album, Giant. They were the first producers to truly build Mariah’s sound from scratch, giving space for all the complexities within her to shine.
Mariah has multiple versions of herself, not just Alien Mac Kitty. There is Onyx, Ms. Geraldine, and others, and this project allowed each of those sides to come to the forefront.
And there is one constant across them all:
“I am not the bitch to ever fuck with. All of myself, every last personality. You cross that barrier with me, you gonna see a whole different fucking side of me.”

On previous projects, where she used beats that were sent to her, the music often felt like a reduction of who she was. One person advised her, “You need a sound curated for yourself, because you have a different style, you have a different sound.” Before that, she had been constantly trying to fit into other people’s sonic worlds, ones that did not fully reflect her or apply to her artistry.
2EZ was an opportunity to write a new era.

At first she was nervous, carrying the same hesitation every woman in the industry learns to have when collaborating in a male-dominated space. But soon every session became a blend of therapy and art. They would start by talking about the week, then build the sound from whatever surfaced. No two songs sounded the same. The process was vulnerable, immersive, and capable of holding every version of Mariah.

“I mean, we’ve cried in the studio, we’ve laughed, we’ve screamed, we’ve all had moments of being vulnerable together. There is a real trust and responsibility that comes with that. Because of it, I was able to let myself give them the same vulnerability. It was beautiful,” said AMK.
The project, sculpted over countless studio sessions for nearly two years, has pushed Cam and Tajin of 2EZ just as much as it has pushed AMK.

“I will say this collaboration with her has been the most freeing collaboration we’ve had in the last year, year and a half. It has allowed us to grow in our musical production, our taste, our character, in a big way. The range is huge,” said Cam.

She has learned to set her ego aside, understanding that respect comes first. She listens to 2EZ’s direction and knows that being at her best means recognizing when to be a student and when to lead, when to follow and when not to.
“One reason why we work so well with AMK is because she’s so raw and has so many good ideas, but yet is always”

“It’s unleashed, it’s unhinged, it’s emotional, it’s a roller coaster. It’s everything. It’s energetic. It’s truly a very special thing we all have, and I think it shows in the songs we’ve made,” said Cam.

stories.title: DJ Day$: Crowd Control
paragraphs: After a ten-hour flight from SFO, DJDay$ landed in London in the thick of July’s heat. Everything felt unfamiliar, from the accents to cars on the wrong side of the road. It was only his second time abroad, the first being a brief trip to Canada just weeks before. He and Karri were in the middle of touring with Isaiah Falls when they took a quick detour to open for Drake in London.

Still exhausted from the flight, he landed already in motion, preparing for his DJ set while simultaneously stepping into the role of impromptu tour manager, coordinating between Drake’s team and Karri for Drake’s 2025 Wireless Festival performance at Finsbury Park, a 50,000-capacity venue.
The feeling was indescribable, and yet it was only the beginning.

Grayson, better known as DJDay$, had been manifesting this life since eighth grade, when he quietly added “@4karri’s DJ” to his Instagram bio. It began when he transferred to a new middle school in San Francisco. Shy and unsure of himself, he made an early mistake, calling Karri trash at basketball. Karri gave him the cold shoulder for a week, but after patching things over, the two became inseparable. Today, they’ve moved through every era together, from middle school, to early music experiments to releasing albums, and playing sold-out shows.

Music had been a throughline for Day$ long before sold out crowds. In eighth grade, he was just a kid who loved the radio and supporting his friend’s music. By freshman year of high school, he joined the DJ Club, though he was too nervous to actually spin in front of people and share his work. But everything shifted after Rolling Loud. Watching Travis Scott, Playboi Carti, and his favorite artists move entire crowds made something click. I want to do something like that, he thought. He quickly realized he couldn’t rap, but every artist had a DJ. That was his in and he was ready to take it more seriously.

In sophomore year, a haircut changed everything. His cousin Zmo—also a DJ—turned the appointment into a crash course in how to get started DJ’ing. When he returned home, Day$ pulled out his iPad and downloaded every app Zmo mentioned. He began experimenting. He started producing on Ableton, creating drum loops and tweaking BPMs until something felt right. Then when school went online, he finally got a laptop, saved for his first mixer, and spent COVID teaching himself to DJ from scratch.

By the time he returned to school as a senior, the DJ Club had fallen apart, many of the seniors and juniors leaving after COVID. But he still showed up faithfully. Slowly he built the courage to share mixes online. SoundCloud, Instagram, Snapchat—bit by bit, he let the world hear the ear he’d always had.

By senior year, when he applied to USC, he imagined a double life: journalist by day, DJ by night. He’d worked on his high school’s newspaper and assumed that would be his “real job,” with DJ’ing as a side gig. Batman, but with a press badge. But then the breaks started coming.

The summer of 2022, before Grayson left for USC, a friend asked him to open up for an artist at Brick and Mortar. His sound, hip-hop, trap, underground rap, rage music, made people move. The crowd loved him. Confidence began to bloom. For the first time, he wondered if DJ’ing wasn’t just an option, but option A.

Freshman year at USC further solidified his instinct. He was out every weekend, not because he chased nightlife, but because DJ’ing placed him at the center of it. It helped him meet people, connected him to businesses, and built his name. He DJ’d his first frat party on Halloween. Suddenly, everyone wanted “their DJ,” and for the freshman class, he became that person.
Soon, the stages got bigger: opening for Baby Smoove, D Savage, Wifisfuneral. Then, performing for crowds of 1,500. He watched as the room jumped under his command.
He loved how people found comfort in an album and used concerts to alchemize their energy. DJ’ing wasn’t just a job; it was a service, a way of giving people a place to feel good.
“I just wanted to put a smile on people’s faces,” he said. “I want people to leave a show with a good memory. That’s the whole point.”
He continued to grow at USC, DJ’ing more parties, at a bigger scale. At the same time, his middle school best friend Karri, was charting his own artistic path.

But as senior year of college approached, pressure crept in. Friends, artists he admired, were hanging up their dreams for careers. He felt the pull of “real jobs,” and the urgency of adulthood calling him. Still, something in him resisted the idea of stepping away. Instead, he leaned in harder: planning events, supporting Karri with artist management, eager to uplift others in the music industry. He never wanted to look back and wonder if he could have made it if he’d just kept going.
“I’m always trying to keep that hunger,” he said. “That hunger is what drives the best work.”

Through everything, he stayed grounded. He recalled a time, back in 2019, when he and Karri worked a funnel cake stand at Outside Lands, slicing strawberries while P-Lo performed onstage just yards away. They laughed about how badly they wished they could watch the show.
“We have the same energy, just a bigger stage,” said Day$.
This was the payoff of years of showing up, practicing alone, spinning at lunch, posting mixes when he was scared, and claiming “@4karri’s DJ” before he was even ready.
And he’s not done.
What started with an iPad and a haircut has taken him across the world. And somehow, it still feels like he’s just getting started.

stories.title: Falilou
paragraphs: Fueled by Muhammad Ali’s legacy and an unwillingness to accept limits, Falilou moved beyond expectations to build a life driven by ambition, creativity and self-made success.

Growing up in France, there was always an unspoken expectation that children like Falilou should settle for less. Less in school, less in career, less in life. Whenever the news mentioned Black or Muslim communities, it was filled with stigma and racism. While Black people were visible in sports and entertainment, they were rarely seen in executive roles or government positions. So from a young age, Falilou began searching for examples of Black excellence he did not see directly in the world around him. He turned to American culture. The figure he gravitated toward most was Muhammad Ali.

Muhammad Ali’s career represented everything Falilou wanted to embody, even at a young age. He admired Ali’s ability to push people out of their comfort zones and inspire them towards their goals. He watched his fights, his demeanour, his resilience, his interviews. For Muhammad Ali, success was meaningful, but inspiring others to believe they could do better meant even more. Ali fought against segregation, advocated openly for his beliefs, and spoke his mind. He was unapologetic. He excelled to the highest peaks. When someone wronged him, he held them accountable. And he was Black and Muslim.

The tenacity and fervor of Muhammad Ali always resonated in Falilou’s spirit, and he was determined to create a life beyond the limitations others placed on him. He excelled throughout grade school, both academically and in sports. But when it came time for high school, he encountered a barrier that had nothing to do with his abilities.

In France, all students took an exam before entering high school, a test that helped determine their next step. The results mattered, but the final recommendation came from a student’s lead professor. Falilou had performed exceptionally well, both in school and on the exam. He did not want to attend the school closest to him. He set his sights on the largest and most prestigious high school in the area. After acing his exams, he felt confident about the next step, until his professor informed him, along with three or four other Black and Muslim students, that they would not be a good fit.

Falilou, barely thirteen years old, rallied his fellow classmates, all except one who likely feared retaliation or rejection, and challenged the decision. By the fall of the following year, Falilou was attending the most prestigious high school in his area.
He excelled over the next four years in high school, both in sports and academically. The teacher who originally said he wouldn’t be a good fit later went on to apologize.

In his senior year, he sat in math class while conversations buzzed around him about what everyone planned to do next. Falilou, however, felt unsure. Before entering high school he had known exactly what he wanted, but now nothing seemed to spark that same excitement.

As the teacher filled the board with equations, Falilou quietly opened his laptop in the back of the room. He put one headphone in and clicked on Chadwick Boseman’s 2018 Howard University commencement speech on YouTube.

The video was just over thirty minutes long and was celebrating the 150th commencement of the university’s history. The first image that flashed was a black t-shirt that said, “Howard is our Wakanda” in red, yellow, blue, and green writing. Falilou turned on the French subtitles and listened closely as Boseman received the same honorary degree once given to Jackie Robinson and Martin Luther King Jr. As he watched the speech, questions began to swirl in his mind. A Black university? Do those exist? Where is this? He was captivated. He kept watching as math class droned on, completely captivated. It did not take long before he began to imagine what his life could look like if he went to school surrounded by people who looked like him.

He continued the video, sneaking occasional glances at the board to convey mild interest, when something caught his attention early in the speech. Chadwick Boseman described his early days on campus and how an otherwise average day was transformed the moment he crossed paths with Muhammad Ali. Boseman said he walked away feeling lighter, ready to take on the world, and added, “That is the magic of this place. Almost anything can happen here.”
It took only ten minutes and one mention of his childhood hero for Falilou to feel it. In that perfect moment of happenstance, he knew exactly where he needed to go next: Howard University.

Falilou applied to Howard, but he was not accepted because of complications with international students traveling during the pandemic. Still determined to bring himself one step closer, he decided to move to the United States and earn his associate degree at Northern Virginia Community College (Fun fact: Jill Biden was his professor.) After completing his degree, he applied again to Howard, along with schools like NYU, UCLA, and several colleges in the DMV area.

He was accepted to every school he applied to, except Howard. He was devastated. He had come to a new country with one goal in mind, and despite his fierce persistence, his dream suddenly felt out of reach. He decided he would enroll at the school nearest to him, the one with the best financial aid, even as he quietly hoped that something would shift.
On the final day to confirm his enrollment, as Falilou typed in his debit card information, an email from Howard University appeared in his inbox.
He threw his computer across the room and began yelling, screaming, “I got in, I got in.” His aunts and uncles rushed to him, screaming in joy. He was going to Howard.
“Mr. GQ”

His first days on campus were surreal. Everything he had aspired to since being a young boy watching Muhammad Ali in France was coming into fruition. At Howard, he quickly became accustomed to expecting the unexpected. Suddenly, he was at one of the most prestigious Black colleges in the world, brushing shoulders with notable figures and sharing space with people he had long admired through a screen.

Falilou quickly became known for his style and presence on campus. People constantly asked if he was a model. This was not new to him. In high school in Paris, his English teacher had repeatedly suggested he try modeling. She introduced him to a friend in the industry, and Falilou took headshots that were sent to major agencies. They all wanted him, but when he told his parents, they were hesitant. Their perceptions of the modeling world were tied to drugs, partying, and instability. They wanted him to focus on school, so he did.

But here he was in the United States, and the same words were being spoken to him again and again. A photographer reached out to take test shoots, then another, then another. He began posting his photos online, and before he knew it, modeling had seamlessly become a real part of his life. He was excited to show a different side of modeling, one that didn’t center the partying or extracurriculars, but focused on the art.

Around this time, he was sending out his headshots to modeling agencies in New York. It was different from his high school experience, when people were sending his photos for him, practically begging him to take a chance on the biggest agencies in the world. This time, he was ready. But when he sent out his headshots, no one responded, and the few who did were not interested. It was humbling, but ultimately it became a blessing and a redirection. He would remain independent.

Falilou went on to land brand partnerships, leading to features in GQ, and people on campus calling him “GQ man.” At the same time, he aligned himself with the creative community at Howard, joining the Warner Brothers Music program spearheaded by Jasmine Young, who had led million-dollar marketing campaigns for artists like Jay-Z, DMX, and more (this program was also his introduction to the Good Compenny team).

His modeling experience allowed him to hone his styling and creative direction skills. In almost every shoot, he had a heavy hand in producing the vision. He played an integral role in taking small brands he modeled for to major viral moments, which led to athletes and celebrities wearing the same pieces. Like every other part of his life, once Falilou accepted something into his world, he wanted to make it the best it could be, and he quickly became masterful at curating his ideas.

Using his growing reputation as “Mr. GQ,” he ran for several roles on campus, creating full marketing campaigns that included merchandise, influencers, and even celebrities he had met through his modeling work. He brought them to campus to support his campaign and hand out free clothing to students. He was selected as one of twelve Warner Brothers Fellows, a scholarship awarded to exemplary students who received specialized coaching, curriculum, and mentorship. Whatever Falilou touched turned into excellence, but he would not have it any other way.

When senior year approached, people were quick to ask what he planned to do for his senior pictures, a tradition meant to commemorate your time on campus and flex your creativity. Expectations were already high, and he felt nervous, but he knew he had to rise to the occasion. He assembled a team, including a photographer and a creative director, and he styled the shoot himself.
“I want a bison,” Falilou said.
“A bison?” His team looked at him, confused.

Falilou started calling farms to find one, only to learn there were no bison in the DMV. At least, not alive. To avoid losing time, they shot the photos pretending a bison was there and planned to figure it out in post-production. Months went by as they tried to superimpose a bison into the images. Dozens of attempts with AI and Photoshop failed. Nothing looked right.

Then Falilou made a random connection with a digital effects expert from Senegal, his home country, someone who would eventually bring the bison to life. The final photos were so iconic that Howard University shared them, creating yet another viral Falilou moment.

Falilou wrapped up his senior year at Howard in the spring of 2025 and went straight to New York, already carrying a wealth of connections who had been patiently waiting for his arrival. He attended his first fashion week, walking seven shows in a matter of days and closing out Calvin Klein without ever auditioning for the role. Now he was in the city to see what he could create. His expectations were nothing short of the top. He wanted Model of the Year. He wanted to lead some of the biggest campaigns in the world. Fresh off releasing his Vogue feature, he was only getting started.

The same fire he carried as a young boy in France still guided him, driven by a deep belief in himself and an unrelenting commitment to excellence. And much like Muhammad Ali, he did not wait for opportunities. He made them.

stories.title: Juvenile, LaRussell and Richie Rich at Great America
paragraphs: Rows of green bleachers stretch upward in front of the stage. Parents squeeze in beside their kids, arms loaded with tacos, wings, chopped cheeses, and bottles of water. Towels cover heads. Hats wave in front of faces. Umbrellas pop open. People stand on the bleachers, fanning themselves with one hand while bouncing babies on the other hip.

The stage is wide. Instead of squeezing into corners, there’s enough space for everyone to move comfortably. At the center sits a truck, a foldout table standing on the bed. Kenzo’s DJ board rests on top, his office for the day. To the left stands the traveling pergola, a nod to the origins of GC. Center stage is the choir. To the right is the band.

In the crowd, a sign reading “Thank you, LaRussell” stands out against the cloudless sky. A few rows back, Sarai stands with Cairo, who wears oversized noise-canceling headphones that nearly swallow his head. Off to the right, a roller coaster rises and falls in an endless loop. During the gap between soundcheck and showtime, band members rush to squeeze in rides before the lines grow too long. They return soaked from water rides, shaking out wet hair and pant legs before climbing back onstage.
Backstage, Juvenile waits with his wife and a small crew as Avery pulls him aside for a quick interview. Moments before the show begins, choir member Rain moves through the stage, passing out roses.

Kenzo kicks things off with “Tell Me When to Go,” then flips seamlessly into “She Was a Fairy.” Young kids and Good Compenny members alike raise one leg and throw their arms out, perfectly synced in a TikTok dance. He glides into “Vans” by The Pack, then into “Love” by Keyshia Cole, somehow hitting every generation in a three-minute sweep.
Michael follows, wearing an “I Am Black” bucket hat and a brown hoodie. Phones shoot up instantly, everyone eager to capture whatever magic he brings beyond the music itself.

By the time Juvenile steps onstage, generational lines crack wide open. The older crowd sings every bar back to him, word for word. Parents set their kids down when “Back That Azz Up” hits. Some children retreat further into the crowd as adults push forward, untethered, when Juvenile shouts, “Where my hot girls at!”

Juvenile jumps straight into the three-hundred-person crowd. Children perch on parents’ hips. Teens clutch agua frescas. Parents shield themselves with towels draped over their heads. Hands reach out in every direction. The crowd screams, desperate to touch him.
“Y’all don’t act like this for me,” LaRussell laughs as the crowd, completely enamored, surges toward Juvenile.

LaRussell jumps back in with “When I Get Home,” then slides effortlessly into “GT Coupe,” bending genres without breaking momentum. His crowd control is impeccable as the audience moves from ass shaking to locked in, somber in his words. Juvenile cuts back with “Ghetto Child,” Kenzo scratching underneath while Clay and Simon drive the chords forward.

Richie Rich cuts in with his verse, and for a moment LaRussell, Juvenile, and Richie Rich all sit together on one ledge. It is a rare moment where eras of hip-hop merge, creating an experience that feels just as meaningful to the parents as it does to the kids watching from below.

The show moves forward in an effortless flow of improvisation, with LaRussell directing the energy between everyone onstage. By the end, hair is slicked to faces and babies have settled into their naps despite the noise.

But instead of heading home, the crowd drifts back into the amusement park. It is a chance few people get after middle or high school to move in a group of hundreds, eating together, celebrating, laughing, and letting themselves feel like kids again.

That is the magic of LaRussell. Gathering people like this, especially as adults, feels nearly impossible. Class field trips and group birthday parties fade with age, but moments like this recreate that sense of collective joy on an entirely different scale.

For a few hours, adulthood loosens its grip. Parents dance. Kids run free and indulge in sugary drinks. There is something radical about joy like this. At the end of it all, the truth is simple: people want to gather. They want to celebrate. And sometimes, they just want to be kids again.
