stories.title: Outside Lands
paragraphs: Kenzo leads a prayer over LaRussell moments before Good Compenny and the Co-LLab Choir take the Outside Lands mainstage. The two squat on the carpeted ground, surrounded by artist trailers nestled just offstage. Kenzo places one hand on LaRussell’s shoulder and holds his other hand tight. Their eyes are closed as Kenzo’s words of protection, encouragement, and purpose move through LaRussell and cover the space around them. After a few moments, they stand. LaRussell turns to the team, now gathered around them, and flashes his signature smile.
“Let’s do this.”

A shawl of fog wraps around the shoulders of Golden Gate Park. The blanket of gray is broken by towering redwoods. A clearing down the center allows the view to stretch the length of a football field. The landscape is speckled with people in fur jackets, art installations, and food stands.

On stage, the Co-LLab Choir settles onto the three-tier risers as Yee Section members check their instruments one by one, in-ears dangling from their clothes. Behind the board, Jacob and Donavan adjust levels. It is Saturday, still early in the festival. The set is scheduled for 2:45 p.m., and the crowd is not yet full. The people at the front are the dedicated ones, staking their claim early, securing their spot for the closer.
The team exchanges glances, snaps selfies and dances before the show starts. Disbelief and giddiness wash across the stage. Friends and family are visible despite the massive space.

Kenzo rotates the turntables on his DJ board. Two scratches cut through the air before he lets the record go and drops the first song. More than twenty people onstage erupt, jumping with wide eyes as they trade looks between one another and the audience. Within the first few notes, the crowd, still only about a quarter full, begins to thicken. The patchwork of grass slowly disappears beneath a growing sea of bodies.
LaRussell walks onto the stage in an all-red outfit, a GC racer jersey and a cow-print beanie pinched at the top to form ears. Splash follows close behind.
“Wow,” LaRussell says as he reaches center stage, beaming at the crowd.
He introduces himself, then invites everyone to close their eyes and step into his world. A single, solemn keyboard note cuts through the air. The choir rises.
“We go dumb, we go dumb, we go, we go, we go dumb,” they chant into the mics before the band snaps into “What We Doin.”

The crowd, that was still moments before, breaks into motion. LaRussell’s command of the space is immediate. Hundreds surge toward the stage, pulled in by his energy as the set fully ignites. It’s not long before LaRussell jumps off the stage, Splash and Jason chasing after him like a lead in an action movie. He cuts through the middle of the crowd, his mic cutting with him, surrounded by thousands of people trying to figure out where he is.

Over the next forty-five minutes, LaRussell guides the crowd through his artistic journey, walking the audience through his childhood, growing up hyphy in the Bay, surrounded by love, light, and the talent that first budded in Vallejo before blooming across the world. He also opens the door to deeper truths, revealing the weight of gun violence, single-parent households, and generational trauma through Kage’s story. He ends it where it all began with GT-Coupe, an early cult classic, but not before taking a stop by his major milestones like multiple Hit-Boy albums, P-Lo collaborations and his infamous solo projects.

Throughout the set, LaRussell weaves in the history of hip-hop, sampling classics like “This Is How We Do It,” “Thizz Dance”, and “Tell Me When to Go.” He traces the genre back to its roots of storytelling and resistance, an art form born from Black survival and expression. Even further, the performance becomes an ode to our ancestors who endured unimaginable conditions, whose paths made it possible for tens of thousands of people to gather and bear witness to this moment.

When the choir sings “Wade in the Water,” a hymn born in the nineteenth century, the meaning is layered. The song carries biblical imagery, but it also served as coded instruction during the Underground Railroad, guiding people to move through water to avoid capture. It speaks to divinity, protection, cleansing, faith, and survival. In the middle of Outside Lands, in a crowd that does not reflect much Blackness, the moment stands as a testament to Black culture, its endurance, its impact, and its roots that refuse to disappear — especially in the Bay Area — particularly in San Francisco.

The crowd witnessed more than a performance. It was a continuation of a long lineage of resistance, hope, community, spirituality, and history. In that moment, dozens of lives converged to create something larger than music.

stories.title: Reece Take ’Em to Church
paragraphs: From Oakland church pews to gold plaques, Reece traces faith, loss, and perseverance in a deeply personal chapter of his career.

The drums were Reece’s first love. Growing up in Oakland, California, he was always banging on things, playing loudly and unapologetically. The drums became the perfect outlet for that energy. Church was the place that held his earliest musical memories. Between the choir, percussion, and keys, he had space to experiment freely, surrounded by gospel music and community. That foundation later inspired his producer tag, “Reece take ’em to church,” a phrase that now precedes some of his hardest-hitting beats. His credits range from “All Me” with Bay Area legends Kehlani and Keyshia Cole to Mozzy’s “Excuse Me,” both of which earned him gold plaques.

Now signed to EMPIRE, Reece has spent years shaping the sound of artists including YG, Rexx Life Raj, 22nd Jim, P-Lo, and E-40. When he’s not producing, he is quick to jump on an instrument, his versatility allowing him to move effortlessly between roles in the studio. While he has firsthand experience working with some of the biggest names in the industry, this year marks a shift. Reece is opening up a more personal chapter with the release of his own album, created in memory of his cousin Snacks, who passed away from a fentanyl overdose in 2022.
Snacks was one of the first people to teach Reece how to program beats and play the keyboard. That bond, and that loss, sit at the heart of this project.
Church and Reece’s sound are inseparable. The emotion, the release, and the sense of connection he felt growing up all carried over into his music.
“Church is my whole field,” Reece said during an interview at EMPIRE earlier this year.
That influence shows up not just stylistically, but emotionally. He recalled a moment in the studio that captured the power music has always held for him.

“I was in the studio, and I was playing the keys when I kept hearing someone who sounded like they were crying. I kept looking back, thinking I must be tripping. The third time I looked back, I asked, ‘Are you okay?’ And she said, ‘Whatever it is that you’re playing, whatever you’re doing, it just keeps making me cry.’”

That same feeling Reece experienced throughout his life in church is what he aims to translate into every record, no matter who is on the track. His love for music has brought success, but it has never come without sacrifice. Being a producer means long nights, fourteen-hour days, and pushing through an industry that is not inherently built for people to thrive. It means showing up even when you do not want to.
“You know, I just try to stay prayed up and grounded,” Reece said. “God, a higher power, whatever you believe in, helps keep my mind steady, because this job is insane.”

This album is an invitation into Reece’s world. Not just the plaques and the hits, but the trials that exist alongside them. More than a year and a half in the making, the project is meant to be experienced, tracing pain, resilience, and survival. Even the rollout reflects that intention.

Rather than only releasing singles on streaming platforms, Reece has been revisiting the places that shaped him. He has returned to old schools to speak with teachers who once guided him. He has gone back to the two shelters where he lived at twelve and thirteen with his mom and sister, talking with kids who now occupy the same spaces. Walking through those buildings again, he was struck by how little had changed.

Grief often goes unnoticed. After memorials and funerals pass, collective mourning fades. What remains is personal, carried quietly or shared only with those closest to you. People learn how to smile, keep conversations moving, and continue living, even as the weight of loss settles deep in the heart. This project lives in that space, honoring what was lost while finding a way forward.

stories.title: Teeko
paragraphs: Remembering D’Angelo, honoring turntablism, strengthening the Bay’s roots, and shaping what comes next.

In 2004, Teeko was fresh off a trip to Shibuya Japan, where he and fellow Bay Area DJ’s were invited to design their own turntable. It was a rare chance to customize the sounds a board could hold, and to innovate in an era that was still largely static. He described the starting point like water: he could add anything to it. Teeko worked closely with engineers who did not speak his language to create the turntable of his dreams. A year later, he got the equipment. The result was a melodic, fully expressive instrument that became the Controller One Turntable, released through Vestax Engineering. He returned to his regular spots in San Francisco with his new customized sound.

Years later, in 2008, Teeko was performing at the Elbo Room in the Mission District using his Controller One turntable. His friend, Dojah, filmed the set along with performances from other Bay Area DJs to share with a manager he knew, someone who had previously launched a DJ booking agency and was now working with major artists. The video of Teeko was passed along.

Less than a year later, in 2009, Teeko received a call, the person on the other line was Dom Trenier, who at the time was working with artists like Janet Jackson, Questlove, D’Angelo and Mark Ronson. Trenier was immediately enthusiastic about Teeko’s background and talent. He was willing to do whatever it took to work with him, even saying he would come to Teeko and stay on his couch if that was what it took.

A few days later, Teeko was on the phone with Mark Ronson. Days after that, he was boarding a flight to New York. He had been to New York City before. The crowded streets and yellow taxi cabs were familiar, but as he walked through Manhattan, he knew he was stepping into an entirely new world. Teeko arrived at the major label studio, was greeted by Mark Ronson and soon found himself meeting Q-Tip and working on Ronson’s Record Collection album.

After a surreal few days, Teeko found himself in a cab with Traineire, heading back home and reflecting on everything that had just happened. Traineire praised him for the work he had done and made his intentions clear: “I’m going to get you in the room with D’Angelo,” he said.
In September 2011, Teeko was back in New York, this time in the studio with D’Angelo as he worked on his third and final studio album, Black Messiah, at Electric Lady Studios.

The first few days were spent smoking, breaking down government conspiracy theories, going over Funkadelic and Prince deep cuts, dissecting favorites from Earth, Wind & Fire, and connecting on an intellectual level. No music had been made yet.

After two days of deep dives and chopping it up, Teeko finally stepped into the studio, tasked with laying scratches on multiple projects. First, he worked on turntable melodic scratches for the song “Prayer.” At the time, there was no Pro Tools. Everything was recorded to tape, and you only had one chance to get it right. The process was slow and meticulous between takes. The sound engineer had to rewind the first tape, take it down, load a new one, and reset the machine, leaving about fifteen minutes before anyone could record again.

To pass the time, Teeko hopped onto the grand piano in Electric Lady Studios, right next to Questlove’s drum room. He assumed he was alone, playing bass chords with his left hand, until he felt someone behind him. D’Angelo was standing there. As Teeko played, D’Angelo grabbed a bass guitar, threw it over his shoulder, and jumped in, kicking the bassline. The two started jamming together for a moment that felt like forever and two seconds at the same time.

When they finished, D’Angelo set the bass down, placed both hands on Teeko’s shoulders, and told him he’d be honored to have him in his band. He then sat beside him on the piano bench and taught Teeko how to play “Prayer” on the keys.
(In a later conversation, Traniere explained that the moment had been D’Angelo’s blessing — like a kiss from the godfather.)

Teeko went on to track funky scratches on “Sugar Daddy,” although his scratches on that song never made the final studio album. (Some said the label had done their own cut, one that strayed from D’Angelo’s original vision.)

Teeko left New York floating from inspiration. Trainiere continued to stay in Teeko’s corner, cheering him on and bringing opportunities his way whenever he saw the right fit as Teeko returned to the Bay to continue music.

Years later, Teeko remained in the orbit of D’Angelo and Dom Trenier despite the tragic passing of Trenier in 2016. Once again, Teeko’s friend Dojah connected D’Angelo’s world with Teeko’s, dropping off Jermaine Holmes, D’Angelo’s right hand man, at Teeko’s studio in the spring of 2025 and essentially saying, “You two need to meet.”
“He literally just dropped him off here and left, and was like, ‘You guys have fun playing together.’ He basically dropped off two kids in a little play area,” Teeko recalled.

The two recorded four or five records and instantly hit it off. Teeko didn’t hear from Holmes for a little while, until he called back with difficult news. He told Teeko to keep D’Angelo in his prayers because he was dealing with some health issues. Teeko prayed for him, and the two spent time on the phone reminiscing about their moments with the star, only then realizing they had actually met years earlier at D’Angelo’s comeback show at the House of Blues in Los Angeles, at the beginning of the Black Messiah run.
Holmes was hopeful about bringing Teeko back into the studio with D’Angelo in the near future, excited to share Teeko’s beats with him.
A few months later, Teeko received the call that D’Angelo had passed.

Teeko’s first emotion was pain, pain for the world, for everyone who knew D’Angelo’s music and understood how true, deep, and authentic it was. His second emotion was concern for the future. D’Angelo was a lineage bearer, an oracle of the music’s rich history. Prince, Stevie Wonder, James Brown, and so many others shaped D’Angelo’s fingerprint, and through him, those legacies continued to breathe. He worried about where that history would go with him gone.
Teeko later talked with Simon and Clay about carrying the torch, keeping your soul in the work, and staying original.
With shorter attention spans and the constant pressure to create quickly, there is a real fear that the craft and the time it takes to make great music could become diluted.
The Roots of the Sound
Teeko has played a critical role in connecting newer generations to their roots, honoring the past while encouraging artists to innovate and shape their own distinct sound.

Born in Puerto Rico, some of Teeko’s earliest memories include sitting on the floor of his family home with a turntable placed in front of him. He would place his small fingers on the large disc and slowly pull it counterclockwise before letting it go, then repeated the motion again. He paid attention to each groove on the record and listened for the subtle variations that emerged as he changed the movement and speed. He grew up watching his dad play piano and while he learned how to catch and throw a baseball, he also learned about 12 bar blues.

At six years old, Teeko left Puerto Rico and came to the Bay, where he moved in with his grandparents and his uncle, who had a record distribution company that was putting out gangster rap records from East Palo Alto. His uncle would sit Teeko in the car, barely seven years old, blasting the loudest music he had ever heard, the dashboard buzzing from the bass.

When Teeko was barely old enough, maybe ten or eleven, he worked at his uncle’s Redwood City record store, helping him pull records, move boxes, and price items. At the end of each week, his payment was one record. He pulled Digital Underground, Tupac, and Too $hort. One day, while he was behind the counter and customers were shopping, he stood in front of a quartz-locked turntable. He looked at it irresistibly, like a kid told not to touch the dessert sitting right in front of him. Against his better judgment, he touched the record and pulled it back. The warped, distorted sound caught the attention of everyone in the store, stopping them in their tracks. He knew he had done something wrong, but at the same time, he had captured the entire room’s attention, and in that moment he also knew he had done something right.

As he stepped into adolescence, Teeko became fully engrossed with the turntable and began spinning at high school dances. He soon discovered world turntablism, the art of using turntables to create new sounds, rhythms, and compositions in real time.

After high school, he began participating in competitive DJ’ing and went on to win the USA finals for scratching in 2003, eventually traveling to Germany to represent the United States in turntablism.

The discipline of turntablism wove itself into Teeko’s earliest steps as a producer. Its pillars became his compass. Originality was paramount. Borrowing someone else’s style was a cultural flag, and something people didn’t let slide. The fingerprints of his turntable years still live in the way he slices beats and reshapes rhythm. And now, he says he is finally chiseling out the kind of signature sound that defined the turntablists he grew up idolizing.

Most recently, Teeko has brought his decades of musical experience to Empire as one of their signed producers, signing in February of 2025. Now Teeko is standing at the crux of a vital moment in the Bay Area. He grew up watching the region’s music scene take shape, and today he is witnessing it evolve into something new: the Bay Area renaissance. The Bay has long set the tone for the musical diaspora in this country, but its influence has often been tethered to the geography. This next era is different. A growing lineup of heavy hitters share the same mission: to take the Bay Area global.

Teeko plays a crucial role in that movement. He passes down history, game, and lessons drawn from his own journey, while staying a student of the craft and continuing to shape his own sound. He serves as a mentor to many, whether it is Yee Section members Clay and Simon or the duo 2EZ. He is a fountain of knowledge, continually pouring into the next generation of Bay Area artists. And his story is still being written.

stories.title: The Yee Section
paragraphs: An oral history told by Harry, Simon, Clay, Jimmy and Kenzo.
The Origins

Simon: Maybe we’re just an entity. We’re a unit, an army, a force of creativity. The best way to put it is if you think about how The Roots play behind Erykah Badu or D’Angelo, that’s kind of what we are for the Bay. A collective of talented musicians and human beings who are all really good at their craft.

Kenzo: The Yee Section is a collective, a band of individuals from the Bay Area who came together around LaRussell’s movement. We started as the band, but it grew into something bigger. We just did our first show today, and I’m excited for what’s next. I feel like I came in at the perfect time, like it was meant to happen that way.

Harry: Yeah, it’s just a group of musicians who all kind of met through LaRussell. We grew up in the Bay Area, so that’s where the connection really started. There’s this shared rhythm, that Bay swing, it’s something you feel more than you read off paper.

Clay: The name actually came from that. We were talking about how a lot of beats are just eight bars looping, and we’d add a new section, switch it up. So we started saying, “Yeah, you got the A section, but do you got the Yee Section?”

Jimmy: I joined before it was even called that. It happened organically, just showing up at the pergola with my flute and getting thrown into the mix. I’ve known Simon for years, we’d played in a lot of bands before this, so when it started forming, it felt natural.
The Sound

Simon: Everything we do is on command, played by ear. We never know the set list, and that’s the magic. If we don’t know what’s coming next, neither does the crowd. It’s like scoring something live, in real time.

Kenzo: I still feel like I’m finding my way, because when you’re a DJ, you’re used to controlling everything. But in a band, it’s different. You’re not leading, you’re assisting. You’re filling in, seeing where you fit, and sometimes you don’t. It’s been humbling and really fun to learn that balance.

Harry: A lot of what makes it different is that we weren’t practicing for a long time. Sometimes we’d be on stage hearing a song for the first time and just have to pick it up. It’s all improvisation, each show becomes a new experience.

Clay: It’s a lot of improv, a lot of learning songs on the spot. I’ve grown so much as a piano player because of it. When you’re surrounded by people who listen and leave their egos out of it, it’s just fun. No one’s tripping, no one’s mad, everyone’s easy to be around.

Jimmy: What makes it different is the musicianship. We don’t rehearse much, but everyone shows up prepared. The music stays authentic and unplanned, it just happens organically, and that’s what keeps it alive.
The Descriptors
Kayla: I want to go down the line, say a word or animal that comes to mind for each member.
Harry: Michael, visionary. Geo, bubbly. Clay, suave. Jimmy, mysterious. Simon, maestro.
Clay: Geo’s a puppy. Michael’s like a lizard. Harry’s an ostrich. Jimmy’s a flamingo. Kenzo’s a lion.
Kenzo: Harry, fantastic. Geo, rare. Jimmy, extraordinary. Clay, calm. Simon, genius. Michael, brain. Everyone in the Yee Section has something unique about them.

Jimmy: Geo’s a butterfly. Simon’s a chameleon, he can adapt to anything. Kenzo’s a silverback, strong leader energy. Clay’s a kangaroo, just bouncing into any zone to make music. Harry’s a giraffe, tall and funky. Michael’s some kind of aquatic animal, maybe a dolphin.
Simon: Harry’s a Bengal tiger. Kenzo’s a hyena, always laughing. Geo’s a swan. Jimmy’s an owl. Clay’s a peacock, colorful as hell.
The Collective
Clay: We’re all on similar waves. Everyone’s hungry for this music thing, and there’s no ego. It’s like Simon’s the MD, so we listen to him, but it’s not about control, it’s about trust.

Kenzo: I feel like we’re all patient and kind people, and that translates into how we treat the music. When you’re patient and kind with art, it fills you up. It teaches you to step back, to know when to add and when to let others shine.

Simon: What makes a great musician isn’t how much they play, it’s knowing when not to play. When you’ve got ten people on stage, you have to make space for each other. Sometimes I’ll stop playing entirely just so everyone else can shine. That’s what makes us a living organism.
Jimmy: It’s really like a family. We check in with each other outside of music, and that energy shows up on stage. The chemistry comes from actually caring.
The Moments
Kayla: What’s your favorite Yee Section or GC memory?
Harry: Outside Lands. Being backstage, getting free massages, just taking it all in. That was surreal.

Simon: Tiny Desk. Only one percent of artists get to do that, and to do it with your friends, that’s something I’ll never forget. After Outside Lands, we were celebrating in the green room, and Ludacris just walked by. Like, what is life?

Clay: I remember the night before Tiny Desk, when we cooked up a new song in the Airbnb. Everyone was there. It’s those little moments, the creative ones that happen by accident, that I remember most.

Kenzo: When we made “Do You Wanna Be My Best Friend,” that was a really special moment. Even though not everyone was there, it felt like a breakthrough. And watching Tiny Desk from home, I still felt connected, like I was right there.
Jimmy: For me, it’s showing up at the pergola before the band even had a name. That’s where it all started.
The Group Chat
Simon: “Anybody free to do a live session tomorrow?” Either no one replies, or we just send memes.
Jimmy: A lot of trolling. A lot of stickers. But also planning, like where we gotta be, what time. It’s a mix of business and jokes. That’s what keeps it fun.

Kenzo: We organize live sessions, talk about future shows, send motivational texts. Sometimes I’ll finish a five-mile run and drop something encouraging in there. Sometimes we just talk nonsense, but it’s love every time.
Looking Ahead
Harry: I think we’ll all keep thriving individually, but that’ll open doors for the Yee Section to grow. Maybe like how Anderson Paak’s band became its own thing.
Clay: Right now we’re all balancing other projects, but I could see us getting booked on our own one day. Maybe when things slow down a little, we’ll build something bigger.
Kenzo: I live in the now, but if I had to look ahead, I see Grammys, headline shows, stadium tours. We’ve got something special, and the world will see that soon.
Jimmy: Five or ten years from now, I see us as one of the greatest to come out of the Bay. Not just a band from here, but a band that travels, collaborates, and keeps pushing what live music can be.
Simon: We’re still at the beginning. The Yee Section isn’t done becoming whatever it’s meant to be.

stories.title: WithdifficultyWithpleasure
paragraphs: Sunday stood at the front of Heron Studios in Oakland, California. The room was warm and the lighting intimate. A few rows of chairs in a small room. A mic and soundboard in the front. The typical rowdy Family Not a Group crowd, is speckled with elders, chatting, waiting in anticipation for Sunday to preview her July release, WithdifficultyWithpleasure.

Sunday sat on a stool, her hair full and framing her face, her skin glowing under the low lights. A mic rested lightly in her lap as she waited for everyone to settle. The album was a culmination of five years of collected sounds and recorded pieces coming together to capture the past, present, and future of her story.

Sunday opened the listening party with her song “U Dnt Knw Me,” a slow, deliberate introduction to the soft soliloquies that shape the entire project. As she invites listeners into the most vulnerable parts of her life, she also reminds them of an uncomfortable truth: you only ever see parts of her, and that may always be the case.

Across the ten-track album, Sunday’s exquisite vocals, layered with metaphors and lyrical storytelling, illuminate her struggles in music, her process of accepting loss and love, the complications of creating art, and her desire to show people what exists beneath the bubbly persona that has lately felt more suffocating than freeing lately. As you move through the record, you are invited into emotions she usually keeps to herself, feelings that might frighten people if she expressed them in the moment, but carry less risk when transformed into music.

The album draws from R&B, soul, and neo-soul, but not without surprises. Her playful lyricism weaves in deep-cut anime references and even an entire song about menstruation, a detail you might miss unless you listen closely. But the album isn’t without its surprises. “Mustangs in Mojave” channels the carefree euphoria of jumping on your bed as a teenage girl, belting out Avril Lavigne lyrics at the top of your lungs, giving you a taste of Sunday’s rockstar persona.

For Sunday, the album is a declaration of self. It represents showing up authentically as the weird girl, the high-functioning sad girl, the anime girl, and the girl who is done tiptoeing around other people’s feelings. It is the voice of someone no longer willing to push her emotions aside to comfort the world behind her.
